the rapporteur. - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, my report is actually a set of four separate reports. in this respect, i would like to pay tribute to commissioner schreyer for her presence. i hope that through him the more specific people responsible for the management of the structural funds, both in the commission and in the member states, will take note of the message of our report and our conclusions, since in this case we are dealing with the structural funds, which, as we know, are generally and directly managed by the member states. so there are four separate reports: a report on additionality of aid, a report on the conversion of industrial sites, a third report by the court of auditors on measures to help young people's employment under the european social fund and the eaggf guidance section, and a fourth report on the international fund for ireland and the peace programme in northern ireland. i am particularly grateful to the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism for its contribution to my work on this report. we have taken over all the amendments that she has tabled from the cocobu. these four distinct themes, however, lead to similar remarks which can be of three types. firstly, the main criticisms of the commission concern the administrative procedures which the court, like us, considers to be too long and complex and which sometimes hinder the smooth running of projects. it must also be said that the same criticisms are directed at the member states. the controls currently being carried out on the project in the field or from brussels are still insufficient. the lack of resources and staff is always pointed out - others have said so on other issues - and this despite the court of auditors' frequent remarks on this subject. the commission is profoundly reforming its structure and is asking for additional resources. i hope that parliament, which has always believed in the myth of zero growth for civil servants, while the tasks have increased, will accept the commission's proposals, the objectives, to also strengthen its controls and its role. this obviously leads to overlapping funding, since funding is not sufficiently controlled, and therefore to a misuse of european funds. the last criticism that can be made is that of late payments, a recurring problem which the commission seems to have been unable to solve or control. secondly, a major criticism which i would very much like to see highlighted in our contacts with the member states is the misuse of appropriations, often due to the lack of cooperation between the member states and the commission, and the lack of willingness on the part of the member states to make use of the funds. they often appear as donations, as funds to replace national funds. the member states have little regard, under certain conditions, for the principle of additionality, which means that it is cofinancing which must be supplemented by national funding. he believes that the funds cover almost 100% of the funding, which is clearly not in line with the logic of the structural funds and their use. member states should bear in mind that these funds are public and concern all european citizens. they should therefore use them with even more discretion than national funds. to overcome this dysfunction, new regulations were adopted in june 1999 and i hope that they will help to move forward. we ask the commission to use all the means at its disposal when it detects malfunctions, such as suspension of payments, and if the reasons are justified, we will stand behind the commission in supporting it in this process. finally, i think that the commission should itself pay more attention to the eligibility criteria before authorizing the release of funds. this would avoid funding for projects that do not stand the test of time, for the 'all-in-one' projects that are often seen in the member states. these are the comments i had to make. thank you, mr president, for the few extra seconds you have given me.

commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by congratulating mrs oomen-ruijten on her excellent report on the situation of frontier workers and, in particular, the social and fiscal problems these workers face. i should also like to thank parliament for the support given to the commission's proposal to extend the scope of regulation 1408/71 to third-country nationals, the proposal to modernise and simplify that regulation, and for the encouraging support given to the eures network. the commission fully supports your concerns as regards the problems encountered by frontier workers. i therefore welcome your proposal to forward the resolution to the council. allow me to now set out briefly the commission's approach to the points raised in the resolution. first, on social security and the labour market, the report calls on the commission, before the end of this year, to organise an international conference for the member states and applicant countries concerning the position of frontier workers. this is an excellent idea and advantage can be taken of the experience accumulated under the eures network. such a conference could identify best practices and initiatives that could be launched both at community and national level, and the european parliament will be involved in its organisation. on the idea of coordination provisions for supplementary pensions, i would remind you that the commission has committed itself in its social policy agenda to propose in 2002 a directive on the transferability of supplementary pensions. this initiative will complement the already existing directive in this field, which was adopted in 1998. as the proposal will be based on article 42 of the ec treaty and rely on the codecision procedure for its adoption, parliament will be fully involved. furthermore i can confirm that a study covering the extent and nature of frontier work is already planned to be carried out under the eures auspices in 2001. on the initiatives taken by social security agencies for closer cross-border cooperation in order to facilitate access to health-care benefits, i am very much in favour of such initiatives and can confirm that it is the intention of the commission to encourage such initiatives and to promote exchanges of experience and best practices. in fact the commission is already giving support to such a project involving the inhabitants of the euregio meuse-rhine, which covers part of belgium, germany and the netherlands. with regard to the follow-up of the decker and kohl judgments, there are important legal questions currently being debated in new cases before the court. these questions concern hospital care and the dutch health system. the commission will await the outcome of these judgments before taking a position. on obstacles to the mobility of stagiaires, students, volunteers and researchers, the commission has already taken the initiative and presented a proposal for a recommendation of the european parliament and the council on mobility within the community for students, persons undergoing training, young volunteers, teachers and trainers. on 9 november 2000 the education council adopted its common position on this proposal. i wish to thank parliament for its support on this matter and i hope that the final discussions will enable parliament and the council to adopt the recommendations shortly. on the idea of a proposal for a directive on the introduction of frontier effect reports, whereby member states would be required to test their legislation as to the effects for frontier workers, i should make it clear that it is already the commission's task to ensure that all provisions of national legislation are compatible with the treaty and the secondary legislation of community law. the commission will certainly continue to use the powers laid down in article 226 of the treaty and to launch infringement proceedings against member states when they violate community law. however, i understand that the suggested proposal for a directive aims to provide for a more general socio-economic impact assessment of the consequences of national legislation, that is in itself compatible with community law but might cause further difficulties to frontier workers. the commission is not sure that it would be appropriate to propose such a legislative instrument. it seems to the commission more appropriate to stimulate cross-border cooperation of the partners involved in the different regions and at community level in order to prevent any negative consequences of national legislation on frontier workers. finally, my comments on tax. unlike social security, there is no community legislation at all on personal taxation. indeed member states are extremely protective of their sovereignty in this area. that is particularly true of their competence to enter into bilateral tax treaties. therefore, there is little chance of the commission being able to secure successfully the adoption of measures by member states, as requested in the report. unfortunately this will not change following the treaty of nice. as you are aware, contrary to our common wishes, the requirement of unanimity in council was retained for tax matters. opinions are, moreover, likely to be divided about the merits of the recommendations made in the report concerning taxation in the state of employment. in fact, the prevailing view in tax administrations is that the state of residence rather than the state of employment is best placed to take account of the overall situation of taxpayers. in conclusion, i wish to thank mrs oomen-ruijten again for her stimulating report and to underline the commission's determination to maintain its efforts to overcome the problems faced by frontier workers.

- oral question (b5-0556/2000) by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy to the commission on the poor implementation of certain environmental directives (pcbs and pcts, habitats, nitrates).
commission. – mr president, first of all i thank mrs jackson for her important question. i would remind all the members of the european parliament that implementation of european community law covers both the transposition of directives into national law and their application to individual decisions. it also includes fulfilment of other obligations such as adopting programmes, making designations and monitoring. the difficulties encountered by the committee on the environment in these three reports are indeed not limited to the three directives chosen but extend to all ec environmental directives. the commission, and not least the environment dg are aware of these difficulties and have for some time devoted efforts to improve their performance in this field and i can assure you that next week when the commission discusses the sixth environmental action programme the whole implementation issue will be a very important point in that programme. we have a number of tools at our disposal to improve implementation. we can, for example, disseminate information to give a more up-to-date picture of the state of play and i know that we have also forwarded some of these reports and annual surveys to parliament and that we can do much more to ensure some media attention as well. we can develop tools to aid in the analysis and evaluation of progress in implementation. we can take legal measures to follow up implementation. since 1997 specific initiatives have been pursued on a number of fronts including environmental liability, which of course will put pressure on the member states to follow the existing rules and regulations; complaints and investigations procedures at national level where we have been involved in playing a consultancy role; access to justice, magistrates' training courses – also very important because this is also about education – and the publication of this annual survey on the implementation of environmental law. we have also worked to create a clear link between implementation of the directives and community cofunding which has proven to be very effective as well as ensuring a close relationship with the life financial instrument, because when they see that the money is threatened if they do not comply with the regulations this will definitely put pressure on the member states. in may last year we had a first name and shame exercise, as we call it, on bathing water quality. a second exercise will take place in march this year and i will continue to follow this up so as to give us a scoreboard of how member states are implementing community legislation. just last week the european parliament and the council, as mrs jackson said, reached an agreement on a recommendation which will establish minimum criteria for environmental inspections in the member states. all these initiatives are intended to increase the level of knowledge of and compliance with european community and environmental law. of course, i acknowledge that there is still much to be done. we have to look for new ways to encourage the proper transposition and application of environmental legislation. for example, we need to work to improve the involvement of people at the local and regional level. greater public awareness at these levels would lead to closer scrutiny and to public demand for effective implementation of environmental legislation. we must remain vigilant and active to ensure that the situation improves and i would like to confirm to the european parliament my personal commitment and that of my services to ensuring the highest possible level of compliance with european community environmental law. to this end i will apply all means available, including the formal infringement procedures set out in articles 226 and 228 of the european community treaty and 141 and 143 of the euratom treaty, which may lead to imposing economic penalties on non-complying member states. i would be more than happy to receive more resources and personnel from the european parliament to work on this. today we have about 45 to 50 staff working full or part-time on implementation, and, of course, we would need more than that. but i also think that it is for every civil servant here to actually look at the implementation part of introducing new legislation. i have been very clear from the beginning that i will put more emphasis on implementation. that needs the three i’s: information, integration and implementation, which should be the guidelines for the future. i hope that you will agree with me that we are starting to make progress on improving implementation and if both the commission and the european parliament continue their efforts to highlight the problem and act on it, further progress will surely be made during this parliamentary term.
mr president, as mr jackson has very effectively illustrated, the picture emerging from the analysis of the application of the three directives in question is truly disturbing. although these measures differ widely, it appears that most member states have been seriously behind in their practical implementation. this is a serious phenomenon which, beyond the technical considerations specific to each of the three directives, should make us reflect on the reasons behind this situation. i would like to emphasize two aspects of this story: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is based on the principle of the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment as a whole. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. the mistake is that environmental investment is ultimately seen as an imposed obligation, an unnecessary additional cost. but the environment is our future and we cannot rely on the will of the people alone, or even on the punitive power of the court of justice alone, to defend it. i also agree that if the fifth environmental action programme has focused mainly on a sectoral approach to environmental policy, perhaps in thinking ahead to the sixth environmental action programme we should instead place greater emphasis on involving the social and economic actors, as well as local authorities, in achieving the objectives defined from time to time, so that the protection of our environment becomes increasingly an element to be integrated into overall planning. in this context, it will be important to ensure, as we say in our motion for a resolution, that the best and worst results achieved by the member states in implementing environmental directives are widely disseminated, including via the internet, in order to highlight the different commitments made by each of them in this area and to subject the behaviour of the member states to the judgment of public opinion, which is almost always even more effective than that of the court of justice. in order to facilitate monitoring and comparison between the different situations, i think it is even more important to continue to deepen research on common environmental indicators. environmental protection knows no national boundaries and is a paramount area of community action. for this reason too, and even more so in view of the forthcoming enlargement to include the countries of central and eastern europe, we cannot accept that the decisions taken by the 15 governments and by us should be ignored. the natural environment is a common asset and our commitment to the objectives must be able to set an example for the candidate countries, which are so laboriously engaged in the difficult task of restoring often very serious degradation situations. to improve the situation, each of us, whether we are representatives of the community, national or local institutions, or just ordinary citizens, must do our part.
commission. – mr president, i should like again to thank all the members of the european parliament for their statements. i could not agree more with most of what you have said, except for any accusation of complacency. may i remind you that, as of today, 45% of all the complaints are on environmental issues and cases – 700 complaints, 30% of the infringements – about 400 – are on environmental cases. so there is a heavy burden on us and we are trying to do our best but also look to the future. that is why i am saying that we also have to look out for new instruments and ways to do more. mr sacconi's point was that we need the good examples of what economic gains can be made from complying with environmental legislation. we could do more on that. we could do more with the scope, such as the habitats directive. it is no coincidence that the habitats and nitrates directives are chosen as examples of bad compliance because they are very far-reaching. they are ambitious directives and in some cases it means the member states need to review fully their agricultural practices. we know this from some of the member states. this should not be taken as an excuse, but an far-reaching and there are consequences for the member states which they perhaps did not realise when the decisions were taken. we must not give in now, we have to carry on because we will finally start to see results. what we have done, which is very effective, is to establish the link between european funding and compliance with environment legislation. we have to draw on that. we can do more on education and information. we have started activities like this. we use our experts to go to member states or to carry out seminars to teach the member states how to best implement it. we try to use all these available instruments to improve implementation. in an enlarged and more diverse union, clear and legally binding targets, as well as education and methods for measuring, monitoring and calculating results, become more and more important. i hope for the european parliament's support and backing in our further attempts to improve the implementation of our european community environmental legislation.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, i shall omit the definition of intermodality and take for granted the definition which the commission itself has tried to give in the past. it is increasingly important, however, to define the measures to support intermodality, and this is necessary for a number of reasons: the need to streamline traffic and optimise freight travel times; the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the transport of dangerous goods by road. intermodality today presents a set of critical issues related to the lack of integration of different modes of transport, as well as to specific inefficiencies of some of these modes. the level of efficiency of the rail services offered is of primary importance for the development of intermodality, which in many member states is characterised by poor quality and efficiency and a high cost-effectiveness ratio. moreover, as the commission has repeatedly pointed out, infrastructure continues to develop mainly on a unimodal basis, whereas intermodal transport requires a network approach based on complementarity and interconnection between different modes. finally, there are still no open intermodal information systems capable of efficiently managing intermodal transport and network services and of ensuring a streamlined and continuous flow of information and communications in real time. specifically, when analysing the friction costs associated with intermodal freight transport, it is shown that the elements of greater criticality, compared to traditional unimodal transport, can be identified in high prices, longer times, increase in average distance travelled, reduced quality, higher risks of damage to the load, restrictions on the type of goods that can be transported, more complex administrative procedures. these clutch costs are due, firstly, to the lack of coherent system networks and interconnections between them, which create a loss of efficiency and increase transfer costs. moreover, different modes of transport enjoy different levels of efficiency and quality of service which are ill-suited to a logic of customer satisfaction and real-time transfer of goods. the causes are due to the lack of widespread electronic communication systems between the various partners in the intermodal chain and the lack of goods identification and information systems organised on an intermodal basis. finally, a series of bottlenecks, linked to the lack of harmonization of times and schedules between the different modes of transport, characterizes the whole system, causing inconsistencies between the needs connected with the chain of transport of goods and the operational needs of the resources used in the process: for example, the working hours of drivers of crews not adapted to intermodal operations. terminals cannot always accommodate the 24-hour train and ship schedules. it is clear that the intermodal transport framework within europe is quite differentiated, with totally different situations in the different member states. it is therefore necessary to monitor these different conditions as a matter of priority with the support of the intermodality task force, in order to identify specific lines of action to address emerging priorities in individual states. the objectives which the european union intends to pursue in developing intermodality are linked to the need to create an integrated system of different modes of transport offering door-to-door services oriented towards the customer and allowing efficient and profitable use of the transport system, which favours competition between operators. in the report on intermodality and intermodal freight transport in the european union, the commission outlined the objectives to be pursued in the field of intermodal transport, dividing them into priority areas of intervention addressing specific challenges, the so-called 'key actions'. the first key action concerns infrastructure and integrated transport; the second action, interoperability and interconnection in traffic operations; the third action is the services and regulations common to all modes of transport. the aim is to establish an information system enabling real-time transport management and the use of electronic transactions in transport through the development of intermodal real-time electronic transaction and information systems. the harmonisation of edi-based communication standards, procedures and transport documents; standardise the liability regime in order to offer the end-user a clear set of conditions and transparent procedures for liability for cargoes that may be damaged or lost en route; developing information society technologies for the benefit of intermodal transport by creating an open architecture that allows the movement of goods along the intermodal route to be tracked; to enable paperless transport by harmonising documentation rules and creating a single electronic window. the commission has also planned a series of horizontal activities through targeted research and technological development projects aimed at introducing innovations aimed at using new technologies for the development of innovative services and for increasing productivity. it is clear that talking about intermodality implies a strong cultural change in the business culture. globalisation and the liberalisation of markets are already leading to a significant increase in demand for the movement of goods and services. the high growth rates will lead to competition which will increasingly take advantage of the volumes transported and, consequently, the process of aggregation of operators in the sector will be absolutely inevitable. finally, i would like to thank the members who have actively participated in the drafting of a resolution which is broadly agreed. i would also like to say that as far as the amendments are concerned - few indeed - that have been tabled, i agree with them in principle, except for amendment no 3, which has some perplexities about state aid.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, i am pleased to present this own-initiative report drawn up by the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism of the european parliament to take a step forward on a subject which i hope will seem a little less complicated after our work here. the report was born, as is well known, of a commission green paper of 1995, which called for measures to internalize external environmental, safety and congestion costs, in order to make the charging of transport infrastructure costs to users more fair and efficient. it essentially asks the commission to take action by harmonizing the definitions of internal and external costs, by harmonizing or identifying methods for calculating and measuring them, and then naturally leaving the application of these measures to the subsidiarity and intervention decisions which the member states will take. the report's main thrust, in my view, is to make this application of the 'polluter pays' principle part of the wider principle of the user-payer. this is the contribution that you make, with two consequences that i want to highlight in this presentation: the first is that if, thanks to the methodology which we hope to obtain from the commission and to be able to approve, we succeed in having a clearer definition and allocation of internal and external costs to users, we will create the conditions for being able to shift the problem of financing infrastructure from purely public resources, from general taxation to users as such. this makes it possible to imagine the great effort that europe - today's europe, tomorrow's europe - is facing in the process of restructuring its possibilities, the effort to involve private capital in this operation, which would otherwise not be possible if we were unable to identify this situation. the next step is to consider that, whereas the imputation of some of these costs no longer has any meaning - i am thinking of the italian motorways, which have been largely depreciated - these costs which exist today could constitute funds to be used in a cross-subsidy hypothesis, so that certain costs imputed to road users are used to improve infrastructure in competitive ways, certainly more environmentally friendly. the whole system - i repeat - of shifting the financial burden from the state to the users must be safeguarded, and it is the last principle introduced, according to which those who are in the most difficult conditions, those with disabilities or who live in rural or peripheral areas of difficulty, can to some extent be exempted, and therefore a set of interventions, including state interventions, can be reviewed in this direction. the ambition pursued in this report is to bring together some of the fundamental principles which i have already mentioned: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. how can this be done? the methodological suggestion that is made here is that there is now a set of good practices in europe, which we have tried to explore and put together in a seminar, the documents of which we will make available to anyone who wants to study the problem in depth and which we have been able to finance with the help of the commission. i believe that these practices can now be generalized and made available to everyone. the result would be - and i believe the time is ripe - the possibility of having operational indications for making european policy move concretely in this direction.

- mrs karamanou, i do not think that the lack of representation of women, or perhaps even of young people, in our parliamentary assemblies is due to an excess of democracy, but to a deficit, and i believe that the electoral lists prepared by the parties, even prepared - as you hope in your report - as blocked lists, where it is not even possible to express the preferential vote, constitute an excellent system for having a proportional representation of the parties, that is to say of party officials and candidates chosen by the parties, whether women or men, in our assemblies. i believe that the delay in the representation of women, or even young people, in our assemblies is due to electoral systems which prevent candidates from confronting each other, from competing and being chosen, perhaps by means of primary elections, by the people rather than by party secretariats. i do not think that there is any particularly clear statistical evidence one way or the other - i do not know what margaret thatcher or hillary clinton would think of his position on the majority system - but i think that a lot of data and evidence proves the opposite of his arguments. another recommendation, which you make in the explanatory statement to your report, is that of giving public funding incentives to those parties which have the largest number of women in parliament. i believe that, although this is a well-intentioned approach, it risks being the bureaucratic and subsidized approach to representation and representativeness in our assemblies, and i do not think that is the way to go. we need more, not less, democracy for women's representation.

in writing. - the report adopted in committee struck a very careful balance between those who want to move faster towards advancing the community transport pricing framework and bringing it into line with concrete measures and those who feel that public opinion is not yet ready for such a radical overhaul of the way society finances the use of its transport infrastructure. the rapporteur is satisfied with the substantial agreement reached on the basic principles of the report, namely that it is up to the community to establish a common methodology for calculating transport costs; that external costs should be included in such assessments; whereas the revenue should be used to reduce environmental damage and to promote alternative and less polluting modes of transport; whereas implementation should be subject to the principle of subsidiarity; whereas users and polluters should contribute in proportion to their use of the infrastructure; and that exceptions should be made for the least mobile members of our society and people living in rural areas. for all these reasons, and even though i sympathize with many of the amendments tabled by the green group/european free alliance for concrete measures, i cannot support these amendments because they would threaten the consensus reached on the above principles and could be considered later in the course of implementing a pricing framework.

tribunal. during the past year, the commission bilaterally, and together with the eu member states, has called on the cambodian government to express its support for the process leading up to the law was adopted by the national assembly on 2 january and by the senate on 15 january. it is now due to be ratified by the constitutional council and king norodom sihanouk. while we welcome the adoption of the legislation regarding the khmer rouge tribunal, both by the national assembly and by the senate, it should be borne in mind that we are still awaiting the official statement from the united nations on the draft text. there are indications that the text is not completely in line with what had been agreed with the united nations. nevertheless, the first reaction from the un after receiving an unofficial translation, has been cautiously positive, and the commission hopes, therefore, that the remaining outstanding issues can be resolved so that the un can improve the new court and the agreement between the cambodian government and the united nations can be implemented expeditiously. one other outstanding issue which the commission will follow closely is the question of which khmer rouge leader will be put on trial. although prime minister hun sen has given assurances that nobody would be immune from prosecution, he has also indicated that this is a very sensitive the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, mr wieland, perhaps this one of mine could be sexier, because justice is generally naked, or at least there is an attempt to strip it off so that it does not work. in fact, i believe that this motion for a resolution can be a first step which is quite practical and significant, since it is aimed at the concrete. i would like to make one point, however, and that is that the member states, often out of a misunderstood sense of power, try to prevent what may appear to be a surrender of sovereignty, especially in the field of criminal justice. so it is not easy to reconcile community sovereignty and the sovereignty of the member states in this area. the introduction of a mechanism for mutual evaluation by the member states, provided for in the amsterdam joint action plan of 1997, which - albeit with some delay - has now come into force, gives us a first framework. the first five countries have been selected: denmark, ireland, greece, luxembourg and the netherlands, and there is a committee of three experts. the country concerned does not provide for the presence of its own national expert and so the action is, shall we say, quite free. this first evaluation led to the discovery, firstly, that there is often strong political interference in the justice system, especially in requests for judicial cooperation in relation to urgent measures, seizure of property, searches, and this is acted upon in different ways, either by the minister of justice or by judicial authorities other than the one to which the request is addressed, etc. of course, there are also some positive aspects, for example, a computer system in the netherlands, called kris, which is used as a model. of course, today we face a far more sophisticated organized crime that uses advanced technology. they change the methods and therefore we also have to respond differently to crime. the reports of italy, belgium, spain and finland are also ready, but only unofficially, not officially. it is hoped, however, that there will be a review of this evaluation mechanism which should, in the future, be entrusted to the court of justice, a wish which parliament has also expressed on several occasions. in fact, the main thrust of this proposal is to emphasize that certain rules of approximation must be put forward. the commission has also been active in the fight against fraud, and has been involved in the preparation of the european court of justice's annual report on fraud. we are thinking of a crime which is prescribed for one of the member states but not for the others. it has happened, for example, that luxembourg refused to comply with requests from the judicial authority of another country to be the prescribed offence under national law. there are therefore various obstacles, which if we fail to address, judicial cooperation will in fact end up being just a word. so, to make it effective, there is already another motion for a resolution on the mutual recognition of final judgments. i have also called for it in this motion for a resolution, so that we can have a mosaic, a complete package of measures aimed at making this judicial cooperation more functional. we all feel the urgency of having an electronic archive, a documentation centre, at least of the final judgments, at least of the community framework. it is clear that it would be very useful to be able to have, in a timely manner, the response of final sentences against defendants or already convicted persons, at a wider level of europe, but already a good platform would be this computerization, which should not be a stratospheric thing, since today, through informatics, rather rapid and important results should be achieved. the motion for a resolution also calls for a fairly rapid intervention by eurojust - as we have already seen on several occasions - and above all by the european public prosecutor, the so-called european prosecutor who, at least in the area of serious crime - organised crime, electronic crime, white collar crime, the mafia - can effectively give the go-ahead in a united manner. the cooperation of the judicial authorities, the mps and the judges of the various member states is therefore also called for, and they will then be part of the european mp as a support at the level of the various states. in summary, it is a proposal that aims to support the european judicial network and the so-called 'good practice': i would like to emphasize this because, in the end, common sense, good practice in the rules is above all the direct transmission of requests between judges.

- mr president, i am surprised that some members are joking or making a point of controversy about the fact that a member of parliament has been arrested in a territory of the european union; i think that is a very serious matter, and it is connected with the very things we are discussing and have been dealing with for some time in the legal affairs committee. on the subject, the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights proposes that mr ribeiro and mr castro's parliamentary immunity should not be waived. this proposal - and i would like to ask my colleagues to reflect on this - is based on the contents of the treaties and on certain principles which have become well established. first, immunity is a guarantee of the independence of the european parliament and its members from any other power; secondly, immunity has no legal effect upon waiver of immunity. thirdly, the immunity covers any period of time, including members' transfers. fourthly, european parliamentary immunity is autonomous from national parliamentary immunity, even if the legislation of the member state of origin is applied. fifthly, reference must always be made to the political content of the facts, the fumus persecutionis hypothesis, the political moment of the request for revocation, the possible delay in that request and the seriousness of the alleged facts. sixthly, there are sometimes differences between the actual offence and the corresponding sanction in the various member states. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. on this basis the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights calls for the zimeray report to be adopted. i should like to take this opportunity, mr president, to stress two points on which, i repeat, i believe that this parliament and all our colleagues have a duty to reflect deeply. the provisions of articles 9 and 10 refer to the time when the european community was born, when the representatives in this parliament were members of national parliaments, and so the reference to national immunities is obvious. but we must also be aware that the european parliament today has a very important role in the institutional balances, and i think that the need to guarantee its full independence from the member states is a very important fact. parliament must always be informed of the proceedings which are intended to be brought against its members and if this information function is not carried out by the judicial authority of the place where the facts occur, the members have the duty and the right to carry it out directly, since it is this parliament which must decide which provisions are to apply, as happens in some european countries. mr president, i would not like to be forced to seek political the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this directive regulates the protection of copyright and related rights in the information society. it is an important directive, very difficult. we are in the second reading and parliament is called upon to express its opinion on the council's position which, as you will recall, was forwarded to us eighteen months after the adoption of the first reading. the reason is that it was a difficult and delicate compromise between all the interests involved in the directive. i consider this difficult and delicate compromise to be a step forward, not least because it covers many of the points which parliament proposed at first reading. but there were some things that needed to be improved, and that's what i tried to do. despite the adoption of some compromise amendments in the legal affairs committee, there are still divergent views, firstly on the article on technical copying, or caching, and the article on private copying. there are many amendments on this point which i do not agree with. the reason why the compromise amendments adopted by the committee were an important innovation in support of authors in the area of private copying is that they state that this private copying - and i quote - 'must not have commercial or even indirect purposes, must be made by a natural person for private use and must generate fair compensation for the rights holders'. this amendment introduces a new principle into community law, in that it restricts the concept of private copying to the benefit of authors, while at the same time safeguarding the legitimate interests of consumers. this amendment, which was approved by the committee, has stopped the proliferation of unauthorized exchanges of copies between users of sites such as napster, and it will no longer be possible to classify the exchange of unauthorized works between users of napster as private copying. i think that was a step forward from the text of the common position. as regards the other aspect, that of technical copying, i believe that the balance achieved in the common position is more than sufficient to protect the rights holders on the one hand and the consumers on the other. all the amendments tabled on this subject - article 5 (1) - although they are intended to provide greater protection for copyright, which is a laudable aim, cannot be accepted, not least because they concern the scope of application and not the regulatory sphere, which is the scope of this directive. the amendments also aim to introduce a system of dual authorisation of works on the internet, one for hosting and one for caching, placing a heavy burden on the management of networks. so, in the end, we have seen with the vote in the legal affairs committee that it is possible to gather a broad consensus, to adopt the directive and to improve the common position in a way that does not expose us to the risk of a long and exhausting conciliation; all this after three years of debate, controversy and confrontation. i think this is an opportunity which the european parliament must seize: if you support the agreement reached in the legal affairs committee tomorrow and approve the amendments which are the result of a broad compromise between many political groups, we will finally be able to approve this directive. this will not only be useful for the european union, which has been waiting for legislation on this subject for a long time, but it will also be useful, and above all for the rights holders. the directive adopted will not only bring into force the still controversial exceptions, but also and above all the rule laid down in article 2, which provides for the principle of the authorization of rightholders for the use of works in the new digital environments. for all these reasons, i think and hope that tomorrow it will finally be possible to approve the text of the directive.

mr president, i should like to congratulate mrs emilia müller on the great balance she has shown in this report. as a researcher, i cannot help but appreciate the scientific rigor with which such a sensitive subject has been dealt with, in which a varied and sometimes contradictory picture has been noted. i thank the commission for having also approved my amendment on the need to follow good manufacturing practice in the preparation of various vitamin and mineral supplements, as this is the highest quality guarantee for consumer protection. similarly, an overly permissive position on the doses used was not rightly adopted; in fact, these were kept within the daily reference range, thus overcoming the notion that the higher the dose, the greater the effects. as a pharmacologist, i must point out that, for pharmacokinetic reasons as well as for pharmacodynamic and toxicological reasons, for example, excessive doses may also produce effects contrary to those desired or, even, after long periods of intake, damage to important organs and systems of the body may result, so there is no need to increase the doses of mineral vitamins to the maximum tolerated level. in conclusion, mr president, i believe that the document approved by the commission can be definitively approved by the house.
commission. – mr president, i am pleased to be here tonight for your consideration of this proposal for a directive on food supplements. this proposal aims to harmonise very divergent national rules by ensuring that consumers will be able to choose from safe products bearing adequate and appropriate labelling. i would like to thank mrs müller for her considerable efforts to prepare this report and for her overall support for the proposal. i know that she has had a very difficult task. this is evident from the number of amendments that were tabled in the environment committee and the number of additional amendments tabled for parliament. the most sensitive issue, judging from the amendments tabled, seems to be the range of ingredients that may be present in food supplements. recital 6 of the commission's proposal recognises that various nutrients, including vitamins and minerals and other substances such as fibre, plant and herbal extracts, may be ingredients of food supplements. it lays down specific provisions only on vitamins and minerals which are nutrients as a first stage, because that is how far scientific knowledge allows us to go today. the intention is to lay down specific rules for other nutrients and other ingredients at a later stage as scientific knowledge improves. it is understood that, until the adoption of specific harmonised community provisions and without prejudice to the provisions of the treaty, national provisions on these other nutrients and ingredients may be applicable. i agree with the last sentence of the justification for amendment no 1. the specific rules on vitamins and minerals laid down in the future directive should be applicable to food supplements containing vitamins, minerals and other ingredients. otherwise it would be very easy for an unscrupulous manufacturer to avoid applying these rules by adding just a small quantity of another ingredient to a product. i can, therefore, accept amendment no 1 in principle with necessary drafting changes that will depend on the final wording of article 2. amendments nos 29, 37 and 41 add to the text of amendment no 1 the principle that specific rules for these other nutrients and ingredients should be prepared when the science enables us to do so. i accept this principle. however, and in terms of drafting, i can accept amendment no 37 with some drafting changes, but i cannot accept amendments nos 29 and 41. amendment no 5 purports to introduce in the definition in article 2 what is explained in recital 6. food supplements are concentrated sources of nutrients and other substances, or ingredients as they are called in recital no 6. this would clarify the definition, an essential part of the directive. i can therefore accept no 5 in principle with drafting changes to ensure coherence of the text. amendments nos 33 and 44 have the same purpose as amendment no 5 and the clarification goes further in stating that these substances have a nutritional function, as have vitamins, minerals and amino acids or a physiological function, as has fibre or some antioxidants extracted from plants. so i can accept amendments nos 33 and 44, provided that the status of the substances that would thus come under the scope of the directive is very clear, both in terms of the criteria that would be applicable for drawing up positive lists and their status until these positive lists are adopted. amendments nos 34 and 46 refer also to article 2 and are acceptable because they follow the same logic as amendment no 33. however, from the drafting point of view the proposed addition should be separate from the provision of article 2(b) so i can accept them with that drafting change. amendment no 45, an alternate to amendments nos 34 and 36, is in line with amendment no 5 which i could accept. here again the proposed addition should be separate from the provisions of article 2(b). i can therefore accept amendment no 45 with the necessary drafting change. amendment no 6 on the same point is an alternate that creates confusion. the justification given in the committee's report would seem to be in line with recital 6 and with the proposed text of amendment no 5 by acknowledging that ingredients such as amino acids, fatty acids and herbal extracts are included in food supplements. but the proposed text is in contradiction with them by limiting such ingredients to those having a nutritional function. i cannot see the reason for this limitation and therefore cannot accept amendment no 6. i can accept amendment no 2 to recital 7 and also amendment no 4 to recital 14, which is a technical correction to the text of the proposal. amendment no 7 concerns the definition of dose form. this is a highly technical matter. i understand that concern is expressed from many sources to have a workable definition that depicts current practices. this is also our aim. i can accept amendment no 7 in principle but with drafting changes necessary to achieve the stated aim of flexibility. amendment no 8 would add a new paragraph to article 3 with the same text as that proposed for addition to recital 6. as for amendment no 1, we have no problem with the principle but the inclusion of the same text in that article is not necessary. therefore i would not accept amendment no 8. amendment no 51 has partially similar aims to amendment no 8 and goes further to set rules concerning the principle of free circulation of products. i hope you agree that this cannot be done in a few lines in this specific directive and i cannot accept amendment no 51. amendment no 9 refers to article 4 and the purity criteria of substances listed in annex ii. i can understand the wish to be more concrete here. in fact, since the tabling of this proposal, appropriate wording regarding purity criteria has been agreed and included in community legislation, namely the directive on nutritional substances that may be used in the manufacture of foods for particular nutritional uses. this text refers to community purity criteria that are already adopted for some of the substances in annex ii and to purity criteria recommended by international organisations. for the sake of coherence, the same text should be included in this proposed directive. i can accept the spirit of amendment no 9 but with drafting that is in line with already agreed community texts. amendment no 3 on recital 9 is one of a series of amendments concerning procedures and the working rules for managing the directive. regarding the revision of the lists of the annexes, the commission may respond to a request by a member state, a stakeholder including a manufacturer, or take the initiative to set in motion the procedures for adding to the annexes, or it may reject the request of the manufacturer. amendment no 3 is not acceptable because it constitutes a restriction on the commission's right of initiative. amendment no 10 reduces the procedure of modifying the annexes, which includes both scientific assessment and the subsequent adoption of a commission directive, into a procedure of evaluation of the safety of substances. it also aims at specifying in this directive working rules for the scientific committee for food. this is not a subject for legislation. therefore, amendment no 10 is not acceptable and for the same reason i cannot accept amendment no 25 which also lays down working procedures for the scientific committee for food. amendment no 11 poses the same problems that i mentioned regarding amendment no 6. it also poses problems from the procedural point of view. the commission must preserve its right of initiative as to when to present proposals. therefore, i cannot accept amendment no 11. for the same institutional reasons i cannot accept amendments nos 35 and 47 despite the fact that they include references to ingredients with nutritional or physiological functions. amendment no 13, the last on procedures, proposes that the comitology procedure referred to in article 5(3) shall be subject to the principle of transparency. of course, i would not deny this but i have a problem dealing with this issue in a specific vertical directive on food supplements. the principle of transparency is a general one to be applied to procedures dealing with products across the board. you are currently considering our proposal for a food act which includes provisions on transparency applicable to all foodstuffs. therefore, i cannot accept amendment no 13. amendment no 12 to article 5(1) makes a valid point that requirements of children and adults be taken into account when setting maximum levels for vitamins and minerals. the principles can be extended to take into account, and i quote, "sensitivities of different consumer groups" and not only children and adults. further, the point may be inserted in a more appropriate place in the article than the one suggested, therefore i can accept amendment no 12 in principle, subject to drafting changes. i now move to a number of amendments that concern the labelling provisions of the proposal. amendment no 14 refers to the name of the product. in terms of labelling there is very little significant difference between the name of the product and the labelling. the name of the product must be set in eu legislation otherwise member states can do that at the national level. this would create confusion for consumers. for this reason, i cannot accept amendment no 14, however i take note of your request that the name of the product should include the words "food supplement". the text proposed by amendments nos 15 and 28 does not express a different principle than that in the text of the proposal. they are drafting amendments and i am not convinced that they achieve greater clarity on this point and therefore i would not accept amendments nos 15 and 28. i consider that a statement to the effect that food supplements should not be used as a substitute for a diversified diet is important for consumers both for information and education. therefore i cannot accept amendment no 16 that proposes the deletion of this provision. i can accept amendment no 17 that proposes to include on the label a statement to the effect that food supplements should be stored out of the reach of children. such a statement would provide additional safeguards to avoid accidental ingestion of these products. amendment no 18, although well intended i am sure, raises a number of complicated issues. any food supplement intended for infants under the age of one year would, be to my mind, a product for particular nutritional uses and would be excluded from the scope of this directive as mentioned in article 1. the case of supplements for pregnant women could give rise to a similar debate. amendment no 18 would be potentially contradictory to article 1 and i cannot accept it. i can accept amendment no 19. i can also accept amendment no 20 in principle but with drafting changes that would be in line with the justification for this amendment provided in your report. amendment no 21 proposes the addition of two sentences to article 9. the principle expressed in the first sentence that excess doses should be avoided is already covered in article 6. the second sentence deals with the issue of tolerance limits for declared quantities of certain nutrients that have stability problems. this is a highly technical issue that needs to be considered by appropriate experts and, if necessary, dealt with through technical implementing measures. therefore i cannot accept amendment no 21. amendment no 22 proposes to adopt the principles of good manufacturing practices by legally binding measures. this is not the practice in the area of foodstuffs and would set a precedent. we have horizontal rules on hygiene and control that apply to all foods and will apply to food supplements also. we have purity criteria for many of the substances that are listed in annex ii and intend to adopt criteria for the rest. these binding horizontal rules seem to us to be enough. therefore, i cannot accept amendment no 22. of course, nothing stops the relevant industry voluntarily adopting specific gmps for a specific product. this happens often in the food area. amendment no 23 would make it obligatory for member states to require manufacturers to notify authorities of food supplements when marketed. the commission proposal allows member states to waive such requirement if they can monitor these products otherwise on their territory.member states are opposed to such imposition because they feel this is an issue of subsidiarity and wish to have a free hand in how they monitor these products. i cannot accept amendment no 23. amendment no 24 also relates to procedures and aims to impose strict time limits for commission decisions. such decisions may depend on advice delivered by the scientific committee for food, positions of member states and other factors beyond the control of the commission. for this reason i cannot accept amendment no 24. amendments nos 26 and 27 add to annexes i and ii more minerals, - doc. a5-0015/2001 by mr lange, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending directive 97/24/ec on certain components and characteristics of two or three-wheel motor vehicles (com (2000) 314 - c5-0334/2000 - 2000/0136 (cod)).
- mr president, the proposal for a directive we are about to vote on represents a concrete step forward in the union's desire to pursue ambitious objectives in the field of limiting air pollution. we are in fact faced with a paradox today: although motorcycles account for only 2-3% of the total transport volume, their share of total emissions is increasing. the amendments proposed by mr lange, as well as virtually all those adopted in the committee on the environment, improve the commission's proposal. in particular, the insistence on the definition of specifically calibrated test cycles for motor vehicles and units throughout europe, but also the request to submit type approval to the confirmation of the functionality of pollution control devices, are signs of the european parliament's willingness to take firm action in such a sensitive area. in this connection, it seems important to me to emphasize that most of these objectives are broadly shared by the companies in the sector. this means that mr lange has been able to negotiate well with them and that the producers are also becoming more aware of their duty to contribute to improving our environmental conditions. the choice to fix now not only the date for the revision of the first set of limits - 2006 - but also the limits themselves of this second phase is a symbol of parliament's choice to push the companies ever further. the introduction of a possibility of revising these limits, linked to the desired technological development, is a sign of the will to continue the dialogue with producers.
the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to thank the european parliament and in particular the rapporteur, mr lange, for the rapid handling of this matter. the rapporteur supports the commission's proposal for limit values to be applied from 2003. the rapporteur proposes a second phase, however, in which the mandatory limit values would be respected from 2006 onwards. this phase would be based on the passenger car test cycle. the commission recognises the need for a second stage. we will make a separate proposal on this subject by the end of 2002. the future proposal will build on further studies looking at the technical performance and economic feasibility of improved emissions reduction devices. in this next step, the emissions shall be measured in relation to the improved test cycle. this will be matched to the actual driving dynamics of motorcycles. the commission did not include in its proposal mandatory limits to be observed from 2006 onwards, as it does not yet have data to support the introduction of a new test cycle in a scientifically convincing way. the commission actively supports the development of a global and uniform motorcycle test cycle. the work started in 1999 and was formally commissioned by the un economic commission for europe in may 2000, with the support of the eu member states, japan and the united states. the work programme is proceeding as scheduled. we therefore believe that the new cycle will be introduced in time to be applied in 2006. this approach is also in line with the view of the rapporteur, mr lange. the commission cannot therefore support the amendments which now call for the start of the compulsory second stage in 2006. the matter is dealt with in amendments nos 3, 5, 10, 11, 23, 24 and 25. but the commission is of course prepared to contribute to the establishment of a comprehensive interinstitutional agreement as soon as possible. the rapporteur mentions a number of measures to better ensure the effective operation of the emission control devices throughout the life of the vehicle. the commission recognises their importance in ensuring that emissions are effectively reduced while driving. however, as a technical product, a motorcycle is very different from a passenger car. the application of the requirements to motorcycles has significant implications which require a careful assessment of technical feasibility and cost-effectiveness. i could answer mr de roo on his question on rail transport that it is under consideration but there is no proposal yet. the commission accepts in principle amendments which invite the commission to examine the above aspects. however, we reject amendments which set dates for the mandatory application of the requirements or which do not take into account the completion of the final research results. this refers to amendments nos 6, 13, 14, 15, 20 and 22. the same commission position applies to amendments nos 8 and 17 on co2 emissions from motorcycles. the report contains a number of amendments which the commission can support, such as amendments nos 4 and 12, if member states are given the possibility of encouraging the retrofitting of emission reducing equipment and components in older motor vehicles. the same applies to amendment no 1 and the second part of amendment no 9, which propose a one-year derogation for a special category of trial motorcycles, and to the first part of amendment no 9, which defer application to existing vehicle types from january to july 2004. the commission has, however, rejected amendment no 26, which postpones application to existing vehicle types for a full year. in principle, the commission also supports amendments nos 7 and 16 on the requirements for switches and other bypass systems and considers that these requirements can be incorporated into the present proposal. the commission can therefore accept amendments nos 4, 9, 12 and 18 and, in principle, amendments nos 2, 7, 8, 16 and 21 and, in part, amendments nos 1, 4, 19, 20 and 22. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 13, 15, 17 and 23 to 26.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0039/2001), on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on special provisions for vehicles used for the carriage of passengers and comprising more than eight seats in addition to the driver's seat, and amending directives 70/156/eec and 97/27/ec (a5-0039/2001 - c5-0456/2000 - 1997/0176 (cod)) (rapporteur: mr miller).

mr president, the radical members of the bonino list will vote against the council's own-initiative proposal and therefore, while voting in favour of some of the amendments proposed by the rapporteur, will also vote against the report as a whole. why would you do that? the first is a fundamental reason, which concerns these and all other initiatives which affect the framework of criminal law in the union. as a european federalist, not a eurosceptic, i consider it a monstrosity that criminal law legislation is adopted and put into effect without any approval from a legitimately and democratically elected parliament, which is therefore entitled to do so. the european union is taking a monstrous course on this and other issues. criminal law cannot escape parliamentary debate: the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval, and the council will be consulted on it. the only track on which european integration policy is moving forward is the track of repression, because that is where it is easy. the decisions are prepared by groups of officials from the ministries of the interior and justice, whose only concern is the efficiency of the repression mechanisms, without any other consideration - it is not their fault, it is their profession, their professionalism - without any concern for social, economic, labour, international policy, development issues. we are moving very fast on the track of repression, while on the other tracks, those of the guarantees of the right of asylum and the guarantees of the right of defence, the european parliament, the european union, the european commission and the council are unable to move. this is the first reason why we cannot accept the council's proposals, just as we cannot accept a report which does not reject them clearly and totally, because on this point too the european parliament is consulted - as usual - without any real powers. as regards the substance of the matter - as my colleagues boumediene-thiery and frahm have said - it is an illusion to ignore the fact that the strengthening of prohibitionism on immigration only leads to the strengthening of illegal immigration, the strength of the illegality that overwhelms us. our borders are overrun by the illegality that our prohibitionist laws produce: that's the reality of the facts. let us not think that we can solve the problem by increasing the penalties for the transport of illegal immigrants here and there, without democratic consultation. if possible - let us hope not - we will only make it worse. at the same time, the underlying economic causes are not being addressed. at the european commission, commissioner lamy had put forward a bold proposal for unilateral liberalization of trade in goods from the poorest countries: this is a way of attacking the root causes, not by bringing charity, alms and assistance, but by opening our markets to agricultural and manufacturing commodities. everything but arms, that was the name of the proposal, which was scuttled by the lobbies in the european union and so the pressure on migration is getting stronger. the lamy proposal is therefore being ignored, and at the same time we are deluding ourselves that we can solve the problem by increasing the penalties for those who practice a trade which we have given them for the profits which we, with our laws, make possible. but we must not be under the illusion - i say this to mr ceyhun and to my colleagues on the left - that the partial improvement - we are in favour of some amendments - of this repressive framework will turn the situation around. we do not think that the distinction, which we will support as the lesser of two evils, between the economic benefits of immigration and humanitarian immigration solves the problem, because you teach us that on the left, when you say that economic causes are the basis of immigration. so how can you claim that economic causes are the root causes, while at the same time taking a very hard line against entrepreneurs and those who profit from illegal immigration? prohibitionism is not just about immigration, but also about the labour market, new forms of work, parttime work, fixed-term work, fixed-term contracts, seasonal contracts, and it is a prohibitionism for which the left, and also the trade unions, are largely responsible in europe. we do not think we can then set our conscience straight by attacking the entrepreneurs and those who exploit labour, because in the eyes of those who are exploited, of those who are condemned to die in their own country because of hunger and the absolute lack of means of subsistence, the european entrepreneur-exploiter is probably the only possibility of development and salvation for himself and his family. i therefore conclude, mr president, by confirming the negative vote of the radical members of the bonino list.
