mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i do not want to repeat what has already been said by the previous rapporteurs, and i will not therefore tell you what the content of this amending budget, proposed by the commission and already approved by the council, may be. i would rather take this opportunity to stimulate two reflections which have been central to the debate in the amendments proposed in the committee on budgets: first, the compulsory expenditure. as we all know, parliament has little power over these expenditures - including agriculture. the council has the final say, although the cap has always been synonymous with the european community before and the european union now. i think it is time to move forward and give this house greater powers: as elected representatives of the european citizens, we have a duty to represent their demands in all areas. as a branch of the budgetary authority we should have the right to influence all its parts in a significant way. second thought: the commission has also proposed that the burden be shared between the member states and the union. the liberal group has tabled several amendments on this point, which, as you know, aim to revise the intervention rates, aiming at equality between the union and the member states. i don't think it's the right choice, and i want to explain why. first, given the difficult political situation created by the bse crisis, citizens would see such a decision as a distancing from the european institutions. in short, it would send the message that the union is ready to intervene to ban state aid or to fix milk quotas, but equally ready to wash its hands of the matter when it needs to. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's farmers are not left behind in the crisis. it is he who must be protected, and we will certainly not do so by shifting the burden of the problem onto the member states. secondly, if we support this political position we would be sending a signal in favour of the renationalisation of the common agricultural policy, an absurd signal at a time when the debate on the post-nice period is not about the abolition of community policies.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the telecommunications sector in europe has, thanks to the impetus of the community institutions and the innovative drive of the market, moved in a short space of time from a situation of national monopolies to a regime of general liberalization; the dynamic market and technology drives have fuelled the process, with results in terms of competition and new entrants sometimes exceeding expectations. the process of reviewing the current regulatory framework in the telecommunications sector, which is currently being considered by the european parliament, therefore aims to outline the general objectives from which the regulatory principles of the new framework are derived. in essence, the new framework aims to move the telecommunications market from the phase of market liberalisation to a phase of effective competition. the approach to market regulation should be geared to the future market environment, where conditions will be highly competitive and differentiated, with a rapid spread of innovative services and geared to the application of competition law, replacing ex ante rules, which are defined from time to time. this can be achieved by means of ex ante legislation harmonized at european level, characterized by the characteristics of transitorious and exceptional nature; ex ante regulation must therefore provide for the conditions for its elimination once a sufficient level of competition has been achieved, since excess regulation is contrary to the market. with regard to the content of the directive for which i am the rapporteur, parliament, through its committee on industry, has identified certain priorities. the definition of 'access' is: the commission's proposal was extremely broad, and a problem of unclear definition of terms could have led to problems in relations with the regulator; in particular, the rules and instruments defined in the directive risk being used indiscriminately in relation to very different conceptual situations, such as access to terminal services, network elements, system elements, networks, roaming, by operators and users. a more detailed examination was also needed of roaming, which i do not think should be considered a form of access since it has different connotations depending on whether it is the ability of a user, subscribed to a foreign operator, to access the mobile service in another country and vice versa - so-called international roaming - or whether it is the possibility for a new entrant to be able to use the facilities of existing operators in his own country while waiting to complete the installation of his own network, so-called asymmetric roaming. principle of light regulation: the report stressed that light regulation and flexibility, which are the cornerstones of european legislation, should not be synonymous with discretion. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are applied in the community. access and interconnection management requires a balance to be struck between the right of an operator, the owner of infrastructure, to be able to manage networks and infrastructure for its own benefit and the limits of other operators, service providers, to access essential infrastructure. level of market competitiveness: another area which needed clarification was the assessment of the level of market competitiveness. the achievement of a good level of competitiveness is the precondition for the reduction of regulation in favour of the application of antitrust law alone or, conversely, for the subjecting of operators, which are notified as having significant market power, to regulatory obligations, with consequent cost-oriented negotiations. the definition of 'new significant market power' originates from the judgments of the court of justice and refers to a kind of reduced dominance: one of the attributes of dominance is that it prevents competition, since it is a restrictive legal concept of an ex post nature. the proposal for a directive applies the concept of 'new' significant market power or reduced dominance which, amended by its 'negative' attribute relating to the possibility of preventing competition, leaves room for ex ante intervention. obligations of operators national regulatory authorities may impose obligations on operators notified as having significant market power in terms of transparency, non-discrimination, accounting separation, access to and use of specific network elements, price control and cost accounting. the rules for the application or revision of the obligations arising from the application of the current system and those arising from the new regulatory framework are also specified. the most immediate comment concerned the application of the obligations on operators notified as having significant market power. notification does not automatically impose any obligations but the national regulatory authorities must specify which obligations are to be imposed on each notified operator. however, the existence of significant market power does not always coincide with an actual abuse of that position. the national regulatory authority, in assessing whether or not an undertaking has significant market power, should assess the effective use of that market power in imposing the obligations laid down in the directive. finally, the environmental impact. a particular issue which is of particular concern to me, also in my capacity as a local administrator, is the reduction of the number of antennas in the towns. increasingly, technical requirements require operators to install infrastructure that has little to do with the landscape. the community institutions, as well as national and local authorities, have a duty to reduce as far as possible this impact on the landscape and the environment. in order to safeguard the importance of competition in the telecommunications market and its development, all policy-makers at all levels have a duty to seek regulatory solutions that allow the optimisation of the use of the currently available infrastructures, taking into account the environmental landscape impact and the socio-cultural consequences for citizens. there are also some points relating to the various tax regimes, for which harmonization is called for, and the necessary coordination by the european commission. in view of all these considerations, the assessment of the proposed directive can only be positive, since it aims to stimulate growth in the sector, stimulate future investment, improve the competitiveness of enterprises, facilitate price reductions by improving efficiency and contribute to economic growth as a whole.
- mr president, we welcome the commission's initiative and consider it an important step towards simplifying, if nothing else, legislation at european level. however, we would first like to point out that there is a serious contradiction in the electronic telecommunications sector which, if left unaddressed, could ultimately render any effort to create a competitive environment for the benefit of consumers useless. the contradiction is the situation of a real conflict of interest in which many european states find themselves, being at the same time regulators and holders of economic and political interests, arbiters and players. this is true in the field of telephony, but also in the field of digital television, where the public broadcasters have a very strong influence thanks to the large investments financed with public funds. we must therefore bear in mind this basic flaw, but the overall assessment of the package - i repeat - is positive. following the recent success of the unbundling regulation for the local loop, the aim is now to provide a first solution to a situation in which those operating in the european electronic communications market are faced not only with the many directives and regulations that have been layered over the years, but also with a plethora of national regulatory authorities acting in profoundly different regulatory contexts, with the most varied criteria, often not even foreseeable for operators, in a situation of fragmentation and sometimes serious legal uncertainty. the commission's proposals have the advantage of rationalizing existing legislation in a few directives and of creating a telecommunications market which is becoming increasingly pan-european. it is also important to stress - as i believe the rapporteur, mr brunetta, has mentioned - that the objective to be pursued is to achieve, as soon as possible, a situation of effective competition without the need for the heavy regulatory burden of the authorities. we must move beyond the role of national authorities and reach a situation in the electronic communications sector where the general antitrust rules apply to all markets. we can only do this when we have succeeded in tackling at the root of this fundamental vice of collusion and conflict of interest, which still exists at the state level, with the weight of the state in the economy of electronic communications: only then will we be able to bring this sector into line with the ordinary antitrust rules applicable to other sectors.

mr president, i too congratulate mr avilés perea on the excellent work he has done and on the fact that he has brought this report to the table this evening. but i am sure that two things must be emphasized, which are also the result of the discussion that took place in committee and of a series of majority votes that in some way created or favoured, within the report itself, the presence of certain positions which are, in my view, questionable. i shall therefore divide the report into two parts: the first, which i entirely agree with, is that the rapporteur is very courageous in expressing a great demand for legality, in some way anticipating in this report the need, which is present in all european states, to tackle the problem of immigration in its entirety for a long time, now that we are aware that the countries of the union can no longer have individual and different policies in this very difficult and delicate field, and in defining what are the rights and duties of both immigrants and the host countries. at the same time, within this policy, the role of the most vulnerable groups - women and children - certainly needs to be examined very carefully. in this respect, this aspect of the report is very useful, especially since it takes up some of the guidelines and decisions already expressed by the tampere council. i am, however, uncomfortable with two things in particular. i too share the difficulty of accepting an additional observer - i consider observers to be stiffening and difficult elements - and the difficulty of accepting this term 'european citizenship' or even 'euro-mediterranean citizenship', which has no legal status at all and is confusing.
commission. – mr president, it is a common misconception that globalisation trends and related policies are gender-neutral. this is important to bear in mind when we discuss the problems of immigrant women in europe. the commission considers that zero immigration is neither realistic nor justified. the policy has never been fully implemented, not only because of the legitimate need for family reunification, but also for economic reasons. in the future, demographic factors – the ageing of our workforce and population as a whole – are likely to make immigration more, rather than less, necessary and understood. in this process we have to prevent gender-based discriminatory practices. the promotion of proactive gender equality is very necessary. in its communication on a community immigration policy presented on 22 november last year, the commission stated that, in the short term, immigration can be an important element of population growth and could accompany other responses to demographic change. it will not in itself be an effective way of dealing with labour market imbalances, but can help alleviate skills shortages within the context of an overall structural strategy. migrants, including women migrants, may have a particular role to play in some of the areas particularly affected by the increase in the number of older people, while legal migrants, the majority of whom will be of working age, will play a part in reducing the financial burden of the elderly on the population of working age. in december 1999, the commission launched a draft directive on the right of family reunification which, among other matters, gives family members the right to immediate access to education, vocational training and employment. the next steps will be the presentation of a draft directive on the status of long-term residents and a proposal on the admission of third-country nationals for the purpose of employment and self-employed activities and for the purpose of study on the territory of the member states. the treaty of amsterdam explicitly includes gender equality among the objectives of the european community. this applies to our domestic, as well as external, policies. in addition, there are several political decisions which explicitly call for gender-equality concerns to be acted upon in development cooperation. in order to strengthen the promotion of gender equality as an issue which affects all policies, programmes and projects, i will, in the near future, present to the college a programme of action for the mainstreaming of gender-equality development cooperation. the trafficking in human beings is facilitated by globalisation and by modern technologies. trafficking in human beings, and in particular girls and women, not only involves sexual exploitation, but also labour exploitation in conditions akin to slavery. the traditional flow between certain third world regions and western destinations continues. what gives rise to even greater concern is the increase in the numbers of women and children trafficked into the eu from central and eastern european countries. the commission has taken significant steps against this violation of human rights. freedom from discrimination is a basic human right, be it on the grounds of nationality, sex, racial or ethnic origin, religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. that is why the commission very much welcomes that the treaty of amsterdam gives the community powers to combat discrimination on all these grounds under article 13. the promotion and protection of human rights is an integral part of the eu’s human rights policy. immigrant women are particularly vulnerable to discrimination and social exclusion. the employment strategy and the social funds are both designed to combat discrimination and secure inclusion in society. two directives recently adopted deal with discrimination, one related to employment and the other to racial discrimination. both integrate the gender perspective and the programme will support transitional activities. turning to the position of women in the labour market, let me recall that the community’s employment strategy with its priorities of employability, entrepreneurship, adaptability and equal opportunities is about supporting member states’ efforts to introduce structural reforms into their employment, social protection and taxation systems. this is a matter of equality. it is also a matter of replacing discrimination with the economic good sense of engaging the enterprise and creativity of all those who need and want to work. this requires our social model to be reformed to engage all our people, both women and men, in an inclusive economic and social europe with equal access to opportunity, skills, personal development and the support this implies. the european structural funds play a major role in this process. to secure the rights of immigrant women is now fundamentally about good governance on the basis of shared values in a changing world for both sexes. it is about tolerance, modernisation and improvement of the various tools of policy. it is also about democracy and solidarity. equal representation is a key issue here. the participation of women in political and civil life is fundamental to good governance, whether in europe or elsewhere. women’s voices are still not being heard sufficiently in major policy areas. structural changes are required to make them more audible. institution-building to meet the challenges of globalisation must be accompanied by equal and shared participation of women in the political process. many of these things are well-known, well-established challenges. hopefully the new thing we can do is to face those challenges with a more rigorous will to do what is politically needed.
the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i should like to thank the commissioner, because he has returned to the committee on development several times for this report, thus contributing to and enriching the debate which has taken place within the committee itself. i should also like to thank the chairman of the committee and all the group coordinators and all the colleagues who have contributed to the preparation of this report, and who have very sensitively accepted my invitation to make this report a document which would have the widest possible support and a very broad parliamentary majority, in order to take account of all the positions which the european parliament can express. finally, i would also like to thank my colleagues on the other committees: i am pleased to note that the commission has taken the initiative to present a report on the situation in the community in the field of the environment. the report is based on a number of fundamental principles: the restoration of the natural balance with a view to protecting the environment; the protection of the food chain, to protect the ecosystem; the protection of biodiversity; the search for a self-sufficient subsistence economy; the limits on industrial monocultures which constitute an exploitation; and then, the restoration of the natural balance also with regard to anthropological progress and responsible relations between man and woman, between adult and child, between worker and elderly person, starting from a social embryo which is represented by man, woman, children. another principle is that of conscious and self-managed development, as a cultural factor, of the need, of the search for a better living condition: projects that are self-generating in order to promote the evolution and the overcoming of the local cultural experience; and then the awareness of the institutional role and the need for private involvement with programmes consistent with development; finally, a special, very special attention to the world of children, who are an invisible part of society for the political class, without a voice and without rights; the commission has also proposed a strong role for women, recognising the role they have always played in the social fabric, starting with the family and the workplace. these guidelines were used in the debate in committee on the european commission's communication, which we found to be somewhat reductive in relation to the prospects for the european union in this world of development. and since it is not possible to make a coherent report on such a complex task, i would just like to say that the situation of the poor today is worse than it was in 1960, that is, 40 years ago, that the rate of schooling has decreased and that we cannot talk about the individual, the person, the individual, but we look in statistical and economic terms at the whole complex of poverty in the world. the debt problem is also a problem that can and must be tackled, provided that we manage to monitor the budgets of the states to re-qualify the posts and to allocate them to the eradication of poverty. similarly, rural development needs to be improved, emphasised and increased, also to counteract the rush to build megacities. as regards conflict prevention, i think that it has been dealt with in rather comprehensive terms in the opinion of mr carrilho for the committee on foreign affairs, and i think that it can also be dealt with in terms of the regionalisation of development policies. one last point i would like to make: i think there is a tendency to tackle the problems of development and poverty eradication by giving this task to the multinationals. i do not think they are adequate for this task. i think that the role of ngos, which must have a priority relationship with the people of developing countries, should be enhanced. in conclusion: i do not know whether this report will be able to deal with these problems. i just think there are so many children, so many women, so many men who need our help, and we have to defend them.
mr president, commissioner, i voted on the gemelli report in committee and i shall vote on it again in the house. i very much agree and, like all my colleagues, i have no reason to criticize a work which i believe has been done with great care and dedication and with the cooperation of all my colleagues in the committee. i shall take advantage of this time to raise two or three other problems. the question that arises, as some of my colleagues have said, whenever i discuss development and development cooperation, not only in this house but also outside it, is: why? if we look at the situation 40 years ago and look at it now, we see that the gap between north and south has increased, that the gap between the richest countries and the poorest countries has increased. why would you do that? we must try to answer this question, otherwise we risk being frustrated every time we talk about it. why, as my colleague mr gemelli said, are there more poor people, less education, new diseases, and a worse situation for children, children and women? what are the reasons? i think there is one, basically. we are talking about development policy, we are talking about public resources: a small, tiny stream that runs from north to south. then there's a huge stream, a huge river of private resources that runs from south to north. the question then is whether the member states and the european union and the other rich countries can organise a development policy which is capable of fostering a coherence between public and private policies; the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. that's the point, otherwise we're the ones emptying the sea with a spoon. what is the risk now, commissioner nielson? you know better than i do: the problem is that in today's globalised and information society, those who have been excluded from wealth are also excluded from knowledge, that is, they suffer a double exclusion. this is a serious risk. that is why drastic decisions must be taken now, at this historic juncture. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. however, only one of the 15 eu countries - sweden, which has the honour of holding the eu presidency - is meeting this commitment. we need new support for development policy, which has not been there until now, support from the whole of the economic systems in which we live, not just from the states or public institutions. one last point, commissioner nielson: the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i have also read the commission's action programme, but we are not discussing that. we had asked for an information campaign in europe on cooperation policy and public aid policy. i didn't see any sign of it. a development policy cannot be sustained without the support of european public opinion. and how can we get this support if there is no information campaign inside the european union, not outside?
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i must say that i very much appreciated the initiative taken by the commission to bring together in a single text all the provisions applicable to large migratory species, although i agree with mr piétrasanta that it would have been better to wait until the autumn round of meetings on fisheries had concluded, so as to incorporate the decisions taken at those meetings into the rules of procedure. for species defined as highly migratory, the total catches are very high. in fact, in 1997 3.5 million tonnes of large migratory fish were caught in the atlantic, pacific and indian oceans and, as we know, the european union is actively involved in this fishing activity in the world's oceans. the last period has seen the emergence of a number of regional organisations to regulate fishing activities for these species. these organisations adopt recommendations which include limitations on the capacity of certain fleets, restrictions on catches in certain periods and areas, technical measures on sizes and weights and, if no objections are raised, recommendations become binding on the contracting parties. i would also add that the regional organizations continue to take effective measures to solve problems of various kinds, such as those listed above, but it will certainly not be easy for them to remedy a problem common to all areas and not easily solvable: the commission has also proposed that the fishing fleet be reduced to a minimum. hence the need for concerted action and cooperation between the rops and national governments to prevent shipowners, who feel overwhelmed by the regulations in force, from changing the flag of their ships. in conclusion, let me draw your attention to the fundamental role of the rdps in this context, where, given the vastness of the subject and the local specificities, it would be difficult for the community institutions to respond adequately to the different needs, as the rdps are able to do.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i express the full support of the eldr group for the reports by mr marset and mr salafranca of the committee on foreign affairs of the european parliament on the eu-chile association agreement and the interregional agreement with mercosur. in both cases, as the two rapporteurs have rightly said in their respective explanatory statements, these new association agreements with chile and mercosur are currently the most important priority of the union's foreign policy towards latin america. the scale of economic relations between the european union and these countries, the need to strengthen the political role of the european union as an autonomous and authoritative actor at international level against the preponderant influence of the united states, the union's concrete support for all initiatives aimed at strengthening democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights in south america, make it imperative to move to a new phase with respect to the transitional framework agreement, which entered into force in 1995 for mercosur and in 1999 for chile. the european parliament, as the only democratically elected institution, cannot simply deliver an opinion; in the context of the next institutional reform, our assembly must be able to play a more decisive role by obtaining an explicit assent. it is an important moment, therefore, mr president, a moment not to be missed. as chairman of the delegation for relations with south america and mercosur, i can only call for europe and south america to continue their efforts to find a solution, regardless of the outcome of the multilateral negotiations of the world trade organisation. today europe still has the opportunity to build a special relationship with the countries of mercosur and chile, a relationship which will open a new chapter in relations with this land which is close to our continent for many reasons, a land in which we can still play a leading role. it is therefore necessary to give a new impetus to these global association agreements, which must be implemented without further loss of precious time and which - it is extremely important to stress this - must not only have an economic and commercial connotation, which is extremely important, but must also integrate the political and development cooperation aspects. these are the characteristics which make up the specificity of europe, our heritage, of which we are proud and which we cannot and must not renounce.

commission mr president, i should like to begin by thanking mr schwaiger and the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy for this very good report. it provides invaluable support for the european union's positions and i have noted, as has mrs mann, that it has aroused a great deal of interest in your ranks, which i welcome, at least judging by the number of amendments tabled. in substance, the considerations and concerns you express in this report are broadly in line with those of the commission and, of course, as many of you have said, go beyond the framework of the embodied agenda which is the current objective in geneva. like us, you want to frame trade liberalisation within a commonly accepted set of multilateral rules, you want to ensure greater transparency in the wto negotiating mechanisms, you want to improve the integration of developing countries into the multilateral system, you want to preserve our european model in the fields of agriculture and public health, you want to do the same in the fields of the environment or public services: this is basically a summary of the european union's agenda for the new round of negotiations. we have always considered that progress on the embodied agenda, which is the subject of your report, would be facilitated if it were part of a broader agenda. your report makes essentially the same argument, and in saying that i am responding to mr berthu's observation on this point. we are making very slow progress in geneva in what is really the preparation of a negotiation on agriculture and services, which we know very well that only a global cycle can really catalyze the start. this is where we are today. i shall try to comment briefly on the few subjects you have mentioned in your report, and in particular on agriculture, services and intellectual property, which you have mentioned extensively in your speeches. on agriculture, i have no quarrel with you. firstly, agenda 2000 is the framework for the union's negotiating position today. secondly, the needs of developing countries are at the forefront of our agricultural concerns, and that was the aim of the 'everything but arms' initiative, which i thank you for supporting. thirdly, you want to safeguard the european agricultural model, given its multiple functions in social, environmental and food matters, and this is something that franz fischler and i fully agree on. i can assure mr seguro and mr cunha that the promotion of non-commercial considerations in agriculture and the preservation of our own agricultural model remain key elements in our negotiating objectives. as regards the precautionary principle you have just stressed, i think it is clear that bse and more recently foot-and-mouth disease inevitably raise the question of whether we have the necessary multilateral framework to deal with these issues. it seems to us that at international level the sps agreement - sanitary and phytosanitary matters - is appropriate as it stands and therefore does not need to be renegotiated as such. however, the commission, like the council, shares the wish expressed by mr kreissl-dörfler to examine the precautionary approach in this sector. we have made proposals on this and we will continue to discuss this issue in the multilateral negotiations. this is part of our agenda. finally, on agriculture, and to answer mr clegg, there is indeed a 'peace clause', or more precisely a non-aggression clause, which excludes agriculture from the dispute over subsidies until the end of 2003. we believe that this non-aggression pact benefits everyone and that this is a reality that everyone should bear in mind when this issue is settled, that is, at the end of 2003. the 'peace clause' is not a sword of damocles over one head, which is europe's; if it is a sword of damocles, it hangs over several heads that are around the negotiating table in geneva. as far as services are concerned, our position is as follows. firstly, as the world's leading exporter and importer of services, we have aggressive commercial interests. secondly, we want to take development issues into account. thirdly, and i am responding to mr herzog and mrs fiebiger here, we are fully aware of the implications for public policy of a negotiation on services and therefore we fully agree with your recommendation on the specific nature of public service provision. the agreements concluded or to be concluded under the gats, that is to say the general agreement on trade in services, do not commit our states to privatization or deregulation. in the sectors related to the state and public services, health, education and culture, we must and will preserve our legislative prerogatives, our socio-cultural identity and our high levels of safety and consumer protection. as regards intellectual property, i must stress a point raised by mrs kinnock which is indeed in the news recently in a lawsuit between the south african pharmaceutical industry and the south african government. i will not comment on the case itself, because it is a sub judice and it is not the commission's custom to do so, but i would like to explain very clearly the commission's policy on the question of communicable diseases affecting developing countries. we've been working on this case since last summer. a high-level international round table was held in brussels in september and recommended a comprehensive approach based on three pillars: one, to strengthen support through development policy; two, to lower prices of essential medicines; and three, to resume high-level research on these medicines. following this round table, which brought together governments of the third world, international organizations and member states, as well as a number of non-governmental organizations, we have just adopted a specific action programme based on this approach, and i believe we are beginning to see the first tangible effects of this with a number of price reduction commitments by several pharmaceutical companies. what is the role of intellectual property in this context? we believe that this is a key area for stimulating innovation and research. that is what the gatt trips agreement says, but we are equally clear, mrs kinnock, that there are cases where exceptions to patent law are allowed, provided for in the intellectual property agreement. this is called compulsory licensing and is provided for in cases where public health or health emergency grounds justify these exceptions. the agreement allows and provides for this flexibility and our position on this point is the one i have been making public for several weeks: the whole agreement, nothing but the agreement. it is true that there is still no real international consensus on a balanced interpretation of these provisions, but we have committed ourselves to promoting this clear position: the preservation of intellectual property, but the maintenance and use of exceptions where they are provided for, both in the wto, in the wipo and elsewhere. i shall answer mrs mann in a second, at the risk of taking a little longer than the five minutes i was given. we have indeed begun to readjust our pre-seattle mandate in the direction of the concerns that have been expressed by a number of developing countries. we do not need, at this stage, a formal amendment to the mandate. we'll get to that when the time comes. on the part of the question she asked about the united states, it is true that i spent part of last week there. i come back with a rather positive feeling from the administration, but with this evidence, which i must reiterate to this house, that the united states' trade policy depends more on congress than on the administration. that is why i shall now turn to the institutional aspect of your report. we agree on the increased involvement of parliaments in wto discussions. as you know, we lost the battle of nice, which we fought almost alone, in terms of our internal procedures, and so we are now back to the spirit of the framework agreement on relations between parliament and the commission which we adopted in july 2000. i think that in this framework agreement we have everything we need to organise our cooperation and if we still have some problems on the part of the procedure which concerns the settlement of disputes, i am prepared to discuss them, provided, however, that the settlement of disputes is not a negotiation, it is not the creation of internal legislation, it is an executive prerogative. so, i am perfectly fine with discussing and informing, but let's not confuse, let's not confuse, management and dispute settlement with legislative prerogatives. the next step, ladies and gentlemen, is the qatar ministerial conference, from 9 to 13 november this year. it is clear that we will continue to work very hard with the committee responsible on the agenda and the progress we can make. i would stress that the time has now come to consider our practical arrangements for participation in qatar. i intend to follow the practice we had in seattle in terms of the composition of your own delegation, and i therefore count on the active presence of some and some of you to promote in qatar what clearly appears, from this report, to be our common objectives. the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. before i comment on the substance of the matter, let me express my sincere thanks to the rapporteur, mr daul, and also to the committee on agriculture and rural development and the committee on industry and budget, whose members were involved in the very detailed examination of the proposal for the reform of the sugar market regulation. the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. the commission considers that a fundamental reform of the sugar market organisation is necessary. but such a reform can only be justified on the basis of a thorough analysis. the commission has therefore commissioned two studies, the results of which are expected to be available in mid-2002. the first study examines the conditions of concentration and competition in the sugar sector, but not only in this sector but also in other major agricultural and food sectors. the second study will examine the various options for a fundamental reform of the common organization of the market in sugar. in the meantime, the commission proposes to extend the main mechanisms of the present sugar market organization for two marketing years. the total quota is to be reduced by 115,000 tonnes, equivalent to 50% of the structural surplus under the wto export restrictions. the storage reimbursement is to be abolished in order to increase competition and reduce the incentive to produce c sugar. this also means that the eaggf will save 300 million euro per year in expenditure. the obligation for producers to maintain minimum stocks should be abolished, as such stocks are no longer justified in the light of the actual supply situation in the union. finally, production refunds for sugar used in the chemical industry will be paid by the sector itself. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the amendments tabled by mr daul, in particular, are intended to extend the current sugar market arrangements for a period of five marketing years, without the amendments proposed by the commission, as provided for in amendments nos 2, 15-18, 22, 26, 29, 68, 69, 70 and 71. the commission can accept the extension of the current sugar market regime for a longer period than the proposed two years, but only if the other key elements of the commission's proposal are accepted. the commission cannot therefore accept a number of amendments for the following reasons. amendments nos 3, 4, 23, 24, 31 and 56 provide for the scope of the basic quotas and the estimated maximum supply requirements of the refining industry to be left unchanged. this cannot be accepted, because the reduction of at least part of the structural surpluses envisaged by the commission is indispensable to comply with our obligations under the wto. the commission is also unable to accept amendments nos 36, 45, 57, 60-62, 65, 67 and 72-75, because they will either increase the quotas even further or they will reduce or redistribute them very, very drastically. amendments nos 1, 5, 8, 12, 13, 19, 25, 27, 28, 30, 39 and 40 are aimed at maintaining the compensation for storage costs. i cannot accept this either, because the abolition of the compensation system will increase competition, remove the incentive to produce c sugar and also bring about considerable savings in budgetary resources. amendments nos 6, 21 and 40 provide for the maintenance of the minimum stocks. i cannot accept that either, because given the scale of the current surpluses, such an obligation is not justified. amendment no 40 calls for the continuation of the eaggf contribution to the financing of the production refund for the first 60 000 tonnes of sugar used in the chemical industry. i do not think that makes sense, because within a self-financing system exemptions are no longer justified. amendments nos 19, 14, 37 and 38 seek to restore the possibility for italy, spain and portugal to grant national aid. these national aids have been granted for too long and have caused significant distortions of competition. the commission has already decided to abolish them in 1995. it would therefore be a serious mistake if we were to reverse this decision of 1995 now. as regards amendments nos 33, 63, 64, 66, 76 and 77, i can assure you that the commission will make every effort to ensure the necessary coherence between the sugar proposals and development policy. there is therefore no need to do so in the proposals. amendments such as amendment no 20, which seeks to derogate from the concept of refinery for the azores, or amendment no 36, which seeks to adjust quotas to meet wto obligations, must also be rejected. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. in conclusion, i would like to thank you again for the work you have done and i hope that you will accept that the commission's willingness to go beyond extending the scheme for two years is also a significant step towards parliament.

behaviour. i said this very clearly and that is why we are applying pressure. there is the preparation of the wto action and there is the preparation of the temporary focused support mechanism. of course, and several speakers made this point, the system that we had in place until the end of last year was not really a good one. why? it was unhelpful vis-à-vis the korean threat and harmful to our own single market. the fact that it was unhelpful relative to the korean threat is more than demonstrated by the facts. the korean threat has persisted in spite of the contract-related operating aid. this has brought about major distortions within the single market and i found expressed in very different ways and words the concern about this adverse impact within the single market by a wide range of speakers from mr paisley to mr paasilinna. a second theme that clearly emerged is that there must be a number of measures to support shipbuilding in europe. i agree with the remarks to that effect made by several members and i would like to thank in particular mrs langenhagen for her kind words of appreciation. all the attention has been focused on contract-related aid which is no longer there. let us have a look at the list of those other forms of aid providing an incentive effect to eu shipyards which are still there after 1 january 2001 under council regulation 1540: aid for environmental protection in line with the general community guidelines for such aid, aid for research and development in line with the general community framework for such aid and i have already underlined this, aid for innovation which is not allowed in any other industrial sector except the automobile sector, regional investment aid for upgrading and modernising existing yards, but not involving the creation of new capacity, subject to certain caps below the normal regional aid ceilings, aid for rescue and restructuring in line with the general community guidelines for such aid, subject to certain stricter provisions, aid for partial and total closures contingent on genuine and irreversible reductions of capacity. in addition to these forms of aid, aid in the form of credit facilities for shipowners in accordance with oecd rules will also continue to be permitted. in addition, as i said, we are exploring the ways in which further, more intensive use of existing possibilities for aid could be obtained. that goes equally for national aid for research and development as well as possible community funding measures. we can conclude that the previous system was both unhelpful for its declared objective, that is korea, and vastly harmful within the single market. it had to be discontinued. it has been discontinued. this does not mean that the korean problem is being ignored. we are working very hard on it both in terms of a strong negotiating posture and in terms of preparing, if necessary, the introduction of a temporary defence mechanism which, being more focused, would also be more productive than the old-fashioned system that has been scrapped as it had to be.

mr president, i speak on behalf of the bonino list elected members to announce our vote against the kirkhope report and the french presidency's proposal, which is yet another repressive proposal on immigration. there is no doubt that the views expressed by mrs cerveira, mr sörensen and mr frahm, as well as by the last speaker, are sound, but to go into the substance of this report and this proposal we must take account of a matter of principle, namely that we have reached a parceling-out of the problem of immigration policies, because otherwise we would have to declare, or rather the council would have to declare, that it was not able to govern this phenomenon, that it was not able to foresee what could happen, that it was not able to prevent it and that it is still not able to provide government proposals. we are bombarded by proposals from the council and from individual member states which claim to want to build a common and comprehensive immigration policy while, on the other hand, integrating and harmonizing segments of repressive law, without defining in any way the contents and criteria which will - or rather should - form the basis of the future european immigration policy. we do not believe that this report and this proposal can in any way contribute to the development of an immigration policy. we think that it is precisely these proposals that contribute to events like the one in dover, where there were human casualties. this is how you help the mafia get rich.

- the next item is the report (a5-0077/2001) by mr wiebenga, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council directive on minimum standards for the provision of temporary protection in the event of a mass influx of displaced persons and on measures to ensure a balance between the efforts of the member states to welcome such persons and the consequences of such a welcome (com (2000) 303 - c5-0387/2000 - 2000/0127 (cns)).
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission proposal for a directive on temporary protection in the event of a mass influx of people is, in our view, part of a global vision of the establishment of a european asylum system. the european union must have an exceptional mechanism to respond quickly to massive influxes and to provide an immediate response to the need for protection of displaced persons, as we have seen in bosnia and kosovo. the purpose of this mechanism is to support the sustainable functioning of the asylum system while ensuring a coherent link with access to the normal asylum procedure and the geneva convention. we have built our proposal on the idea that temporary protection should be granted in the member states on the basis of a council decision, stating the situation of mass influx, and adopted by qualified majority. this protection is granted for a maximum of two years but the council may also, at any time, if the conditions are met, terminate it jointly. i believe that while the directive allows member states a certain flexibility in managing the asylum system during the period of temporary protection, it also guarantees absolute access to the asylum procedure for beneficiaries and, in any case, at the time when the period of temporary protection expires. finally, we have established not only fair rights for those who benefit from temporary protection but also principles governing returns. at tampere, the heads of state or government stressed the need to ensure solidarity between member states in the field of temporary protection. and we know how much the european parliament is committed to this principle. i think i discussed this with mr. nassauer over seven years ago. the commission has therefore tried to give concrete expression to the concept of community solidarity and to elaborate the content of article 63 (2) (b) on the balance of efforts and responsibilities between member states. solidarity is first of all a financial component, thanks to the links established with the european refugee fund. i know that the financial allocation of the fund is not very ambitious, but perhaps this is an area where we could work more reasonably by asking how the fund can contribute to strengthening financial solidarity. at the same time, and i should like to stress this, we have retained in this proposal the principle of the distribution of responsibilities in terms of the physical reception of refugees. this solidarity in the reception by the member states is expressed by the principle of double voluntariness. i understand mr von boetticher's problem and i even agree with his observation that there are difficulties. the idea of dual volunteering was born under the german presidency and has made its way. of course, this double voluntary nature presupposes the willingness of the member states to take in and also the willingness of the beneficiaries who are not yet in the territory of the member states. the decision to grant temporary protection therefore sets out from the outset the capacity of member states to take in new displaced persons or the exceptional reasons why they cannot take in new displaced persons. but i want to emphasize that these must be truly exceptional reasons. the basic idea is that the refusal to accept new refugees in the event of a decision to grant temporary protection must be entirely exceptional. in addition, the dual voluntary service introduces a system of transparency. and this system of transparency in decisions is essential, because peer pressure has a role to play: it must lead everyone to accept a joint effort in the field of reception, including physical reception of beneficiaries of temporary protection. i can't guarantee that the system will work. but we have tried to develop an instrument which guarantees both the principle of solidarity in physical reception and that of financial solidarity. i am very grateful to the members for their contribution to this debate. i would like to emphasize in particular the contribution of the rapporteur, mr wiebenga, whose report is excellent. i'm a little nervous today because you've taught me a lot about this subject and i feel like a student in front of a teacher. i'm a teacher by trade. so you know what i'm talking about. but i would like to say that we have taken very good note of all the amendments that have been proposed. i think that these amendments, including those on solidarity, are a source of inspiration for the few weeks of negotiations that await us in the council and which should lead to a final result in may - i hope we will achieve that at the may council. some of your amendments change the level of entitlement of beneficiaries and the commission remains very committed to a level that is fair and not subject to downward revision. as regards solidarity, we note the strengthening of certain provisions, particularly on reception between member states, and despite the sensitivity of this issue, we are doing our best to achieve a realistic, fair and, above all, feasible result. as long as the principle of double voluntariness is respected, certain amendments, if not in their exact form, at least in their spirit, could serve, as i have said before, to finalise the negotiations.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today's joint debate concerns four initiatives by member states relating to expulsion decisions, the powers of enforcement in the field of visa procedures and the control of schengen external borders and, finally, the right to move within the schengen area without frontiers. i shall begin with the aspects relating to the provisions which form part of the schengen framework. i would first of all like to congratulate mr deprez on his careful and thorough examination, particularly of the institutional relations in the area of the powers of implementation of the rules established by the council, powers which concern comitology as provided for in article 202 of the treaty of the communities. the commission is of the opinion that certain provisions contained in the common consular instruction, the common manual and the specifications of the schengen consultation network should be able to be amended, adapted or updated by a simplified method specific to comitology. we can therefore support the initiatives of the republic of finland and portugal, but we cannot support a key part of the proposed mechanism which reserves the implementing powers to the council without proving in detail that this is indeed a specific case of exception to the general rule laid down by the treaty. the commission agrees with the analysis and argumentation presented by mr deprez in his explanatory memorandum. the common consular instruction, the common manual and the specifications of the schengen consultation network have been incorporated as a legal basis in articles 62 and 67 of the treaty on european communities, i.e. title iv. title iv does not contain any institutional derogation from article 202 of the treaty. moreover, most of the implementing measures linked to these instruments are purely technical in nature. they are merely the practical formulation of decisions of a political nature adopted by the council in higher normative acts which are themselves governed by the relevant provisions of title iv. i therefore wish to express the commission's full satisfaction with the position expressed by parliament, which is in line with that of the european commission. and for the time being, the commission not only agrees with the rapporteur but also wants the rapporteur's arguments, which i hope parliament agrees with, and the commission's arguments to be heard and accepted by the council. if interpretation is different, other measures will probably be considered to respond, ... (applause)... measures which the commission and parliament can also share. the commission can support the objective of the portuguese proposal for a regulation on the period during which third country nationals who are exempt from the visa requirement may move within the territory of the member states. article 62 of the treaty calls on the council to adopt, within five years of the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, measures laying down the conditions under which nationals of third countries may move freely within the territory of the member states for a maximum period of three months. however, the treaty, and this is clearly in contradiction with the portuguese proposal, sets a maximum period of three months and is by no means limited to the third country nationals who are exempt from the visa requirement. i therefore agree with the rapporteur, mrs frahm, that it is not appropriate to deal with the situation of one category only, and it seems to me that it is obvious that the period of stay in the territory of the member states cannot be extended beyond three months, up to a total of six months, on the basis of reciprocity agreements alone. the commission understands, and one can probably easily share the reasoning behind the portuguese initiative, that the main aim is to enable the safeguarding of a number of existing bilateral agreements between member states and, for example, third countries such as the united states of america, canada, japan or australia.

- the next item is the report (a5-0070/2001) by mrs angelilli, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the initiative of the french republic and the kingdom of sweden with a view to adopting a council decision establishing a european crime prevention network (c5-0070/2000 - c5-0070/2000 - 2000/0824 (cns)).
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, all the studies and statistics on major social emergencies show that the right to security is one of the strongest demands of european citizens. crime, in its various forms, is rightly perceived by our citizens not only as a threat to their physical safety but also as a genuine, intolerable, ever-present threat to their freedom to move, to work and to live a normal life. this psychological unease has generated a growing distrust of institutions and a growing distrust of others. this feeling of insecurity affects just about everyone: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union. in this context it is often very difficult to draw a line between large-scale organised crime, large-scale crime and so-called micro-crime. this is particularly true in cities, and i am thinking here of the distribution and trafficking of drugs, for example. mr president, people used to ask us, first of all, for the timeliness of the repression of crime and the certainty of punishment for criminals. now the situation has changed: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to remind you of the increase in all crimes related to paedophilia and the sexual exploitation of women and children. prevention must therefore be understood - and is understood - as a guarantee of freedom, and citizens are asking us to commit ourselves to implementing all possible instruments to discourage the spread of criminal phenomena. i believe that the value of crime prevention has been repeatedly emphasized by this parliament, which has produced many acts in this direction, and that it has been explicitly and intelligently recognized in the treaty of amsterdam and then repeatedly, until the tampere council which explicitly proposed a strengthening of international cooperation on crime prevention through the establishment and establishment of a network between national authorities for crime prevention. this proposal was then welcomed by the french and swedish presidencies, which, through a proposal for a legislative initiative, intend to set up this information network, exchange experience and good practice to prevent crime; the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens and their metabolites is a very good one. it is therefore a question of studying criminal phenomena from their origins, following the great capacity of transformation and of true metamorphosis of crime to adapt also to forms of repression and thus to find new ways to assert themselves. in conclusion, it is a network of information and exchange of good practice. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think it is simply a matter of showing the people that europe is working to create a genuine area of freedom and justice. i thank all my colleagues for their cooperation and in particular mr terrón for the amendment which has enriched and made more complete the work that has been done.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all we must say that we share the spirit in which the commission has drawn up this communication on electoral assistance and monitoring, namely the principle that the promotion of genuine democracies is not only an ethical imperative but also a condition for sustainable development and lasting peace, it is a specific mandate of the union under the treaties, it is the foundation of our foreign policy. i would add that it is also something else: it is a long-term commitment, not a formal one, which cannot be confined to statements of principle but must be built up by consistent and concrete political action. this is the role of the european union and the european parliament in assisting and monitoring elections, if free elections are to be considered a necessary condition for democracy. two council regulations of 1999 provide the legal basis for transforming our role into a substantial commitment. how did you do that? a coherent policy strategy is needed. so far we have collected eight years of absolutely generous assistance and election monitoring interventions, often with excellent results: i am referring to zimbabwe and russia. but these were occasional interventions, and we welcome the commission's communication, which is intended to give us a coherent political strategy. another necessary step is to extend this strategy to all phases of intervention, in the monitoring that precedes and accompanies elections, because the democratic process is a process that is not completed only on the day of the vote but in the proper link between electoral support and development aid policies, in an organized relationship with international organizations, with ngos and with civil society, according to mechanisms that are not those of the delegation, on which we have often relied, but rather mechanisms of genuine political consultation. the contributions which our report has tried to offer: the role of parliament first. this parliament can under no circumstances - and certainly not on this particular occasion - be considered a notary, called upon to ratify an electoral process or the quality of an electoral process. our legitimacy, our function, is political in nature and our presence in the monitoring missions of the union - precisely because of our political function - can be an added value for the european union. it is therefore useful for the european parliament to be present at all stages, including those preceding the monitoring of the elections in the strict sense. it is desirable - where the conditions are right - that the head of the eu mission be a member of parliament. we have had some excellent experiences, though. i am thinking of the case of my former colleague mr schori, who was head of the mission in zimbabwe. the role and political visibility must be won on the ground, and i believe that they are an asset not only for this parliament but for the whole of the european union. another key point: institutional coordination between the european parliament, the commission and the council is needed. we have thought of proposing a permanent consultation mechanism, which we believe is preferable to an interinstitutional agreement, which is more burdensome and requires much more time, management and implementation. we have considered, following the suggestions of some colleagues, a six-monthly calendar which would allow us to keep a constant watch on what is happening, bearing in mind that the accelerations which political history is currently producing are very violent. we thought we would suggest that the commission should set up an electoral service with sufficient staff. our amendment specifically calls for a number of amendments which are commensurate with the task which the commission will have to face. we believe that the criteria for the european union's commitment should be different and more flexible. first elections and regional elections may not be sufficient parameters to understand when it is appropriate to intervene: we are also aware that the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european parliament is represented in the european parliament. there is certainly a need for flexibility in evaluation standards; the european union is not only a political body, but also a political body, and it is a political body, and it is a political body. all this is not rigidity, it is rigor: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the strategy is made up of rules and objectives. in conclusion, we believe - as does the commission - that democracy is a process and not a choice of a day. we know that in many countries, true democracy begins to be built on election day and beyond. we would like to continue to do so by making available our resources, which will not only be economic resources but also our democratic memory and our political commitment.

are of deep concern to all of us. the regrettable violence in recent days and its causes underline the present risks to the political and economic stability that are so important for ukraine, as our common strategy makes clear. the situation is particularly worrying, given that ukraine will share such a long border with the european union after the first round of enlargement. ukraine wants to draw closer to the european union and its neighbours. we welcome that. but, for that to happen, ukraine must be able to demonstrate its willingness and ability to live up to basic values, european values, values which are also set out in our partnership and cooperation agreement. that means strengthening the rule of law. it means making progress in the fight against corruption. it means adopting market-oriented legislation. as the report points out, ukraine has, alas, lost a lot of time, but it is a country with a vast potential in terms of economic and human resources. with the fore not just the issue of journalistic freedom but of a pluralistic society and the way executive power is exercised in ukraine. the house will recall that in early december, shortly after the kuchma the rapporteur. - mr president, the green paper on the environmental problems of pvc, which we are discussing today, was presented by the commission in july 2000, in line with the provisions of the end-of-life vehicle directive, which introduces a new method involving the responsibility of producers for the entire life cycle of the product, from its conception to its disposal. this approach, which aims to encourage manufacturers to design safer products and materials and, above all, to make them more easily recyclable, is also the underlying idea of the green paper on pvc. although it does not directly address the question of the production or use of pvc, it clearly raises a number of questions concerning the disposal of waste, which end up directly affecting the product itself. i want to be clear on this point. although pvc has been the subject of intense debate in recent years and some of its characteristics, such as its high chlorine content, make it particularly difficult to manage once it has become waste, my report does not seek to blame it on other plastics. in my report i have in fact explicitly asked the commission to address the specific problems of this material within a wider strategy for plastics and to address the problem of separate collection as soon as possible in a continental perspective. i also asked for this measure to be extended to all plastics, to avoid eco-marketing. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. but it 's not enough . firstly, because parliament stated in its resolution of july 1997 that it was no longer prepared to accept any voluntary agreement which fell outside the community legal framework. secondly, because the objectives set out in this agreement are frankly insufficient, hardly measurable and therefore hardly controllable. but there is one very important feature of the agreement: the commission's task is to bring together the vast majority of the actors involved in the production, processing and recycling processes, as well as the representatives of the trade unions, around a table to seek common strategies and to define proposals to change the current situation. this will of industry is a positive element and we must not dissipate it in the fire of legislating everything. i have therefore asked the commission to come forward as soon as possible with a proposal for a legislative framework which can serve as a reference for all future voluntary agreements. i have therefore also proposed a new form of legislation which would provide for the adoption of legislation whose entry into force would, however, remain conditional on the failure to achieve the objectives set for enterprises. i am convinced that the implementation of truly sustainable development cannot be achieved without dialogue and cooperation with business. there are many points in my report which i would like to mention, but i will confine myself to two: the elimination of hazardous substances, cadmium, lead and phthalates in the first place, and the multi-pronged strategy for the disposal of pvc. as regards the first point, i would just like to stress how important the phasing out of these substances is, in the immediate future, for the health of european citizens but perhaps even more so for the protection of the natural environment. finally, on the subject of waste disposal, i would like to say that one of the characteristics which make pvc strong, namely its resistance to time, also makes the question of its disposal very complicated. what i have proposed is to tackle the problem multilaterally: first, increase recycling rates starting from certain applications such as window frames, large pipes and coatings by implementing closed-loop recovery systems; secondly, limiting the incineration of pvc to the new generation of plants, which are able to comply with the new community legislation and apply the 'polluter pays' principle; thirdly, to deposit what remains in the landfill, taking account, again, of the new legislation which will come into force from 2002. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to thank all the members who, through the amendments tabled in the committee on the environment, have helped to improve my report. i think the text voted in committee is really balanced: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full.

mr president, commissioner, i think that the speeches i have heard, and in particular those of mr galeote, risk creating a misunderstanding. it would be wrong for parliament to ask the commission to strengthen the golden share, to strengthen the special powers of the state in order to somehow preserve the liberalised markets from being occupied by monopolists with large liquid assets. and i think that would be a misunderstanding. i think, however, that parliament must speak out strongly against the golden share and against all the instruments which prevent the formation of a real and dynamic internal market in the sectors which have traditionally been state-owned in europe in recent decades. i speak for the italian radicals. in 1997 we presented a referendum in italy against the 1994 law which introduced the special powers, the golden share, in italy. in that referendum, 80 per cent of the voters - almost ten million italians - said yes, they demanded, as we wanted, the abolition of those rules which prevented and prevent the formation of a genuine competitive market in the capital market for privatised companies. unfortunately, as often happens, those votes have been thrown away, destroyed in a reality, the italian one, where the constitution and the citizens' pronouncements often become scrap paper. in 1998 the government of romano prodi, now president of the commission, was the subject of an infringement procedure by the then internal market commissioner, professor mario monti, against the use of this golden share. in 1999 a decree was issued which amended the italian golden share without changing its substance. i believe that the articles of the treaty should be sufficient to prevent a state-owned monopoly company from buying a company on the liberalized market. this is abuse of a dominant position, this is state aid. there is no need to provide that companies have the golden share to prevent them from being bought by a public company in a different member state. otherwise - as is the case regularly - this alibi actually gives national governments and the majority parties a veto power over the free market for publicly owned companies. the financial markets are prevented from determining the best, most efficient and optimal allocation of control and therefore of the management of companies in very important, crucial, strategic sectors for europe: we are talking about telecommunications, and energy in particular. with the golden share, the companies that are put on the market bring less money to the public budgets because you buy a company that someone, without having even a penny invested, can decide the strategic choices: you lose money by privatizing the golden share. the golden share also risks nationalizing private savings: citizens, investors buy companies that remain under the heel of the state, governments and therefore parties. the golden share creates an extraordinary conflict of interest between the state, which remains the manager and in some way the owner of the liberalized companies, and the state, which must instead be only the regulator to guarantee competition and protect the interests of the citizens. this is one of the ways in which the european states, in some countries - i am thinking of italy - are in fact still managing important parts of the country's economy and are preventing companies in these sectors - telecommunications, energy - from being able to compete efficiently in competitive markets, companies able to withstand international competition. the fact that enel in italy, deutsche post in germany or france télécom exploit monopoly positions to occupy liberalised markets in other countries must be combated as a dominant position, as state aid, but it cannot be used as an alibi for the countries opening up the market to retain power in the company which is to be privatised. the golden share has in fact been and continues to be an obstacle to the creation of truly european public service companies. the golden share thus removes companies from the dynamics of the market and governments continue to interfere, they continue to think they know better who should buy a company, thus responding to logics that are not the most efficient logics of the market and thus penalizing citizens. we should not think that governments should use the golden share as a shield to prevent companies from being bought on the market, or to steer the purchase of privatised companies towards friendly groups, because these things then, in the long run, lead, as happens, to markets with little competition. it is for these reasons that i raise some doubts about the resolution we are going to vote on thursday. i believe that this parliament must speak out loudly, perhaps avoiding compromise, and fighting between the statists and the liberalisers. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. there is a risk that the state-owned monopolies that still exist will dominate the liberalised markets in europe, a risk represented by the abuse of dominant positions and state aid: that's what you're supposed to bet on.
