the council. the union considers that a culture of impunity cannot be tolerated, especially in the case of serious violations of international law such as genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. when national courts are unable or unwilling to act, the international community has the ultimate responsibility to ensure that justice is done. the union therefore considers it necessary to establish the international criminal court in the near future in order to increase respect for international humanitarian law and human rights. by abolishing impunity, the court will strengthen the rule of law and justice and help to consolidate world peace. the union strongly advocates the establishment of the international criminal court in the near future. with this objective in mind, the union launched an international effort to encourage as many states as possible to sign the rome statute before the deadline of 31 december 2000. the union has also committed itself to contributing to the signature or ratification of the charter by the countries associated with it and offers its expertise in this field to all interested countries. the union is also determined to support the effective establishment of the court. the union expects the rome statute to enter into force in the near future, once the required 60 ratifications have been obtained, including by all the member states of the union. italy, france, belgium, spain, germany, austria, luxembourg and finland have already ratified the rome statute. the other member states have all started the ratification process and for the majority it should be completed soon, depending on national procedures. in this context, it should be noted that the implementation of the rome statute in national legislation is a demanding task, which in some cases even requires constitutional amendment. the situation regarding the ratification of the rome statute in the union is regularly discussed by the presidency at meetings of the council working party on international law.

mr president, commissioner, mr lehne's proposal for a directive is indeed a very substantial and well-articulated one, but i would like to draw attention to three points in it: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat money laundering, such as the extension of the scope of the criminal offences required for money laundering, the remote identification of customers, and the confidentiality of the data received. the first point is that the joint text proposes a definition of organised crime, extending the definition of money laundering to include related offences. this enlargement is certainly to be welcomed. the subsequent extension to other offences - fraud and corruption, at least in serious cases - cannot be accepted, since the existence of seriousness is clear to the extent that these offences affect the financial interests of the european union, if they therefore fall within the scope of article 1 (e) of the second protocol to the convention on the protection of the european communities' financial interests. the determination of seriousness is in fact based on a not particularly clear reference. second point: the text again proposes a procedure for remote customer identification, after the provision for a specific procedure, which was complex and difficult to implement, had been appropriately deleted from the text of the previous common position. the new wording seems excessive, whereas it should be left to the individual countries to determine the rules to be applied in relation to the different practices in use. the concern here is that specific and binding european rules may emerge, linked to the application of rigid procedures which are difficult to implement. third point: confidentiality of the data received. all too often, data provided on suspicious transactions are not given sufficient confidentiality, with obvious danger to the supplier. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the information on suspicious transactions is not disclosed to third parties. in this connection, excessive data passes for information purposes, for example to banks, intermediate bodies, professional categories, and representatives of orders, should be eliminated.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0118/2001), drawn up on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a regulation of the european parliament and of the council laying down rules for the prevention, control and eradication of certain transmissible spongiform encephalopathies [14780/1/2000 - c5-0048/2001 - 1998/0323 (cod)) (rapporteur: mrs roth-behrendt).
commission. – tonight could signal the end of two years of hard negotiations between parliament, the council and the commission on the legal framework to combat transmissable spongiform encephalopathies. this is the first major piece of legislation to be adopted following the introduction of co-decision in relation to veterinary matters impacting on public health set out in the amsterdam treaty. it is both ironic and appropriate that it relates to bse, as it was the bse crisis which led to the introduction of co-decision in this area of community activity. i would like to pay particular thanks to mrs roth-behrendt, the rapporteur, for her tireless work over the years in pursuing a coherent community approach to the control of tses. a great many of the key provisions of the regulation under discussion result directly, or indirectly, from her personal commitment to putting in place a very strong framework to protect our citizens from the threat from tses and this is an objective i fully share and i want to join with mr phillip whitehead in wishing mrs roth-behrendt the very best for her stay in hospital over the next couple of days. when we started our work on this proposal in late 1998, the majority of member states considered themselves free of bse. this was still the case in may 2000 when the initial opinion of parliament, largely endorsed by the commission, was adopted: the ensuing negotiations with council remained blocked as council could not agree on the proposed central role of a scientific assessment for the bse classification of countries. however, after the adoption of new emergency measures for the community-wide removal of specified risk materials and the introduction of rapid tests for bse, a compromise on the legal framework came within reach. the provision for such a large-scale screening allowed council to agree to classification by the commission on the basis of the scientific steering committee opinion provided it was verified by that screening. at its first reading, parliament proposed verification of the scientific risk assessment by statistically valid large-scale screening. in its amended proposal, the commission proposed large-scale screening as a transitional measure for the changeover from the current uniform srm rules to the classification-based rules of the regulation. these two elements allowed the council to come to a political agreement on its common position in december 2000. apart from leading to the council common position, the start of the large-scale screening at the end of 2000 had yet another effect: within days germany detected bse cases amongst healthy slaughter animals. around the same time, spain and italy detected their first cases and a number of bse cases detected in france also rose steadily. consumer confidence dropped to a record low. faced with this crisis, the position of council, parliament and the commission drew closer. aware of the urgency of the matter and the need for a proper legal framework, in particular in relation to bse eradication and imports from third countries, an informal trialogue took place prior to the council adopting its common position. during this trialogue, a very solid basis for agreement between the three institutions emerged. these were hard but very constructive negotiations proving that the three institutions can work together very constructively on key issues related to public health. the council agreed to additional demands from parliament increasing the number of tested animals. the commission committed itself to introduce all new measures, adopted under safeguard procedures after the common position, into the regulation. the commission also committed itself to take without delay all necessary initiatives under comitology after entry into force of the regulation. consequently, the common position of council was adopted by unanimity and endorsed by the commission. this compares with the very sharp differences in approach in the past on bse-related issues. i would finally like to remind parliament of its resolution of 16 november 2000 on bse and the ban on animal proteins in animal feed. in this resolution, parliament asked for several protection measures. these included a temporary suspension of the use of meat and bone meal, increasing testing in all member states and rules for the control of scrapie. the tse regulation, in its current form, provides the framework and, in many cases, the detailed rules for these measures. further amendments at second reading would, however, delay formal action upon this resolution. i trust that this house agrees with me on the need for the proper legal basis to be operational without delay and from what some of the speakers have already said, there appears to be a measure of agreement on that issue. the debates we have had in parliament on this subject since last november make this only too evident. it is vital, therefore, that this regulation enters into force as soon as possible. the commission is therefore prepared to consider only amendments which would substantially improve the text or correct important weaknesses. neither of the two proposed amendments falls, in my view, into these categories. i cannot accept amendment no 1 for reasons of substance also. this amendment, which had already been rejected in committee during first reading, proposes the right for bse-free member states to take unilateral action at their own discretion against the import of any live animal. this is against the principles of laying down community rules. it is also superfluous, as one of the main objectives of the regulation is to create harmonised rules for the marketing of animals in view of bse status. nor can i accept amendment no 2 as it makes the establishment of an epidemiological picture of all member states more difficult. this does not however prejudge future initiatives from the commission on the basis of this regulation in the light of the experience gained particularly on the aid structure of the cases detected by the current screening, and this can be done by comitology. over 1.3 million tests were carried out on healthy animals aged over 30 months in the first three months of this year. these are in addition to the tests on fallen animals and at-risk animals. we are rapidly acquiring a hugely improved picture of the true incidence of bse in the community. if i see any reason in the light of this evidence to reduce the current age of testing, i will not hesitate to take the necessary proposals. i would also add, in this respect, that research continues on more sensitive tests than are currently available. in conclusion, we are now very close to putting in place the proper legislative framework for the control of tses. it has taken much time and effort, but the text of the common position following considerable input of all three institutions provides a coherent set of rules and procedures for the future. may i just comment briefly on some of the contributions made by some members a moment ago. this particular proposal is compatible with the oie international standards. furthermore, let me say that i greatly welcome the views expressed by mrs paulsen when she made reference to the proposals on animal feed and, in particular, the bi-product legislation. let me comment on mrs auroi's remarks on the testing of sheep: i should point out that i am bringing a proposal on random testing of sheep very shortly. in the draft decision, we have foreseen as a first step 170 000 tests on sheep from october 2000 for the first year.

- the next item is the report (a5-0125/2001) by mrs jillian evans, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on animal health conditions governing the non-commercial movement of pet animals (com (2000) 529 - c5-0477/2000 - 2000/0221 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, i wish to thank the rapporteur, mrs evans, and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy for their report on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the animal health requirements applicable to non-commercial movements of pet animals. this assembly is well aware of the importance of this issue which concerns all european citizens who are travelling either for holidays or for longer stays with their pets and do not want to leave them behind. i do not mean that citizens cannot today travel with their pets, but the different regulations applicable in the member states to movements inside the community, as well as movements from third countries, are definitely difficult to understand and somewhat discouraging. it is therefore time to establish a common set of rules applicable to the entire european community, because this issue is directly linked to the free movement of european citizens when they own a pet. the centre of gravity of this proposal is of course the rabies risk linked to movements of cats and dogs, the two major domestic carnivore species involved in the transmission of this fatal disease. on this essential issue, the proposal is based on the recommendations of the international zoo sanitary code, on reports of the scientific veterinary committee and on the conclusions on panels of international experts consulted on the assessment of the rabies risk linked to movements of domestic carnivores. i am most satisfied that the report supports the commission's general approach on this fundamental question of public health. there is unanimous agreement on the safety of the technical provisions relating to the management of the rabies risk, even if a few points of disagreement remain and may need some further clarification. allow me now to address in detail the amendments proposed in the report. i will begin with the amendments the commission cannot accept. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 5, 12 and 13 relating to the legal base of the proposal. the report concludes that article 152(4)(b) of the treaty is sufficient because the essential aim of the proposal is to protect public health. this is indeed true at this stage, nevertheless the commission considers that measures relating strictly to animal disease with no impact on public health could be necessary in the future, and a double legal base with article 37 is therefore necessary. i was asked by one member earlier if we have we enough legal base or enough information to prevent other diseases in animals. this is one of the reasons why article 37 is included as a legal base. i am aware from other proposals brought before parliament that there is a general reluctance in parliament and in the environment committee to support article 37 as a legal base for provisions in conjunction with article 152, probably because article 37 is not a co-decision article. but i would ask parliament to reconsider its view in relation to this particular amendment and consider the question in the light of the need for animal health considerations being relevant, as one member mentioned. hence the need for article 37 rather than article 152. the commission cannot accept amendment no 7 because it goes far beyond the scope of the proposal which is movement between member states and from third countries. this amendment provides an obligation for all member states in relation to the generalisation of electronic identification of all cats and dogs and the establishment of a database to trace any stray or lost animal. on the classification of third countries, the commission proposal adopts the same conditions for imports from certain third countries whose rabies status is equivalent to that of the member states as those which apply for internal movements. amendment no 10 suggests imposing on this category of third countries the criteria provided in the international zoo sanitary code for the recognition of a rabies-free country. this is not consistent with the conditions applicable to internal movements. a number of member states are not rabies-free countries under this definition, even if rabies in domestic animals is under control on their territory. this would be a discrimination which is not scientifically sound, and therefore amendment no 10 is not acceptable. finally, the commission cannot accept amendment no 14. this amendment would delete "ferret" from the list of species which may be moved inside the community with no veterinary conditions. the commission proposal was based on a risk analysis which concluded that this species has no significance in the epidemiology of rabies in europe. i understand the special concerns with regard to this species because it is a carnivore and does bite, but the simple deletion from the list in annex i, part b is unfair to this species, as the only reason is that it belongs to the carnivore genus. i should say to mr davies that i have discovered quite a lot more about ferrets than i knew yesterday and some of my meetings during the day today, including some of the exotic entertainments engaged some member states, might account for some of interest that mr davies supports. i would have been more open to the creation of a new category for ferrets with the requirement for vaccination, which is possible, but no post vaccination test can be foreseen. the amendments submitted by the rapporteur and committee, but rejected, were heading in that direction and would have reached, in my opinion, a solution acceptable to everybody. the commission can accept six amendments: amendment no 4 concerning the commitment for the future on a revision of the regulations applying to commercial trade species; amendments nos 8, 9 and 15 which bring clarification to the proposal and amendment no 11 relating to a communication on this issue to the public by member states. it was with great interest that i discovered in amendment no 6 a real pro-active position in favour of a generalisation, in the short term, of the electronic identification complying with iso standard of animals moved between member states or from third countries. therefore i can accept this amendment. in summary, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 12, 13 and 14. on the other hand, the commission can accept amendments nos 4, 8, 9, 11, 15 and 6. to conclude, i wish to once again thank mrs evans for her excellent report and her support to this important proposal.
- thank you, commissioner byrne. - thank you very much. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11 a.m.
- the next item is the report (a5-0119/2001) by mrs doyle, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the availability of veterinary medicinal products (com (2000) 806 - c5-0105/2001 - 2001/2054 (cos)).
commission. – on behalf of the commission, i would like to thank mrs doyle and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy for this report. there are many different perspectives to be reconciled. unfortunately, no satisfactory solution has yet been found. the communication aimed to present the commission's view on the problem of veterinary medicine availability and noted with satisfaction that the committee and the rapporteur share the general concerns of the commission on this issue. this communication clearly does not bring a direct solution; however, it outlines the options for further action in both the long and short term. it is important to point out that the current veterinary and pharmaceutical legislation provides a framework designed to ensure, amongst other things, the optimal protection of consumer health. this legislation is currently being reviewed. this review will provide a timed framework to further address the availability problem for all animal species concerned in a global manner. any proposal for change to ease the access to the market of veterinary and pharmaceutical products, or to facilitate the use of certain medicines by veterinarians, will be in the interest of animal health and welfare. however, it goes without saying that any of these proposals will have to be compatible with the objective of consumer health protection. with this end in mind, i am cooperating with colleagues, mr byrne, in particular, and i expect the legislative proposal to be finalised within a few months. this will allow an in-depth discussion with the european parliament and the council on all relevant matters. obviously, these legislative changes will take some time. the commission has therefore also announced its approval of the principle of extrapolating maximum residue limits established for some species to other species. such an exploration would only be possible under certain conditions. while we recognise that extrapolating maximum residue limits cannot be a global solution, we believe that it can represent a practical improvement of the situation, particularly in the short term. however, it also raises the complex technical issues, in particular the link with the possible illegal use of certain substances. thus, a need for appropriate analytical methods of control will have to be considered. i am hoping that the further work in close cooperation between the european parliament, the council and the commission will lead to a balanced solution, offering a framework for genuine benefit to animal health, while maintaining a high level of consumer protection.

- madam president, we are in the final act of this important directive. the agreement reached in the conciliation committee is a recognition of the excellent work of the rapporteur and the atmosphere of cooperation that has developed in our assembly on this subject, which is so sensitive to european citizens. the text we are about to vote on is a considerable improvement on the text proposed by the commission, but even more so on the existing situation. for the first time, the rules for harmonizing the internal market took the health of european citizens more into account than the interests of the large manufacturers. this text is, in the final analysis, an important example of how the european union intends to respond to the increasingly urgent demand of citizens to see their health protected. we hope that this example will soon be followed in other areas, such as food safety. without going back to the content of the agreement, i would like to stress two qualifying points. the first is the extension of the obligation to apply the maximum levels of tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide to cigarettes intended for third country markets. this measure was the focus of the debate in the committee on the environment first and then in the plenary. some people argued that the union would not contribute to the improvement of world health by this act, and that it would protect the interests of exporting companies. others preferred to affirm the principle that what is harmful to community citizens is also harmful to third-country nationals, but also supported the need for a transitional period long enough to give operators in the sector the opportunity to reconvert. we believed in this second possibility and the text adopted in conciliation has proved us right. the second key point concerns the definitive regulation of substances added to tobacco products. in fact, in addition to being used to characterize the taste and aroma of a particular product, these substances are also used to increase the dependence of smokers. our directive will not only require manufacturers and importers of tobacco products to disclose the exact composition of the product they are selling, but also to provide justification for the presence of each individual ingredient. the commission will also have to submit a proposal for a common positive list of authorised ingredients by 2004. this is not a matter of secondary measures. together with the banning of descriptors and the increase in the area devoted to medical warnings, these measures can make a real contribution to the fight against smoking.

some debate as to whether they should be more balanced or not. mrs weiler, for example, referred to the social aspects, raising the question of whether they are sufficiently covered. in my view, we detail, but i do not think that the broad economic policy guidelines should play the role that the broad employment guidelines do. it is also true that in the current year the new model established at the lisbon summit and the debate in the european council on two key issues for the elaboration of the broad economic policy guidelines have meant a reduction in the time needed to draw up this document, which has also affected the european parliament. mr von wogau, and also the head of the employment committee, complained about the lack of time for a more in-depth debate on the various issues. it is true that we shall try to overcome these difficulties as far as possible, but it is equally true that it will be difficult, given the commitments we have made, since they all limit the time available for the subsequent debate. let us now get to the main issues. but first i would like to make a small comment on the coordination of economic policies. mr gasòliba i böhm has referred to it, and mrs berès, mrs doyle in a very special way, and a few other speakers. we believe that the coordination of economic policies must be done primarily through the broad economic policy guidelines, which are the key document for coordination. it is true that this document must take account of the stability pact, but in no case can it be regarded as the only element sufficient for economic policy coordination to proceed properly. this is the importance of the document we are discussing today. in the broad guidelines we have to include all the elements. it is true that the broad economic policy guidelines and coordination will be discussed - coordination will be discussed in greater depth later - and this will open up new possibilities for future corrections. i would like to stress, however, a point which has given rise to some comments by mrs berès and mrs doyle on the specific irish problem. firstly, to talk about sanctions in the irish case - although i understand that it is a journalistically attractive language - does not correspond to reality. what the council has adopted (not the commission) has been a decision on a specific recommendation, for lack of coherence with accepted budgetary policy, concerning the budgetary policy pursued by a member state. the von wogau report refers to the consideration of the greater or lesser impact of a country which is part of monetary union with regard to the measures it adopts. in my view, such an option poses obvious risks. of course, if only the large countries are obliged to comply with the broad economic policy guidelines, i think we would end up introducing major contradictions into our model. the european model is characterized precisely by the fact that all countries, large and small, have the same rights and obligations, and i believe that we must be consistent with this general principle. as regards the major challenges, our challenge and approach in this case has been clear. we are talking about three types of options: first, in the short term, to maintain economic expansion; in the medium term, to increase the growth potential; and, in the long term, to tackle ageing. i shall briefly touch on these issues. as far as economic expansion is concerned, our forecasts are more optimistic than perhaps others. we are quite familiar with the european situation and we think that the robust development of domestic demand allows us to be relatively optimistic, and that does not mean that we should not follow with concern the uncertainties arising in other economies and some recent data - to which you have referred - from the us economy. these are obviously facts to bear in mind. in any case, our starting point was a v recovery of the us economy and we hope to get to that situation. the big question is whether the european economic situation, affected by the external situation, can justify a change in economic policies from what we have applied so far. in the commission's view, no. we believe that the still high growth that is going to be produced in europe should continue to allow us to bet on the fundamental idea of going ahead with the consolidation of budget deficits and the reduction of public debt. i do not agree with those who say that these factors do not have a positive impact on employment: it is enough to look at the evolution of employment in the european union over the last few years to see that this policy has produced good results, as has a wage policy that has been consistent with growth and inflation in recent years. i think we have made a lot of progress in reducing unemployment over the last two years and we need to keep going in the same direction. as regards our medium-term objective of increasing growth potential, we all want to achieve the best possible results in terms of economic growth and employment. and we believe that it is essential, of course, to improve the working capacity and the activity rate of our populations, but for this it is absolutely essential to continue the process of structural reforms, both of the markets and of the labour system. we are not forgetting, of course - and some of you have referred to this - the transition to the knowledge economy and the fundamental need to invest in r & d, in new technologies, but also in the public sector. the commission's position has always been very clear on this point. we believe that investment in the public sector is appropriate, it is coherent, but it has to be compatible with our overall budgetary obligations. finally, i would like to make a specific reference to the need to pay greater attention to sustainable development and, specifically, to the environment. in this year's broad guidelines there is a specific reference to this point and, no doubt, next year, after the gothenburg summit, we will include additional elements on this point. the commission is still of the opinion that the problem of the ageing population is a key and fundamental issue which ultimately affects the debt levels of the various member states and is therefore something we must consider. we are aware that the problem is not solved solely and exclusively by reducing public debt, and this is a positive step. we believe that more needs to be done, both in terms of pension systems and in terms of increasing the rate of activity in the different countries. we are not, of course, talking about a problem of broad year-to-year guidelines, but a medium- and long-term problem, but we must also include it in the specific references in the various annual reports. these are the elements i wanted to comment on today, thanking parliament and mr von wogau for their contribution and hoping that the final result that the broad guidelines will bring us is what we all want: greater growth in europe, more sustained growth, growth that is also produced by a scheme of coordination of economic policies which, of course, respects the capacity for national responsibility that each of us has, in accordance with what is established in the treaty.

(fr) mr president, by introducing rules for the recycling of waste electrical and electronic equipment, the european parliament is making a major contribution to the environmentally friendly nature of this industry. in the end, it was the environment that won the battle between the supporters of an innovative industry in electrical and electronic products and traditional industrialists who were putting the brakes on to delay the date of taking on the recycling of this waste. while congratulating the rapporteur on his choice of the clean products route, it is regrettable that the commission has not dealt with electrical and electronic waste and the related chemicals at the same time. the report also calls for the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the directive is implemented in a uniform manner. despite this distorted note, the great innovation of the report is the individual responsibility of the producers, whereby each is financially responsible for his own product, both for products already on the market and for future products. the report gives a boost to environmental concerns and demonstrates the growing political awareness of the danger of industrial waste, especially electrical and electronic waste, proliferating. in the end, everyone will benefit from this forced passage: the commission has also proposed a number of measures to improve the quality of the environment. the report by mr florenz on waste electrical and electronic equipment has benefited from significant environmental guarantees, which demonstrate that european industry must be designed for citizens and policies by fostering an ecological culture.
(fr) the european parliament discussed in strasbourg a report by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy on waste electrical and electronic equipment. the proposed directive provides that the producer or the first importer is responsible for the electrical and electronic waste, which amounts to 16 kilograms per inhabitant in the 15 member states of the european union, a quantity which is expected to double over the next 12 years. because of the specific nature of the situation, luxembourg has almost no producers of its own, but mainly importers. the distribution of products is often organised in such a way that a general importer is responsible for the belgium-luxembourg region. this importer is generally located in belgium and not in luxembourg. if belgium is to hold only one general importer responsible, luxembourg will have to hold a multitude of shops to which that general importer supplies its products responsible. on the other hand, parallel imports of products outside established distribution channels reach a much higher percentage in luxembourg than in other countries. it follows that in luxembourg the commercial enterprises held liable are generally small and in any case smaller than those abroad. this specificity of luxembourg means that particular attention must be paid to the administrative simplification of the management of the financing systems for recycling and recovery to be implemented. therefore, in some areas, it is preferable that the directive should leave sufficient freedom to the member states to develop appropriate solutions. shops, especially in urban areas, often lack a warehouse to store large quantities of waste. recovery by traders should therefore not become compulsory but remain voluntary. if shops cannot take back waste, other systems, such as recycling areas, must be made available to consumers. the cost of compulsory collection would in fact be excessive for many activities. the directive also covers the financing of the recycling of electrical and electronic products already on the market at the time of its entry into force, some of which no longer have any manufacturers. in fact, some appliances, such as refrigerators or televisions, have an average life span of 20 years. the directive should leave it to the member states to choose the means of financing the recycling of such equipment. this would make it possible to agree with the state on measures to encourage consumers, for example, to hand over free of charge the waste they currently store in their cellars. this type of action has been carried out in countries which already have a free collection system. the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the mutual recognition of final judgments in criminal matters raises many problems which we have tried to tackle and solve in the best possible way, thanks also to the contribution of the committee on legal affairs and internal market affairs and its rapporteur, mr joachim wuermeling. this report has not been amended, and that is a testament to the coherence we have found in the proposal. i hope that the solutions proposed will find a broad consensus in parliament to give more weight to the arguments of those in the council and commission of the european union who share them. a common area of justice will only make sense if, within it, the decisions of the courts of one of the member states will have effect in any other member state. in practice, this means that a final decision issued by the competent authority of another member state is enforced in one member state. until now, recognition of judgments between the different states has been carried out through the application mechanism, a slow and complicated procedure with a highly uncertain outcome. in addition to the obvious objective of legal certainty, which is to ensure that the law is applied quickly and effectively throughout the union, mutual recognition is aimed not only at the social reintegration of the convicted person, who is no longer uprooted from the state in which he has chosen to live, but also at the protection of the rights of victims. two possible solutions could be envisaged for establishing a mutual recognition mechanism: or to seek to harmonise the legislative and judicial systems of the member states, or to build on mutual confidence in the adequacy of the legislation of individual states and in the correct application of that legislation in specific proceedings. we have opted for the latter solution because it is more feasible and because we are faced with judicial systems which, although different, are based on a system of procedural rules which guarantee reliable criminal decisions, and therefore capable of being enforced throughout the union. we are aware, however, that, at least in the short term, it will be difficult to agree on an automatic recognition procedure, since no member state will ever be willing to be bound by the recognition of any final judgment which does not respect certain essential common guarantees. it is a question of identifying those indispensable guarantees, such as respect for the principle of ne bis in idem or respect for the rights of an effective defence and not merely formal ones, or respect for the rights of victims. it is also necessary to have common rules on jurisdiction and jurisdiction, in order to avoid double judgments in the first place, as well as common rules on the application of recidivism or the cumulation of penalties. however, some obstacles that currently prevent full recognition of final criminal decisions will need to be removed, and among these obstacles is the requirement of double criminality, which often allows the competent authority of the executing state to review the decision issued by the authority of another member state, in form and in substance. the problem of double criminality must be reduced, since in all the member states of the union the acts which arouse the greatest social alarm are punishable by criminal law. the opportunity remains, and it is shared by many of us, to keep out of mutual recognition a limited number of crimes, such as euthanasia, on which it would be difficult to reach an agreement. this report marks a first step towards the creation of a common area of justice, freedom and security. the route is traced: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
mr president, i fully agree with mr palacio. the excellent report by mr di lello fully addresses all the relevant aspects of a complex problem which, however, must be resolved urgently if the european union is to be an area of freedom, security and justice. the problem of mutual recognition of final decisions in criminal matters is obviously caused by the irreducible, at least in the short term - and i agree with mr posselt on this - diversity of the legal and judicial systems of the various member states of the european union. it can therefore only be resolved if, on the one hand, a precise and common definition, applicable to the various systems, of the concepts of final judgment and criminal matter is adopted, definitions which are fully satisfactory both in the commission's communication and in mr di lello's report. on the other hand, whether mutual confidence is created between the member states in the adequacy of their respective systems and the correctness of the procedures. now, this trust can be based on the shared respect for fundamental rights, which is ensured, among other things, by the supervision of the european court of human rights, but which can be further guaranteed by common minimum standards which can be adopted on specific aspects of procedural law in respect of the rights of the defence, the rights of victims. moreover, to overcome the irreconcilability of certain conceptions of principle on the question of the punishability of controversial conduct - the example of euthanasia or abortion was given here - mutual recognition should simply be excluded in relation to certain limited and exceptional types of crime. in this way, the traditional requirement of double sanctionality can be overcome and the long and difficult process of a recognition judgment for each decision in each country avoided, which, i can personally assure mr posselt, is a long process which really hinders the correct application of sanctions, as my previous experience as a judge can testify. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. i therefore also call on the european parliament to give its full approval to this important and very well-reasoned report. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs hautala, for the serious work she has done and for her willingness to take account of all the contributions and suggestions that all the political groups have made on such a sensitive subject. the previous intervention showed how intense the debate in the committee on women's rights was, because it is true that the 1976 directive played an extraordinary role, but twenty-five years have passed, and social attitudes and the role of women have changed. we have many judgments of the court of justice behind us, but above all we have the treaty of amsterdam, which gives us the opportunity, from a legal point of view, to consolidate and make more effective the legal instruments which - we know that they are instruments, but indispensable instruments for implementing active policies and for making the principle of equal opportunities, including access to employment, concrete and enforceable. the temptation to try to tackle many of the problems facing women with this amendment to the directive has been strong - and mr lulling is right in this respect - but i believe that the result of our work is, from a legal point of view, absolutely consistent with the proposals and objectives of the amendment proposal which the commission has presented to us. the definitions of 'direct discrimination' and 'indirect discrimination' which we have refined on the basis of the commission's proposal are, i believe, such as to make the use of this instrument legally clear. the inclusion of sexual harassment and molestation as an element of discrimination is, without a shadow of a doubt, just as clear as the clarification that the right to maternity, like the right to paternity, cannot be used as a tool to implement discrimination. the possibility of taking positive action, and the possibility given to us by article 141 (4) of the treaty, i believe is an equally clear instrument because the directive - which i hope will be operational by the end of this year and will be an instrument available to all member states, all women, all organisations - will really become an instrument in addition to those which the european union has already made available to so many member states over the years. some people have raised the question of the possibility of too much interference by the european union with respect to the principle of subsidiarity. i do not think that this element can be used as an excuse by anyone, because it specifies the legal instruments that can be adopted, with respect to which there are in some cases constraints, in others opportunities, depending on the laws of the member states. but i believe and hope that today the house will approve by a large majority the proposal of the rapporteur, mrs hautala, who has the support of the overwhelming majority of the committee on women's rights, because i believe that this too will be a step forward in the practical implementation of one of the founding principles of our community, which is the principle of equal opportunities.
mr president, on behalf of the italian radical members of the bonino list, i announce that we will not support mrs hautala's report, not because, of course, we are against the principles set out and the objectives which are to be achieved, but because we believe that, more and more often in the european institutions, the wrong means are being used to achieve just and acceptable ends and objectives. often this is done in a bureaucratic way, always trying to come up with a law, a directive, a new tax. the 1976 directive played a fundamental role - and i will not dwell on this - but the attempt made today with this report, with this directive, to deepen the achievement of equal opportunities through legal instruments, i believe that it may lead us down a wrong road, where the benefits risk being more than offset by the harms. reversing the burden of proof, for example, upsets the liberal principles of the rule of law in the name of the cause to be achieved. the legitimacy of positive action, for example, must be linked to the assessment of its duration and proportionality. the creation of independent national bodies - this applies in this case but, in my view, in all other cases - which carry out pre- or parajudicial tasks would be an incomprehensible duplication with the traditional judicial approach. as regards access to the labour market, i think that we should first of all take into account - and this is true in the italian case - some quite traditional measures - flexibility of the labour market, a review of social spending, which is entirely absorbed, for example, by social security spending - measures which would, and are already in part taking place, to achieve equal opportunities in the labour market, without the need for new laws and new bureaucracies.
commission. – mr president, i would like to congratulate mrs hautala and all the members of the committee involved in this very complicated operation. first, the european union has proposed a combination of political tools to add value in line with the policy of equal opportunities, such as its legislation, the fifth programme, employment strategy, the guidelines, the mainstreaming policies, the social funds, and so on. legislation is one of the most important and effective political tools and there is no need to continually propose new legislation. we must modernise the existing legislation and adapt and adjust it to a world of change. this is what we have attempted to do, taking into account new models of production, the family and society. we have taken into account the new treaty and the new legal basis and, of course, we have taken into account the case law of the court of justice. i would like to briefly answer some of the questions put. first, on codification: yes, we are going to present our work on codification of legislation on the same legal basis. second, there is an expert group which meets three times per year and they examine the problems of compatibility between european and national legislation. thirdly, i was asked whether we are going to continue with new directives going beyond the employment field. we are committed to doing that and proposals will be made next year. as far as sexual harassment is concerned, we have accepted as many of the proposals as possible. there was excellent cooperation between the committee and the commission and i really believe that agreement can be reached on this proposal at the employment and social affairs council on 11 june. it is very important to reach this agreement at this council so that we can move to final adoption during the belgian presidency. i am obliged to refer to each amendment and to explain why they are rejected or accepted, so allow me to read out exactly what the commission's position is. it is very important to say that the commission can accept 49 of the 69 amendments, although we would prefer a different wording for 17 of them and can only accept 17 of these amendments in part. i support amendments nos 7 and 21, which provide for definitions of direct discrimination, indirect discrimination, harassment and sexual harassment in one article. the commission can also accept, in principle, part of amendments nos 39 and 68, which extend the powers of independent bodies to cover all directives in the area of equality of treatment between women and men. however, the commission cannot accept the part of amendment no 39, which provides for funding and human resources for these bodies. furthermore, the commission cannot accept that these bodies could examine and pursue complaints for individuals and organisations without the consent of these individuals or groups. amendments nos 15 and 40 in part would allow law organisations and associations to take cases on behalf of a complainant. the commission can only accept this in cases of approval or consent of the complainant. the spirit of amendment no 10 and part of amendments nos 25, 46 and 69 stress the importance of the reconciliation of family and working life and call for complementary action on paternity leave. we can accept amendments nos 12 and 38 on the protection of victims of discrimination, including employees and trade union delegates against any adverse treatment. amendment no 33 clarifies that the application of the principle of equal treatment concerning membership of, and involvement in, an organisation should not ban organisations of a single sex. the commission never intended such a ban. we also accept: amendments nos 14 and 42 urging member states to encourage employers to establish annual equality plans in order to promote equal treatment; amendment no 41, encouragement of dialogue with non-governmental organisations having an interest in promoting equality of opportunity. the commission cannot accept part of amendments nos 11, 27 nor amendment no 55 insofar as they introduce a definition of positive action into the text of the directive itself. this definition of positive action is already contained in the text of treaty and therefore should not be part of the directive. however, the commission could agree to a reference to declaration 28 of the treaty, which provides for priority for women in positive action measures in the recitals and in the text of the directive. the commission can accept part of the rest of amendments nos 11 and 27, the establishment of reports on positive action every two years but not annual reports and not linked to the employment process. this would be unrealistic and over-complicated. i cannot accept amendment no 1 and parts of various other amendments, which replace "equal treatment between women and men" with "equality for women and men". this would be incompatible with the wording of the treaty. this is the major issue; it is not a question of political differences or an ideological problem. we must use the wording of the treaty and the wording of the treaty is "equality of treatment for men and women". the commission can accept the latter wording. other amendments that the commission rejects are part of amendments no 9 and 59 as a matter of principle since they refer to the need to amend another community directive on equal treatment relating to maternity. a directive cannot provide for future modification of another directive which concerns health and safety at the workplace. nor can it accept amendment no 4, which refers to the necessity for the commission to make proposals on the basis of article 13 to cover areas beyond employment, occupational and vocational training. such a provision cannot be contained in a directive, which does not go beyond these fields. but as i have already said, we are going to propose measures in 2002. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 36 and 61 which extend judicial protection to all cases where discrimination takes place after termination of the employment relationship. this goes beyond the scope of the directive. amendment no 44 which provides for contractual compliance with respect to equal treatment, particularly in the public procurement context, goes beyond the scope of the directive, but we have discussed it with the committee in the past and i have explained to you that there is cooperation between me and mr bolkestein. we are going to issue a communication and support and encourage member states to take this into account. finally, as you can see, the commission can accept most of parliament's amendments. i would highlight our acceptance of amendments nos 7 and 21, definitions of direct and indirect discrimination, harassment and sexual harassment and amendment no 39 in part, scope of powers of independent bodies. i accept in spirit amendments nos 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 15, 16, 20, 21, 32, 33, 34, 35, 37, 38, 51 and 60 and partially amendments nos 5 and 9, first part in spirit, amendment no 11, first part, amendment nos 12, 17, 19, 23, 25, 27, 30, 39, 40, 43 (second part), 46 (second part), 50 (second part) and 69 (second part). many amendments could be accepted in full such as amendments nos 13, 14, 18, 22, 24, 26, 28, 29, 31, 41, 42, 45, 47, 60, 66 and 68. however, i reject amendments nos 1, 4, 36, 43 (first part) and amendments nos 44, 48, 49, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65 and 67. this was the first time that the women's committee had participated in the codecision procedure. it was a first experience and a very successful one, because such complicated work has had excellent results. i would like to congratulate you. i would like to thank you for your cooperation so that we can have this directive in place as soon as possible.

- the next item is the report (a5-0169/2001) by mr ribeiro e castro, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the commission report on the eures activities 1998-1999 'towards an integrated european labour market: the contribution of eures' (com (2000) 607 - c5-0104/2001 - 2001/2053 (cos)).
the commission. - mr president, mr ribeiro e castro's report has given us the opportunity to have a meaningful debate on one of the greatest challenges of european policy, namely the european labour market. the employment strategy, the guidelines and the recommendations have so far been strictly national. the national action plans refer to national labour markets. but it is clear that in all parts of europe what we call the european labour market is emerging. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the training and the qualifications of the young people who are in the labour market. the mobility of workers between european countries is extremely low. it's only 0.4%. the easiest approach to mobility problems is often cultural differences. the question of language, culture, national education systems. but it is clear that this is not all. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social security system is not disrupted, and that the social security system is not disrupted. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work, which would be compatible with the common market. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done on this subject. eures is an important tool towards the creation of this european labour market. parliament has been supporting the commission in this endeavour since 1993, and this year's budget of 13 million is proof of that. eures already has an operational experience. we are witnessing an increase in the demand for information, an increase in its movement across borders, which has reached 40% in the last year, which also proves the need for the existence and expansion of eures. i would like to mention some of the commission's options for promoting and strengthening this tool. first, there is greater cooperation between heads of public services, who increasingly decide to integrate eures into their own databases in order to provide common services to customers. the expansion of the range of services provided, not only to jobseekers but also to employers, is being considered. the commission is to announce in june a new service where eures, via the website, will enable jobseekers in specific sectors where there is a shortage to submit their cvs and, at the same time, employers to register to use this service. after eight years of operation, we have asked the member states to include in their questionnaires the problems or new services that could be requested from eures and the report we will make on the basis of these questionnaires will be brought to parliament's attention. in conclusion, i should like to point out that enlargement will indeed require a new approach to this instrument, but for the time being we should develop it as much as possible between the member states. finally, i think it is interesting to mention the need to revise the legal basis of eures so that it can be adapted and improved to meet the future needs of these services.
