the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i am representing margot wallström on this subject tonight, as mrs wallström had to leave today for the international climate negotiations in japan and australia. i think it is in the committee's interest that mrs wallström should be representing europe in this high level group, because climate policy is one of our most pressing concerns. i would like to thank the european parliament, and in particular you, mr rapporteur, but also the committees involved, on behalf of the commission, for the constructive cooperation and the excellent report. the commission's communication was drawn up in the context of the serious environmental damage caused by cyanide leaks following the 1998 dam collapse in spain and the one in baia mare, romania, in january 2000. the communication sets out the three key actions planned by the commission following the recent mining accidents: firstly, the amendment of the seveso ii directive; secondly, the presentation of the proposal for a new directive on the treatment of mining waste; and thirdly, the preparation of a reference document on best available technologies, in accordance with the procedure laid down in the ippc directive, describing the best available technologies for reducing everyday pollution and preventing or preventing accidents in mining. the final report of the baia mare task force confirmed the need for these measures. the task force was set up by mrs wallström to gather more information on the accident in baia mare and to develop measures to reduce or avoid such risks in the future. in their report they welcome this communication and support the commission's general approach of creating a transparent and coherent framework for greater safety in mining by amending environmental legislation and instruments accordingly. this applies not only to the three key actions just mentioned, but also to legislation which is not specific to mining, such as the proposed environmental liability directive. let me emphasize at this point that the three key actions mentioned have now different timeframes. the proposal for a directive amending the seveso ii directive has already been the subject of public consultation and is expected to be adopted in the course of this year, in accordance with the commission's work programme for 2001. the directive will cover not only mining but also the safe storage of fireworks after the tragic accident in enschede in the netherlands last may. i would add, in the light of the present amendment and the comments made by mrs flemming, that it is true that the two mining accidents mentioned in the commission's communication occurred in the context of activities connected with the extraction of metallic ores. the commission therefore understands the considerations of limiting the scope of the directive to this area. however, i would point out that a gradual extension of the scope of the directive - and only after accidents have occurred - does not take account of the precautionary principle. aristotle said, "it is probable that something improbable will happen". tomorrow there may be an accident in an industrial plant which does not fall within the scope of the seveso ii directive, and then we will correct it again and wait for the next area, so to speak. i would therefore welcome it if parliament would support the commission in its efforts to be proactive rather than reactive in its legislative proposals. a note on the timing of the second key action. work on the proposal for a new directive on the treatment of mining waste is progressing well. the study on mining hot spots will be completed shortly and the consultation of the relevant stakeholders has just started. this proposal is expected to be adopted by the commission in 2002. the work on the best available technologies document started with an inaugural meeting at the european ippc office at the end of june. however, experience has shown that such detailed documents describing the best available technologies take on average two years to produce. the report also calls on the commission to intensify its dialogue with the european mining industry. this dialogue is already taking place. it will play a central role in the implementation of the community strategy on safety in mines. your support shows the commission that we are on the right track. the report gives us the motivation to continue working hard to implement our strategy for preventing mining accidents in the european union and also in the candidate countries.
- thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.
- the next item is the report (a5-0219/2001) by mrs mckenna, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a european parliament and council recommendation on the implementation of an integrated coastal zone management strategy in europe (com (2000) 545 - c5-0474/2000 - 2000/0227 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, as i have taken over the speech from my colleague, mrs wallström, i will speak in english. the coastal zone is very important for europe, as other speakers have said. its resources provide us with food, energy and homes and create opportunities. however, according to the reports of the european environmental agency, conditions in the coastal zone and its resources continue to decline. conditions in the coastal zone can only be improved through a concentrated effort involving all levels of the relevant sectors of government based on the principles of integrated coastal zone management. i would like to stress that this integrated coastal zone management is not a procedure for land-use planning per se. it is more a methodology for introducing a coherent approach to the management and use of coastal resources with the informed involvement of all the relevant stakeholders. in order to encourage member states to assume their full responsibility in promoting integrated coastal zone management, the commission has introduced the proposed recommendation. this calls on member states to develop national strategies for coastal zone management based on an inventory of the actors, laws and institutions involved in the management and planning of the coastal zones. this strategy aims to introduce a coherent approach to the coastal zones across europe but the recommendation intentionally leaves the choice of the format of the national strategies to the member states to ensure that each national strategy is tailor-made to the institutional, physical and social conditions within each member state. at the same time, the recommendation presents a list of features which the member states are encouraged to address through their national strategies, such as the need for coherence between the many plans, policies and programmes for management of the coasts and the need for coordination between the actors that use and manage the coast, particularly those with responsibility for the sea and the land which forms part of the coastal zone. let me turn to the key issues raised in the amendments proposed. i would like to start by noting that the commission can accept many of the proposed amendments. indeed, many of the proposed amendments strengthen the text by clarifying concepts and introducing further information. we thank parliament for putting forward these amendments. there are, however, certain amendments which the commission cannot accept. several of the amendments proposed, namely amendments nos 11, 12, 16, 18, 29, 32, 43 and 49, introduce references to a future community legislative framework. these amendments are unacceptable to the commission for the obvious reason that they prejudge the issue of whether a legislative approach is required. in addition, a reference to a community legislative framework would not be appropriate in view of the wide diversity of conditions in the member states and the commission’s philosophy of coastal zone management. the commission’s present decision to propose a recommendation was based on a thorough assessment of the needs for action at the european level through the demonstration programme on integrated coastal zone management and on a broad public consultation. in the same spirit, the commission cannot accept amendments which introduce compulsory language. "shall" is not the right word in a non-binding instrument, such as a recommendation and therefore the use of this word in amendments nos 29, 32 and 34 cannot be accepted by the commission. similarly, the references in amendments nos 17, 20, 33 and 45 indicating the need for binding instruments within the member states ignore the fact that integrated coastal zone management may be best introduced through voluntary measures in some member states. these parts of these amendments are therefore not acceptable either. otherwise, the six amendments are acceptable in principle or in part. the commission is concerned that amendments nos 16 and 42 might give an incorrect, narrow impression of the breadth of the integrated coastal zone management approach. in particular, in amendments nos 25 and 47, while the commission accepts the need to involve all the parties concerned, this text should not be limited to the special planning process, but should make broader reference to all of the actors involved in the planning and management of the coastal zones and its resources. the commission would also note that it cannot accept two amendments, which make inappropriate reference to other community policies which are better discussed in a different context. the reference to the interreg programme in amendment no 16 is inappropriate as the guidelines for interreg have been set out elsewhere. similarly, the reference in amendment no 35 to the common fisheries policy and the 12-mile derogation is not acceptable as it prejudges the debate on the revision of this policy. in addition, amendments nos 47 and 48 are not acceptable, at least in part, because they could lead to the endorsement of unsustainable traditional practices including those relating to hunting and fishing. concerning the remaining amendments – and this list is longer than the non-acceptable amendments – the commission can accept amendments nos 1, 3 to 10, 13, 15, 19, 21, 22, 23, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41 and 46; and in addition, it can accept amendments nos 2, 14, 24, 36, and 44 in principle. as a result, two thirds of the amendments can be accepted by the commission. in conclusion, parliament has significantly contributed to improving this proposal. i would, therefore, like to thank the rapporteur, mrs mckenna, and the draftsmen from the other committees for their efforts. i am sure that the final text will be an important step in encouraging the application of integrated coastal zone management in europe.
- thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon. the next item is the report (doc. (the sitting was closed at 10.00 a.m.)
commission. – madam president, i am pleased to have this opportunity to talk about the g8 summit. at the suggestion of the italian g8 presidency the forthcoming summit in genoa will focus on the one hand on global development issues, and on the other hand on some key related areas of concern such as the environment and food safety. the commission fully supports this focus for the summit. indeed, it is the g8 leaders' intention that genoa should send a strong signal that the g8 countries are taking the concerns of their own citizens extremely seriously, as well as those of the developing world. following on from okinawa last year, the g8 will be looking at development issues in a much more serious fashion. from the commission's point of view the summit needs to address the following key questions in this area. first, the fight against communicable diseases. the european union has taken a strong lead. the action plan on fighting communicable diseases was adopted by the council earlier this year. following kofi annan's call for the establishment of a global health fund, which was endorsed, i am pleased to say, by the un general assembly last week, it is expected that g8 members will provide their political and financial backing for the proposed fund. mr annan's presence in genoa to take part in an ‘outreach’ meeting between the g8 and other leaders will help to focus attention on the global health fund issue. many issues remain, and we must make sure that the fund's focus and management is in line with the objectives of the european union action plan. but a strong signal of european support in this area will be both natural and expected in genoa. secondly, there is the issue of third world debt. the g8 took an early lead on the debt of the poorest countries – the hipc initiative – and we should now seek to go further. mr prodi and prime minister verhofstadt will refer to the council decision in may this year calling for the total alleviation of all remaining special loans granted to the least-developed countries under the first, second and third lomé conventions. thirdly, there is the question of market access for the least-developed countries. we strongly support the efforts of the italian g8 presidency to broaden the debate on poverty reduction beyond debt relief. in particular, the links between poverty reduction and trade should be highlighted. in this context the ‘everything but arms’ initiative will of course be mentioned, and the commission will insist that other g8 members should follow suit by providing duty-free and quota-free access for all products originating from the least-developed countries. turning now to the environment, g8 leaders will have a discussion on climate change. this will be president bush's first g8 summit. the commission will be keen, as will no doubt the other european participants, to discuss our concerns about the united states' present stance on climate change and on the ratification of the kyoto protocol. we will work to ensure that the communiqué makes a clear reference to the scientific evidence to back up the urgency of international measures to mitigate climate change. we, for our part, will reiterate our determination to press ahead with ratification of the kyoto protocol, and our hope that the reconvened 6th conference of the parties to the climate change convention, scheduled for bonn, can find a means which allows the united states to stick with the process. as regards food safety, the commission is keen that the g8 conclusions include a reference to the precautionary principle. we remain committed to making systems responsive to the growing public awareness of food safety issues, the potential risks associated with food and the accelerating pace of change of developments in biotechnology. these are not the only issues on the agenda of the three-day meeting. beyond the principal themes of development, environment and food safety, there will be a discussion on regional issues focusing on the middle east and the balkans, as well as on conflicts in africa. those subjects will be discussed by the foreign ministers' meeting, at which i will be present just before the main leaders meeting. as usual the g8 summit will also be preceded by a g7 session, that is, without russia, where the main topics of discussion will be the world economy, including oil prices and financial architecture. prime minister koizumi of japan will announce his plan for structural reforms in the run-up to the elections in his country. leaders will also discuss trade with the aim of sending a clear unambiguous message on the launch of a new round at the fourth wto ministerial meeting in dohar in november. also in the context of the g7, nuclear safety issues will be discussed in relation both to the situation in russia and to the need to maintain loan commitments to ukraine, following the closure of the chernobyl plant, for the construction of the k2r4 reactors there. it has become g8 practice to arrange an outreach meeting with some heads of state and government from developing countries. in this vein, the italian hosts have invited leaders from south africa, nigeria, mali, algeria, bangladesh and el salvador to attend a working session and a dinner which should focus mainly on the poverty reduction strategy and the global health fund. as i said earlier, this part of the summit will also be attended by the un secretary-general, as well as by the president of the world bank and the heads of the world trade organisation, the world health organisation and the food and agriculture organisation. the g8 is not an organisation or an institution. it is not based on a treaty, it does not have a secretariat. the group of 8 is an annual gathering of democratically elected leaders of the leading nations of the world. the european commission is invited to participate, not least in view of its trade and other responsibilities on behalf of the whole union. as in the past, mr prodi intends to make full use of this opportunity to convey the views and positions of the european union. it is not enough that world leaders meet and discuss these issues between themselves, however. they must listen to the concerns of third countries and civil society and then enter into dialogue with them. that is why the g8 is increasingly organising side events and meetings with third countries and civil society alongside the summit. i have already mentioned the outreach meetings with other leaders. the japanese last year added an ngo centre in okinawa. the italians continue this year with a number of meetings that have already taken place and others set to take place on the eve of the summit. the commission has extensive experience in its own relations and consultations with civil society – we have been keen to share our knowledge with g8 members, and we hope the encouragement of this type of dialogue will continue and will be developed further. i will just make one final point. however much one agrees or disagrees with some representatives of civil society on issues such as globalisation, it seems to me exceptionally important to have an open dialogue which is not disfigured by street violence. some of the scenes we have seen surrounding recent summits and meetings have, i think, sadly made it more difficult for legitimate representatives of civil society to get their point across to the leaders who are present. i feel that is a tragedy. it very unfairly devalues the case which those legitimate ngos have to make, and i very much hope that they will make that point and that those who have been guilty of violence in the past will get the message. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, let me make a first remark: our resolution refers to 87 countries where the death penalty still exists. i believe that this figure - which amnesty international has given us - is not accurate. this is actually 71 countries that still apply the death penalty, and i think the difference is significant in that the international community is 180 countries, which means that the majority of abolitionist countries are much larger than amnesty international's numbers suggest. i also think that amnesty international should not be seen as a kind of bible for a whole series of things, or as a representative of civil society, which is not the case at all: it is an association that does a certain job and which deserves - i think - a critical look from time to time, if not more. secondly - monica frassoni has said it, mr van den berg has said it, mr manisco has said it - i think our problem is to get to the un general assembly with a resolution on the moratorium. the problem is not to abolish death. i think that there are sometimes temptations to that effect. our problem is to abolish the death penalty because we believe there is a way to do justice without it. the problem is therefore a moratorium, a purely secular initiative, to get other states to consider the arguments against the death penalty and to conclude secularly, wisely, that there is no longer any need for the use of this instrument. i therefore believe that our work over the next few weeks will be important in order to achieve, with the belgian presidency, a resolution on the moratorium to be presented in new york.

- mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr mayer for the thorough work he has done in drawing up this report, including through the hearings he has organised with the committee on employment and social affairs, for a thorough examination of the transposition of the directive. it is clear from this work that transposition into national legislation is generally positive and that a european works council has already been set up in some 2000 european companies; in many firms, the directive has been successful in removing barriers to information and consultation. not only that: the timely involvement of works councils in some decision-making processes has certainly brought positive results, first of all for workers, on issues such as health, safety, equal opportunities, but also for companies in terms of reducing conflicts. that said, the mayer report - which we share and support - also highlights a number of shortcomings in the directive itself, on which i believe it is absolutely necessary that the commission should act quickly to amend it. i would like to stress three points in particular which, in addition to those already mentioned by other members, seem to me to be the most sensitive points on which it is necessary to act in a timely manner. first of all, the timing of the information: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the information provided by the member states is not only available to the public, but also to the media. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. we could mention in this connection cases such as ahlston, adb, marks & spencer and many others. if that is the case, then it is absolutely necessary that the directive be more precise, that it define the time limits for information and consultation before any decision is taken, in order to make the possibility of negotiation operational, otherwise it is useless! second point: i think my colleagues will agree with me that there are no rules in a statute which, if they are not respected, have no effect. it is strange that only in the field of labour and social rights is this almost the rule! the result of this has been a series of disputes and legal proceedings in recent years, precisely because failure by undertakings to comply with the provisions of the directive does not in any way, or even automatically, call into question the validity of the consequences of the decision taken. it is therefore necessary to provide for appropriate and dissuasive sanctions, just as in cases of serious infringement it is necessary to provide for suspension to allow the negotiations to continue.

commission. – mr president, i am aware of the fact that i trespassed on the patience of the house earlier in order to try and make a full reply. i will now try to be as brief as i possibly can in response to the very good points that have been made by honourable members in the course of this debate. perhaps if i try to go through the more salient points made and simply make the most brief answers that will assist the house, especially against the background of the fact that in their post today and probably in their offices already, there is a very comprehensive lengthy reply to every aspect of the oral question set down by mr harbour and madam guy-quint and secondly a very full table of 23 pages going through each of the 98 actions for reform proposals and giving a detailed account of the state of play on each of those at the moment, whether those proposals have been completed and implemented, which several have, or whether they are currently the subject of consultation or whether they have been presented to this house, or to the council, or both, for the legislative amendment required to put them into effect. all the honourable members, including mr pomés ruiz and mr dell'alba and others who have enquiries of that kind can, simply by referring to that table, get the most up-to-date information available to any one in the european union, including the commission itself. in response to mr harbour's questions relating to whistle-blowing and to the code of good administrative behaviour, obviously we require changes to the staff regulations in order to secure the necessary advances on the existing legislation relating to the duty to report suspected wrongdoing that has an effect on the financial wellbeing of the european communities. the proposal has been made in detailed form. we are now seeking the cooperation of the council and parliament in the course of consideration of the modernisation of the staff regulations next year. i am optimistic that this cooperation will be forthcoming. the result will be that the european public service will have the best and most secure provision for safeguarding the interests of staff and the institutions and the european public of any public administration anywhere in the european union. as far as the code of administrative behaviour is concerned, the principles of that code are already set down in the staff regulations. in day-to-day practice, since we have implemented the code, the answer to the question on the oral paper today about whether the code of administrative behaviour is in practice incorporated in the activities of the commission is yes. on the career structure question, it appears that people have either adopted misinformed views or been given misleading opinions. i assure the house that the intention behind the reform generally, and specifically the intention behind the proposals we have made in relation to career structure, is not to try to emulate some form of private sector multinational. it is to establish, to make an assessment upon, to recognise merit and to provide reward in the development of an individual's career according to the very best principles of accountable, efficient, independent, professional civil services at european union level. no more no less. if anyone is trying to give the impression that we are trying to set official against official, to destroy the contribution of loyalty made by officials over the years, to overlook the individual qualities of individuals by making the proposal that we do, they are sadly misled. i am prepared to go into the most thorough detail in order to ensure that we do not get any repetition of the misunderstanding that has led to various communications that have manifested a complete failure to comprehend the purpose and detail of what has been proposed so far. i am very glad to say that in the commission the staff unions, or a majority of the unions representing commission staff members, have gone into these issues in the most thorough detail and have actually developed attitudes and ideas that can lead to significant improvements on the original propositions and options that were put. it is on the basis of that constructive dialogue and negotiation, which has lasted over the past five months, that we are now putting refreshed and reconsidered options which i hope will recommend themselves not only to staff in the commission but to the other institutions. there is nothing to fear and there is everything for the staff, the institutions and the public interest to gain by the modernisation of the career structure of the european union institutions from the inherited structure which is over 40 years old. everything else in the european union has changed and it is time that the career structure and the recognition of commitment and capability caught up with those other changes. can i say to mr pomés ruiz that the answers to the questions that he has raised, for instance on audit, are available in a number of documents which have been conveyed to parliament. but for quick and easy reference, i draw his attention to the set of tables that he will have in his office today or at the very latest tomorrow – i suspect that they are there today – which will give him complete and up-to-date details on each of the aspects of reform relating to the establishment, development and operation, for instance, of the internal audit service. mr miller refers to timing. that is an apposite point. our commitment to sustained momentum is nothing to do with any desire to rush the commission, its staff, parliament, the council or anybody else. the point is that in managing very substantial change that affects our institutions and the people who work for them it is in nobody's interests to delay, evade, or unnecessarily prolong the deliberations. let those deliberations be thorough and the negotiations candid and well-informed. but when the prospect of change hangs over people's heads it can be destabilising, demoralising and demotivating, which is in nobody's interests. that is why we are not rushing. these changes are being considered properly and democratically in a process of consultation and negotiation. we have honoured every commitment on that and we will continue to do so. as regards the early retirement package mentioned by mr miller, the package we have now has retained its attractiveness for staff and its cost neutrality. we have kept our promises. what we need now is for the council to act quickly and effectively, because the increased efficiency and cost neutrality and the benefit to the operation of the european union that can derive from the commission's proposal last year could be drastically reduced or even lost altogether if any part of the council prevaricates. that is not in anybody's interests. i take mrs jensen's point: what we are proposing is to link effort to recognised assessment and reward. i think i have covered mr marinho's point relating to the nature of what we are seeking to do, which is consistent with principles of public service, but now i come to mr dell'alba's point about language. he is a member of this house for whom i have great respect despite our political differences. his point about language hegemony was a cheap point, which regrettably diminishes my respect for him, and what he says has absolutely no foundation at all in anything that i or my fellow commissioners have said or done. he might have intended it as a joke but i do not think that in the european union of 2001 we should joke about things like that. we have been told that, in the two years we have had as a commission, the only reform has been to get rid of the medal for 20 years' service. but when i look back over these two years i see that we have kept promises to establish, for the first time ever, an independent, professionally led and staffed internal audit service, a central finance service, audit capabilities in every directorate-general, an audit progress committee that bears comparison with any comparable mechanism in the private or public sector anywhere in the european union. we have drafted a new financial regulation which came to this house on time and to the council on time and we are waiting for its enactment. we have developed a strategic planning and programming system. it is capable, with the use of activity-based budgeting and management, of being implemented in the european commission, on time, provided that we get the necessary support from elsewhere. on time, in keeping with the promises we made on 1 march 2000 we have set out the most complex and extensive set of proposed reforms for personnel management and conduct in the european commission and european public service comparable to the work that has been undertaken in the administrations of member states over five and ten years. it is a slur on the people who work in the commission and the huge commitment that they have shown, in working 75 hours a week or more, month after month, to suggest that this commission has done nothing in two years. i will not tolerate that kind of attack on the officials of the commission and the way in which they have demonstrated their dedication to the public interest by seeking to fulfil the mandate given to the commission by this elected house. we have not finished the reform. it will be some time before we have even implemented the mechanisms of reform, let alone securing the changes in attitudes, conventions, behaviour and so-called ‘culture’ that will result. one group of people really does deserve credit: the civil servants of the european union, both those who have contributed to the design and development of the reform programme and those who, in a time of turmoil, have shown patience, understanding and commitment in thinking up the ideas, considering the proposals being made, suggesting improvements and showing the goodwill that demonstrates a high standard of professional commitment to the cause of europe. we will continue along that path, hopefully with the cooperation and constructive support of members of this house and the council. but if in the end we do not succeed in making all the changes that are needed in the time available, one thing i want to ensure is that every tax-paying citizen and every voter in the european union understands that a failure to meet the targets and deadlines is in no way the responsibility of the european commission or the people who work for it. the responsibility for failing to fulfil the mandate lies elsewhere – maybe with the very institutions that gave us the mandate in september 1999. i would much prefer to be able to show people in the member states that parliament, the council and the commission heard and heeded the demands for change and modernisation and have worked together to bring about the changes needed to ensure that the citizens of europe have the high quality, efficient, transparent and professional administration they deserve. the commission and its staff have committed themselves to that. i hope that this house will continue to show the same commitment.

enlargement is not just a matter of extending the union geographically, economically and politically, involving ten, twelve, perhaps thirteen countries, mainly from the middle east, which have gone the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this motion for a resolution is based on a number of simple but not obvious considerations. the first concerns a lack of coordination between the union's cultural programmes, especially between those covered by culture 2000 and those included in programmes financed by the structural funds. the second is the observation that there is a gap between programmes managed at union level and national cultural policies, based on mere mutual information. a positive response to these two observations is motivated by two recognitions: the first is that the principle of subsidiarity not only does not exclude cooperation but requires it. it must not be understood as a bigoted cultural protectionism but in a positive and active sense, as a fruitful encounter of different cultures. the second recognition is that the diversity of national and regional cultures is the richness and specific characteristic of european civilization. the motto of the report is therefore 'unity in diversity'. it is clear that european culture is not a homogeneous unit: it is a collection of different cultures, each with its own historical roots and its own radiation space. i would say it's a symphony in the technical, musical sense of the word, since it unfolds through consonance and dissonance: a symphony not created by a single composer, but resulting from the course of history, through dramatic conflicts and occasional religious, national, ideological massacres. however, today, at last, it is converging on common humanistic values of freedom, equity and, if not brotherhood - which would be asking too much - at least solidarity tolerance: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy. a common european culture was recognized by the time of thomas more and erasmus of rotterdam, when erasmus rode on a mule to oxford to bring his friend the eulogy of madness. there was a lingua franca but no monetary union, so on his return they confiscated his honestly earned pounds. today, we no longer travel on mules because we use airplanes, we no longer have a lingua franca, but we have our very good simultaneous translators. in short, there are all the material conditions for a european culture to spread its peaceful and civil message throughout the world, for europeans to be able to engage in rich cooperation in the cultural field. this cooperation is affirmed, indeed invoked, in the treaties and in official speeches, but the intendency does not follow as it could and should. the commission's proposals are not only a means of achieving the objectives of the treaty, but also a means of ensuring that the community's cultural policy is not disrupted by the failure of the council to take decisions. the present motion for a resolution is an attempt to respond to this paralysis, to promote cooperation between european countries in the field of culture in a pragmatic way, starting with the obvious need to adopt a common language, comparable statistics, mutual information, systematic comparison, a selection of best practices and the opening up of areas where it seems most convenient and appropriate to adopt common attitudes and policies. i hope very much, mr president, that the commission, by making its commitments as they are, will give the resolution the follow-up it desires, placing the problem of culture and cultural cooperation at the heart of the great european undertaking. we are different and united at the same time: this is your chance to prove it!
president of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport. mr president, this resolution is the first legislative initiative of parliament on cultural matters based on article 192 of the treaty and it is different from the other resolutions adopted by parliament in the cultural field, not only in its content but also in its procedure, which is certainly the most authoritative currently permitted by the treaty. the resolution comes at a delicate time for the european union, on the eve of major institutional reforms. the commission's proposal is therefore to be seen as an indication and a contribution by parliament to the debate on the future of europe. if this is true, of course, you will allow me, mr president, to express my sincere congratulations to the rapporteur in my capacity as chairman of the committee - as we usually do as a formal clause when we vote - because i really believe that this is a step forward, a great revolution that parliament is about to make. the lack of coordination of cultural programmes, as the rapporteur has pointed out, is in my view the most important factor in the growth of europe, and, as mr ruffolo has said, culture has hitherto played a much smaller role in the economy. the maastricht treaty has improved its position, but it is still marginal. nice then found itself paralysed by the constraints of unanimity. this shows how europe can be built, commissioner, not just on the economic side, but also on the cultural side, and this parliament must take full account of this. this resolution, which was unanimously and passionately wanted by the committee, wanted by the rapporteur and discussed and wanted by the committee as a whole, is, i believe, a sign of a new division, a new diversity, a new reason for this parliament, which is part of a strategy which must bring us, on the cultural level, to the unity of the cultural diversity that this great europe has, in order to have a future in a real strategy in the coming years.
commission - mr president, if i say thank you to the rapporteur, it is not a formula, it is simply a heartfelt thank you because the ruffolo report comes at the right time to relaunch our reflection on the future of cultural cooperation in europe. i regret, mr rapporteur, i regret, ladies and gentlemen, that the debate on this report is taking place at practically midnight, in front of an empty house, not qualitatively but quantitatively, because i think that what is really being discussed - and i am not just saying this as the commissioner responsible for this matter - is the future of europe. the future of europe, even if the current topics are the euro and our economic development in a globalised environment, will depend on the following question: how will we manage our culture, our cultures, our cultural diversity, which is based on common roots, has much in common and is very diverse, all of which together make up the unity of our european cultures? so now is the time to speak and act. you know very well that the move to qualified majority voting for article 151, which parliament and the commission had requested, was not included in the treaty of nice. so we have to substance of the motion for a resolution, mr president, point by point. as regards points 1 and 2, the importance of culture and cultural cooperation for european identity, a long development is not council, which is currently discussing a draft resolution by the belgian presidency on the place of culture in europe. i hope very much that parliament and the commission will do everything possible to ensure that this resolution is carried through. point 4: culture and the information society. you are aware of the many initiatives of the commission: e-europe in the audiovisual field, e-content and, in the field of education, e-learning. it has presented a draft resolution to improve access to culture via the internet and we will be organising a seminar with the belgian presidency on 22 september on 'culture and the internet'. the seminar will focus on the european cultural electronic network and the presence of culture on the internet. points 5, 8 and 10: strengthening cooperation. parliament called for cultural cooperation to be strengthened by means of a three-year plan for the member states and the creation of a european observatory on cultural cooperation. these two proposals open up new prospects and i am pleased that the amendments tabled by mr ruffolo, mrs pack and mr graça moura on behalf of the two main groups in this parliament allow the commission to withdraw reservations which were not reservations of substance but formal reservations as these two proposals called for. so we agree on the substance. by strengthening cooperation between member states and between cultural institutions, we can develop a better knowledge of the cultural world and all that this implies. the members of parliament have said it with great commitment and great talent. so, in concrete terms, i would like to say this. the director-general of the directorate-general for education and culture regularly meets the directors-general for culture of the member states. the aim of these meetings is to strengthen cooperation. they know each other, they know what the other is doing, they can work together, they can think of common, concerted actions, and put them into practice. in the same vein, the commission wishes to increase the visibility of the european community's many cultural activities. i'll get back to you. that is why in a few months' time a actors in your member states and your voters know that this exists and that it works. you'll be one of the relays to help spread the word about this portal. i would also like to thank the committee on suit. point 9: the structural funds. we could be jealous because we have decided to allocate 167 million euros over five years to the culture 2000 programme. let me give you some figures on the investment of the structural funds in culture, and i would point out that this is not automatic. the member states and regions must ask for these investments, otherwise the structural funds cannot be effective on the ground. the commission has specific indications for countries which have chosen to allocate part of the funds to cultural actions. i would mention three: greece, portugal and italy. portugal, for example, has voted for a budget of €327 million for culture for the period 2000-2006. the european community is contributing eur 237 million. for a small country - a large country of culture, of course, but a small member state nonetheless - this is a sum which goes far beyond what we have for 15 member states for the culture 2000 action. in greece, the total community contribution to culture will be eur 414 million and in italy we will also contribute by participating in seven regional operational programmes and by devoting a large budget to culture, in which the structural funds will contribute a total of over eur 1 200 000. if we take only these three countries, not the fifteen, mr president, we see that in one year the structural funds invest more than 250 million euros in culture. so you can see that this involves much larger amounts than those available to us as european cultural policy-makers. point 11: the observatory. you have taken the necessary - mr president, echelon as an undifferentiated system for intercepting communications, data and documents exists and represents a considerable step forward. the institutions of the union, especially the representatives of the council and the commission, will no longer be able to say that they are uncontrollable press reports. however, there is a discrepancy between what has been found and the conclusions of the report, because there is a significant violation of the fundamental right to respect for privacy established by article 8 of the echr and article 6 of the treaty on european union. the system, by its technical capabilities, undermines the relationship of proportionality which, precisely in accordance with article 8 of the echr, must exist between the interference with private life and the interest to be protected by interception. this is all the more serious because today, with such technical capabilities, interception is carried out by a third country on the territory and to the detriment of citizens of the union countries, without any possibility of judicial, administrative or parliamentary control. the other problem is that one of the countries operating the echelon system is the united kingdom, a member of the european union, while other member countries, such as germany, have made their territory available for the installation of antennas, listening bases and so on. in short, the group of english-speaking countries running echelon does what it wants with the privacy of european citizens, as is explicitly acknowledged in point 26 of the conclusion, which mrs flesch also mentioned, namely that there is a violation of article 8 of the echr. but instead of, as my country says, 'putting the sheep to the wolves', it was at least necessary to state that the united kingdom had violated this article and also to recognize that the united kingdom's participation in the echelon system was incompatible with the commitments it had made under the european treaties. the effective protection of fundamental rights in the usa is essential to the credibility and democratic legitimacy of your country. but once again, we have chosen and missed an opportunity, at least for us, to affirm a democratic principle. for others, however, at a time when the right to dissent is being clouded by the eu and the world, genoa teaches, it was not even possible to think of suppressing or at least trying to change and attenuate a system of indiscriminate listening, one of the most useful systems for social control and possible repression. mr president, the fundamental right to privacy, so solemnly written into our treaties and the charter of fundamental rights, with this report and the lack of appropriate conclusions, remains a right on paper, indeed, it remains dramatically a right on paper!
mr president, as a european citizen, even before i am a member of this house, i would like to express my indignation at the way the committee has been working. the committee has worked in systematic violation of the rules of procedure, in violation of the obligation of transparency of parliament's activities, in violation of the right of public access to documents. this management of the work, which in no way detracts from the commitment of president coelho and rapporteur schmid, was necessary not to protect european security - which is an abstract concept in this field - but to conceal the responsibility of the member states of the union. the report states with absolute certainty that echelon exists, that it systematically and massively spies on citizens and businesses in the member states of the union and that the united kingdom is part of the system, but it does not openly condemn it because systematic and widespread interception, filtered by search engines, is already being carried out by germany, while the netherlands, which obviously has the technology, is legally organizing itself to do it. the report shows that echelon is a metaphor for those who do not recognize the citizen's right to privacy and subordinate it to national security, which is endangered primarily by the inability of policy makers to predict, prevent and govern threats. in the face of all this, the report calls for a concrete and immediate solution, inviting businesses and citizens to encrypt documents, as if the indissoluble link between the development of cryptographic systems, cryptanalytical systems and interception techniques were not known. mr president, the minority opinion should be the only political response that can be given today, which essentially passes through democratic control.

- mr president, i have the strongest reservations about the soft and in some ways reticent nature of the report, because it underestimates the dangers of global control of communications and does not propose adequate autonomous measures of defence for europe. in theory, the european union could certainly negotiate a memorandum of understanding allowing the member states to use this information, but for the time being and immediately the european union must think of protecting itself autonomously with a cryptographic system different from the current ones, for example the state-of-the-art hermes system produced by european research, with point-to-point teleportation so that the data cannot be picked up by spy satellites. the report seems to evade this precise question: can the use of information collected by echelon by the security services of one of the member states, the united kingdom, lead to actual cases of espionage against european citizens or companies for the benefit of the united states? these are questions that must be asked, since the us congress itself has raised the question of whether the nsa's surveillance of us citizens is unconstitutional. it has been said and it must be said again that even ngos like amnesty international, greenpeace, and even personalities above all suspicion, like mother teresa of calcutta, have been intercepted by the echelon system. that's a thought. the president of stoa, our former colleague mr pompidou, said that many european companies have already paid for echelon, but they do not denounce it because they continue and must continue to do business with the united states. so we ask ourselves: what legal protection is there for european companies against such damage? what chance do they have of proving it? what funding, i might add, for european research in strategic and important areas such as cryptography? these are questions which the report does not answer.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union and its member states are founded on respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, on the guarantee of the dignity of the human person and on the protection of the rights of individuals and of the institutions enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. all these rights can be affected by acts of terrorism. in a framework of full democracy such as that which exists in the union and its member states, terrorist acts can never be justified, regardless of where they are committed or the objective pursued. acts of terrorism should never be considered as political crimes or as politically motivated or related crimes. terrorism should never be considered as a way of solving a problem that a person or a group may have, regardless of its nature. in recent years, europe has seen an increase in terrorist activity within its borders, characterised by a profound change in the nature of the acts committed. the actual or potential impact of armed attacks is increasingly devastating and deadly as a consequence of technological developments in the arms and explosives sector. new forms of terrorism are emerging as a result of the continuing and rapid development of information technologies, electronic records and computer equipment. terrorists can take advantage of the differences in the legal systems of various member states and the difficulties in extraditing them, especially when the act is not regulated in the requested state. this point, as has been said several times during the debate, underlines the inadequacy of traditional forms of judicial and police cooperation in the fight against terrorism. it is therefore more necessary than ever to take measures to combat terrorism by drawing up legislative proposals to punish such acts. the european union institutions, in particular the european parliament, the commission and the council, have consistently condemned terrorism at political level. unfortunately, we have been called upon to affirm this position of the union with unusual frequency in the light of the terrorist actions of eta in spain. our solidarity with the spanish people and, in particular, with the victims of terrorism in spain is unequivocal and constant. this solidarity must be complemented by more effective action. article 29 of the amsterdam treaty therefore specifically refers to joint action in three areas: closer cooperation between police forces, customs authorities and other competent authorities, including europol, closer cooperation between the judicial authorities of the member states and approximation, where necessary, of criminal law provisions. in accordance with article 2 of the europol convention, terrorism is one of europol's areas of competence. in accordance with article 31 (b) of the treaty on european union and the tampere conclusions, which stated that formal extradition procedures between member states for persons attempting to escape justice will be abolished and replaced by a simple transfer, the commission has already announced its intention to present an initiative to abolish formal extradition procedures between member states for certain types of crime and to create a 'european search and seizure mandate' with a view to combating not only terrorism but also other heinous crimes of a transnational nature. the commission also intends to propose the approximation of criminal legislation on acts of terrorism, in accordance with article 31 (e) of the treaty on european union, not only to cover classical forms of terrorism but also new forms of terrorism. finally, the act of directing, promoting, supporting or belonging to a terrorist group should also be subject to a common categorisation. the commission shares parliament's concerns about the protection of victims of terrorism and intends to present a green paper on compensation for victims of crime in general and of terrorism in particular within the european union during the current six-month period. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in conclusion, the commission agrees with the principles of the excellent report by mr watson, whom i would like to congratulate, and with the guidelines of the draft recommendation which parliament is considering today. following the work we have been carrying out for several months, in close consultation with all the member states - i stress all the member states - and not just a few, the commission intends to propose to parliament and the council this september the legislative initiatives relating to the harmonisation of the crime of terrorism, the adoption of the european search and seizure warrant and the replacement of extradition procedures by expedited delivery mechanisms for certain types of crime, including terrorism, thus giving full effect, i am sure, to the requests in your draft recommendation. the council. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, since the end of 1999, there have been massive demonstrations at every major international meeting. we have seen demonstrators from all over the world gather at ministerial meetings of the world trade organization, meetings of the imf or the world bank and the world economic forum in davos. since the end of last year, the meetings of the european council have also been the subject of mass protests. think of nice and gothenburg. the recent g8 meeting in genoa was the latest occasion for mass protest. if these demonstrations were to be non-violent, we should only be concerned with answers to the questions and concerns raised by the demonstrators and those who support them. unfortunately, the protests in nice, gothenburg and genoa were accompanied by a lot of violence, despite the fact that the organizers of the protests distanced themselves from the violence. in addition to the inconvenience to the inhabitants of the towns where the meetings and demonstrations took place, in addition to the material damage to houses and property, people were unfortunately injured during the skirmishes and - much worse - two demonstrators were killed. we are ready to engage in constructive dialogue with civil society, with ngos, with all those who peacefully express their concerns about globalisation, but we reject and condemn the violence that has more than marred the recent demonstrations.
commission. – madam president and honourable members, i am glad to present on behalf of the president of the commission a report on the g7/g8 summit in genoa. from 20 to 22 july this year, the commission president took part in the g7/g8 summit, together with the current president of the european council, guy verhofstadt. the summit took a number of important decisions. however, most of the media attention was focused on events taking place outside the summit, on the city streets. these events confirmed that the g8 needs to engage in a genuine dialogue with civil society and with non-member countries. demonstrators must have the opportunity to express their opinions. this is an inalienable right not only guaranteed in law but also defended in practice. people are genuinely uneasy about various aspects of globalisation, and we must pay attention to their concerns. however, violence disfigures any demonstration, even one held in an honourable cause. we cannot allow peaceful demonstrators expressing genuine fears and concerns to be tarred with the same brush as those who commit acts of violence. to combat violence, whether at gothenburg or genoa, we need to improve european cooperation in the field of law and order. the justice and home affairs council discussed these issues in late july, and the events at genoa show how urgent it now is to take action. but i would like to remind all of you that according to article 33 of the treaty the primary responsibility for the maintenance of law and order lies with the member states. member states recognise, however, that better cooperation is required between their law enforcement and judicial authorities in order to safeguard public order at european council meetings and similar events. the decisions of the justice and home affairs council were built upon the existing structures and existing legal instruments, which means that there will be no specific institutions to deal with these issues. it goes without saying that the commission has always stressed the need for all police and judicial actions to respect the civil and human rights of the citizens and the legislation providing for privacy protection and for the respect of civil liberties. we have to reflect on a political response to the two hundred thousand demonstrators in genoa. it is the profound belief of the commission that the union should promote an active dialogue with bona fide organisations which peacefully exercise their rights to freely express opinion and assemble. we believe that the european parliament should play a major role in promoting this dialogue. the demonstrators want us to tackle the widening gulf between the northern and southern hemispheres of our world, a gulf created by inequality, poverty, disease and war. in spite of our efforts and even some achievements over the past forty years, tragic disparities and social injustice remain and we have a long way to go in overcoming them. this is the challenge not only for the g8 but also for our europe in the years and decades ahead. the union has to support those political leaders, especially in africa, who are on the side of democracy. it has to prevent illegal trafficking in arms between the north and the south. and it has to implement policies that strengthen the economies of the poorest nations. policies such as the “everything but arms” initiative that has opened up our markets to products from the least-developed countries are a good example of this approach. fortunately, public opinion today is increasingly concerned about where the world is going and people recognise that this north-south inequality cannot be tolerated. the commission is well aware of the growing importance of civil society and is eager to involve citizens’ associations and ngos in shaping and implementing eu policies. as the commission president said yesterday, when discussing governance in this plenary, “the union is still the only concrete, practical and democratic response to globalisation”. it is therefore essential that the european institutions operate on the basis of five fundamental principles: openness, participation, accountability, effectiveness and coherence. we need to engage in an open and systematic dialogue with civil society and to involve all stakeholders in designing the union’s policies. it is also essential to strengthen the union’s voice and influence in the world so that europe can make a greater contribution to international prosperity and stability. multilateral institutions are the key to harnessing globalisation, but of course we underline that we want to help reform the multilateral organisations, making them more open, more accountable and more democratic. in this connection, a particularly important event took place in genoa – the “outreach” meeting with leaders of several non-member countries. this was a very useful meeting, enabling important representatives of southern countries to express their views directly and frankly and to discuss matters openly with the g8 heads of state and government. as a result, the g8 decided to make africa one of the main topics of next year’s summit in canada. the commission for its part can be satisfied with several of the decisions taken at genoa. the documents on trade, food safety, climate change and communicable diseases, as well as the emphasis on africa, by and large reflect the commission’s preparatory contributions to the summit. on trade, there was complete agreement on the need to launch a new round of talks at the ministerial conference in doha in november. this view was, by the way, reiterated last week in mexico city. during the discussion on trade, president putin stated that russia was ready to follow the example set by the european union in its “everything but arms” initiative. on food safety, the european side successfully insisted that the final communication include a reference to the precautionary principle. the g8 had a very long discussion on climate change, opening the way for the conclusions reached at bonn a few days later and i believe you have discussed these conclusions at this part session. the summit also provided an opportunity to launch the global health fund. the purpose of this international fund, which will not be limited to the g8 countries, is to help reduce poverty by dealing with the problem of aids, malaria and tuberculosis. the community, for its part, is committed to providing eur 120 million. as on every occasion when the current presidency of the union is held by a state that is not a member of the g8, the union was represented at the summit by the council president and by the president of the commission. the tandem arrangement worked extremely well and i am pleased to be able to underline that here. we are sensitive to the fact that several aspects of the g8 will have to be changed in the future and not just cosmetically. the commission, for its part, will encourage a return to the original spirit of the g8 summits. indeed a joint decision was taken in genoa to reduce the size of delegations and the summit to be held in canada next year will be much simpler and – we hope – more effective. the results have been tangible and positive. the g8 summit has been reduced to a mere matter of public policy. there is much to be said about what has happened, about the exploitation that has been done in this parliament too, which must not become the arena for debates on major national issues, must not become the place to transfer national debates. we cannot, of course, challenge globalisation - and we must say this clearly - with demonstrations which are legitimate when there are no acts of violence, but we cannot challenge globalisation, we cannot challenge the summits with violent demonstrations, by attacking the police. the investigations by the italian judiciary show that there is also a responsibility for european union citizens who came to italy from outside to organise violent demonstrations. i would like to conclude, mr president, by confirming our solidarity with the italian police forces and also by pointing out the need for greater cooperation between the police forces and the interior ministers, cooperation which perhaps was not sufficient at the g8 summit and on which we will have to work a lot. finally, i find the proposals that have been put forward in this parliament to put italy under observation ridiculous, because i believe that italy does not deserve lessons in democracy from any political force in this parliament.

the rapporteur. - mr president, it is a pity that after a whole day in which parliament has been discussing matters for which it has no legislative competence, it is only in the afternoon and then in the evening that we are going to be talking about the things we are legislators on. it is a bit of a vice of parliamentary degradation and we should somehow try to resist these media-friendly temptations. that said, the european commission's proposal for a directive is an important piece of work and a contribution to the defence of the rights and freedoms of the net, not only with regard to electronic communications of citizens in europe, and for that we congratulate ourselves on the work that has been done. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos, and whether he has not taken a decision on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to asbestos. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to apply the provisions of the directive to the transport of dangerous goods by road. so it is probably this legislative method that should be called into question! that said, however, i do believe that important privacy rules for european citizens are being guaranteed and specified, which the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs and its rapporteur have fully supported in committee and which have been passed. i would now like to focus on two points, perhaps more politically controversial: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the data protection rules are applied in the member states. on the first point, the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs has taken note of the european commission's intention not to grant the kind of 'white card' that some member states would like to have in order to intercept and access the personal data of union citizens, for example by accessing data collected by telephone companies. the european commission is right to insist on this point. we hope that it will also follow us in the further request made by the committee on civil liberties and human rights to put a precise limit on all derogations from european directives and rules which are not completely exceptional, based on a specific law and accessible to the public and limited in time, with the consequence that we have written in the report of prohibiting general surveillance. i think it is important that the european commission can support this, because i believe that the greatest danger to the privacy of citizens lies precisely in the omnipotence of the state in accessing personal data. on the other point - unsolicited commercial e-mails - i preferred, and the committee on freedoms and rights has followed me, not to accept the european commission's proposal to impose a harmonised european opt-in system, but to leave the choice of opt-in and opt-out to the member states. in fact, i believe that both systems are ineffective in stopping so-called spamming: the real spammers who clog up your inbox are people who do it fraudulently, with hidden addresses, and therefore have no interest in respecting either the opt-in or the opt-out. in the so-called opt-in ban i see a danger to freedom of expression, for those who trade correctly: the freedom of expression is not so easy to separate commercial messages from non-commercial messages: there may be journalistic or political texts that are sponsored and, as such, could be treated as commercial messages. i also believe that there are self-regulatory tools, filters, technologies that can solve this problem much more flexibly and effectively than courtrooms can. the costs to the consumer, precisely because of the liberalization of telecommunications which the european commission is pushing for in the other directives in the package, are also likely to fall. so with flat rates, with broadband connectivity, the cost issue also becomes less and less important than a few seconds of connection: that is why, in view of the possible risks of the opt-in system, we have opposed a single harmonised european system.

- mr president, the european commission's communication on the secure information society is a complement to previous initiatives, in particular the overall action plan for a telematic europe, and will require further action in a field which is constantly evolving. the report by mr cederschiöld approves this initiative and enriches it with appropriate legislative measures, suggestions for cooperation instruments to increase the effectiveness of the fight against cybercrime and to ensure a balance between the needs of preventing and punishing crime and respecting the rights of citizens to freedom. this balance, which is guaranteed by the charter of fundamental rights, must always be the compass that guides the work of the european union, and for this reason too the comprehensive and accurate cederschiöld report deserves our full support. the commission proposal for a directive is also very welcome, since it aims to bring the protection of personal data in the electronic communications sector up to date and not to leave things as they are, since harmonization is necessary. the cappato report proposes useful additions to the directive which strengthen the limits on the intervention of public authorities in private life, especially with regard to forms of generalized electronic surveillance, which we discussed this morning. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in other respects, however, the cappato report reduces the protection of citizens' privacy, which is offered by the proposed directive, precisely where we have legislative competence. the commission proposes that data relating to the electronic addresses and mobile phones of european citizens can be included in public lists and disseminated on the internet only if the persons concerned have given their prior consent. the cappato report, on the other hand, proposes that e-mail addresses and mobile phone data should be included in public lists and that anyone concerned should be able to ask for and obtain exclusion from these lists. a similar difference - as we have already heard - concerns the regulation of unsolicited communications for direct marketing purposes. the european commission proposes that messages should only be sent to those who have given their consent, as is the case with faxes today. the cappato report proposes that the opt-out system may also be adopted. if one considers the speed with which a list of e-mail addresses can spread across the network and become known to an unlimited number of interested parties who send unsolicited messages, and if one considers the cost in time and money of deleting these unsolicited messages and of requiring the various senders to stop sending them, one can measure the burden on citizens of the adoption of the opt-out system. this is a prospect which risks discouraging, discouraging the spread of the use of the internet and electronic commerce. in a funny article an italian journalist wrote: "i thought i had bought a mobile phone, but i found a tamagochi, that japanese toy that needs to be cared for like a child. my phone company never leaves me alone, they text me a lot, like a teenager; he asks me if i want to enter a contest, if i know of certain new discounts, he says hello when i go abroad, he welcomes me when i return to my country. "think about when your cell phone number and your email address are known not only to your supplier but to all the possible suppliers in the world, who are no longer just selling you stuff but want you to like their brand, to seduce you, to belong to you. if we want e-commerce to have a future, we cannot force consumers to spend their time deleting unwanted messages or chasing the senders down and begging them to leave them alone. there is no reason why e-mail should not be afforded the same protection as fax. the higher level of protection of rights also ensures greater consumer confidence.
