the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the draft report i am bringing to your attention is based on the proposal for a council regulation no 1969/88 establishing a mechanism for medium-term financial support for the balance of payments of the member states. article 119 of the treaty provides that in the event of difficulties or even a threat to the balance of payments, the council is to put in place 'mutual competition' so as not to jeopardise the proper functioning of the common market. this mechanism may be activated by the council on the initiative of the member state concerned by a difficult situation or on the initiative of the commission. the first thing that should distinguish this institution, at least in its approach, is the speed with which it intervenes and, in response to the loan received, the adoption of all the economic policy measures needed to restore a sustainable balance of payments situation. since its entry into force on 25 june 1988, the mechanism has not been widely implemented. the eib has only been used twice, in 1991 for a loan of eur 2.2 billion, of which only eur 1 billion was disbursed, and in 1993 for an amount of eur 8 billion, of which only the first tranches were paid. it is immediately apparent that many of the european possibilities open to the member states are not being fully exploited. the commission's proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling of foodstuffs is a very good one. more knowledge vehicles might be appropriate in order to encourage and empower members to make better use of the opportunities offered. turning to the draft report, it should be noted that, following the conclusions adopted by the ecofin council on 13 october 1997 and in accordance with article 12 of the current regulation, the commission has submitted a report to the council and parliament on the maintenance of this instrument. in this connection, it should be noted that this attitude is due to the fact that, since the use of this mechanism is possible only for states with a derogation, this possibility could recur with enlargement. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the ceiling is reduced from eur 16 billion to eur 12 billion. the council adopts the decision after consulting the european parliament - amendment no 3, article 9 - and examines the adjustment of the mechanism every two years, not every three years - amendment no 4, article 11. the possibility of subsequent amendments also remains with regard to the ceiling. the committee on budgets' amendment - amendment no 1, recital 6bis (new) - to the establishment of a protection mechanism against potential insolvency risks and related claims for reimbursement was also welcomed. we think that is a rather remote possibility. with enlargement the new member states have begun considerable efforts to put their accounts and balance of payments in order. the community budget is protected against loans to third countries by the guarantee fund mechanism. a similar mechanism, but with a lower financial commitment, can also be considered for financing to countries with a derogation. the conclusions are as follows: first, the loans granted are guaranteed directly by the community budget at 100%; second, the risk of default, which can never be excluded, is covered by an appropriate safeguard mechanism. thirdly, the instrument should be used more and better with the enlargement of the european union. fourthly and lastly, the management of loans is entrusted to the ecb, which replaces the commission previously in charge.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, first of all my warmest thanks to president caroline jackson for the special treatment she has given to this report; i would also like to express my sincere thanks to all the shadow rapporteurs, with whom we have had a very good working relationship, and to the commission officials, the representatives of the various associations and all those colleagues who have contributed to improving this important and delicate directive by making qualified amendments. the directive fills a gap that has existed in europe so far in terms of blood quality and safety standards. the aim of this directive is primarily to protect donors and patients, and ultimately to provide for uniform standards for all member states, ensuring the highest possible level of quality and safety of blood, blood components and blood derivatives, not only of blood available in the countries of the european union but also of blood imported from third countries. the directive provides for a continuous update, at least once a year, of laboratory tests for the identification of pathogens of a bacterial, viral or other infectious nature, as well as an update of the most sophisticated technologies for more effective and safe sterilization of blood and its components. it also makes recommendations to the member states to strengthen scientific research in this field. the presence of a new european directive providing for the same quality standards in individual member states will allow the free circulation of blood and its components at the level of the countries of the european union and the disappearance of undesirable restrictions on the movement of donors from one country to another. high quality and safety standards must be applied at all stages of the transfusion process, from collection to control by specific laboratory tests, to the collection, processing, storage, distribution and use of whole human blood and its components. quality and efficacy assurance should therefore cover the suitability of blood and plasma donors and their components, as well as transfusion medicine facilities, the qualification and training of medical, technical and nursing staff and the mechanisms for verification, inspection and control, and a system for tracing the blood pathway from donor to recipient. the european parliament has provided for the person responsible to have a medical degree, preferably with a specialization in haematology or transfusion medicine or another related discipline. in order to better understand the importance of controlling each stage, we must unfortunately remember those terrible adverse reactions that have occurred and that we hope will not occur in the future, such as aids, hepatitis b and c infections or other infections, sometimes fatal, such as anaphylactic shock or septic shock. the commission accepted the rapporteur's proposal to delete the annexes, since they are extremely sensitive and need to be updated periodically, using a simple and flexible mechanism. finally, the principle that all donations must be made on a voluntary and unpaid basis has been reinforced by numerous amendments from parliament. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this. if donor incentives were immediately and strictly prohibited, given the unfortunately still limited number of donors and the lack of blood self-sufficiency in europe, enormous difficulties could arise for patients, with even life-threatening risks. blood and plasma shortages are a well-known problem in europe. i hope that the house will accept the amendment tabled by the ppe and the liberal group which, on the one hand, safeguards the principle of voluntary and free donations but, on the other, allows for a transitional period for the implementation of this principle. an oral amendment by mr lisi indicates that by the end of december 2008 all donations must be made on a voluntary and unpaid basis. this principle must be an objective which the individual member states must encourage to be achieved, with the necessary gradualness to avoid possible catastrophic effects on man. as regards imported blood - amendment no 43 - it should be made clear that the criteria to which this amendment refers must relate to the quality and safety of blood. in conclusion, mr president, the guarantee of high standards of quality, efficacy and safety of blood, as provided for in the directive, will give citizens of the european union greater peace of mind regarding any treatment with blood, but also greater confidence in the european institutions and in the national authorities.
commission. – mr president, i would be very sorry to shock mr lund and, if i can explain my thinking on this, perhaps it might relieve your concerns. rather than put it the way you put it, i would say that it does not necessarily follow that blood from a remunerated source is any less safe than blood from an unremunerated source and the studies that have been produced more recently on this issue tend to support that proposition. reference has been made to some studies that go in the other direction, but my advice is that those studies are old studies and the more modern view is in accordance with the view that i have just expressed.

the committee on petitions has already adopted a number of amendments. - mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating the ombudsman on his extremely competent work, especially in defence of the rights of all citizens of the union. i would like to thank my colleague, mrs almeida garrett, who has been able to build her position with great skill and has also succeeded in an intelligent mediation. as always, society moves forward and laws follow the progress, however fast, of society, and so there is a slowness of the law in relation to customs. i therefore think it is right that the ombudsman has proposed an amendment to article 3 of his statute, which dates back to the 1990s. i think that the commission has done a good job in this respect, and i hope that the council will be able to take the necessary steps to ensure that the commission's proposals are implemented. this is because there is a difficulty and a divergence, including a legal one, in the control of administrative practices and the control of the political acts of the members of the institutions. a greater balance was therefore needed, even if there was no desire to curb what could be an inspection and investigation activity, for the sake of clarity and above all in defence of the proximity and transparency which are fundamental pillars contained in the union treaties. i believe that the solution adopted, with a partial revision to which the ombudsman also contributed in his last letter, in which he accepts the positions of rapporteur garrett and the commissioner, is the best and that in the future it will be possible to proceed adequately, in compliance with community legislation, also to a more systematic and more legal revision of the same statute, always in accordance with the principle of proximity and transparency which must regulate - and it is desirable that it be maintained - the closeness of european citizens to the community institutions.
chairman of the committee on petitions. - mr president, at the end of this debate i would like to thank all the rapporteurs - mr bösch, mr perry, mr garrett, mr sbarbati, mr camisón asensio - and all the colleagues who are committed to the institution of petitions; i also thank the european ombudsman who, from his vantage point, is taking action to defend citizens. we are certainly working together and we are also working for european citizenship, because the institution of european citizenship finds a champion in parliament, which is the most authoritative institution in this respect. we have made a great deal of progress, and i must acknowledge to the european commission a particular sensitivity, demonstrated by the preparation with which officials present their reports to the committee on petitions. on the other hand, more european citizens are also using petitions to raise personal, social or environmental issues: we must respond to them in a comprehensive and satisfactory way, always less platonic and with superficial answers. the petitions highlight the way forward for the union before the citizens can enjoy a secure life. we certainly do not think that there should be a flat and amorphous homologation in the european union, but rather, above all, we think that cultural differences should be harmonized, taking these differences as the true richness of the institutions. we have entered a period of reform, defence and strengthening of the institution of petitions, and we believe that this reform period will enable us to defend our citizens better and, at the same time, to make the european institutions better known to this growing population.

the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the own-initiative report on 25 years of application of the community rules to mountain farming is on the european parliament's agenda as the international year of mountains 2002 approaches. the commission has therefore decided to launch a series of activities at international, national and local level in the coming year to promote the sustainable development of mountain areas. the main objectives of this year are to raise awareness and knowledge about mountain ecosystems, their dynamics and functioning, to promote and preserve the cultural heritage of mountain communities, and to preserve and develop sustainable resources in mountain regions to ensure the quality of life of people today and in the future. finally, mountain areas account for 30% of the total area and 20% of the agricultural area of the european union, and 10% of the eu population. i am convinced that the european union should also take the forthcoming year of the mountains as an opportunity to give concrete consideration to the specific concerns of mountain regions and to recognise mountain areas as an indispensable habitat. the quality of life in mountain areas must be preserved and protected at the same time as the still threatening migration must be stopped. this report is also the de facto opinion of parliament on the year of the mountains and is intended to serve as a basis and a catalogue of demands for the commission and the council. in the report before you, which was almost unanimously approved by the committee on agriculture and rural development, i am advocating in principle an overall eu strategy for mountain areas. the report contains many new and, in my view, practical proposals in this respect, which i ask you to take up in the forthcoming vote. the commission is therefore invited to present a communication this year setting out the eu's actions in the context of the international year of mountains. i also think it is appropriate that this communication should contain an overall approach to the areas concerned with a view to the future after 2006 and to enlargement. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. i would like to make it clear, however, that the overall approach required must be developed with due regard for the principle of subsidiarity. despite the often similar problems and difficulties, it is a fact that mountain areas also have differences and specificities and therefore there can be no universal patent solution. common problems can be better dealt with across borders. i therefore propose in my report a solution which takes account of the following areas: agriculture and forestry, transport, tourism, energy and water management, regional planning, nature conservation and the preservation of the common cultural heritage. i would like to make a few brief comments on the specific demands contained in the report. agriculture: in summary, this calls for the development of the second pillar of the agricultural policy and thus the development of the rural area, while taking due account of the environmental and landscape-management function of agriculture and the multifunctional nature of agriculture. the search for common problem-solving strategies in the form of regional conventions, the development and updating of criteria and data on mountain areas, as well as the financing of practical and site-specific projects through the sixth framework programme, the development of the necessary basic infrastructure and training and education to ensure that the population is kept adequately informed, the strengthening of transport networks in mountain areas, taking into account the principles of sustainability, in order to safeguard these areas as habitats, natural and economic areas. this means that access roads to yards and alleys, for example, must be guaranteed, while major roads must be built to the strictest ecological compatibility criteria. finally, the need for a specific treatment of mountain areas is also necessary, not least with regard to enlargement. the forthcoming year of the mountains is an ideal time, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, to deal concretely with tomorrow's proposal. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.

to the more specific considerations and recommendations concerning the community: firstly, the education sector is of crucial importance to the strategy of poverty reduction, which is the overriding objective of community development policy. the commission shares the view that clear objectives must be defined, that education must be integrated into poverty reduction and that civil society must also be involved. this is the position taken by the commission in its negotiations with the developing countries on poverty reduction strategies. it is very important for the commission to play an view of the european parliament that better coordination and complementarity between community action and the action of the member states, through the education expert group, and increased cooperation with unesco and the association for the development of education in africa are essential to increase the effectiveness of community assistance. to this end, the commission shall strengthen its cooperation with unesco, in particular by supporting unesco in its task of coordinating education for all partners. the commission also participates in the working group set up to implement the dakar framework for action. it also promotes the objectives of education for all in its negotiations on the acp strategies for the 9th edf. as regards the difficult question of establishing a global fund for basic education, the commission considers that such a fund is not a viable solution because of the commission's procedures for programming and implementing aid. the commission does not, however, reject a global initiative such as that envisaged in the dakar framework, even though the detailed arrangements for its implementation will have to be discussed. thirdly, the issue of children's rights is closely linked to the gender issue in general. the educational objectives for children, and in particular for girls, cannot be fully achieved unless women are given equal opportunities in the family and in different societies. the commission is therefore strongly committed to paying particular attention to the training needs of girls in developing countries. it is currently preparing an action plan on gender equality to address this concern. it also takes gender issues into account in all its own educational programmes. the question before us, mr president, commissioner, is what cohesion policy we should aim to devise in the new context of enlargement. the answer must be articulated on two levels: on the one hand, the principles that will guide cohesion policies from 2006 onwards should be identified; on the other hand, we must set priorities. i believe that cohesion policy should be guided by two principles: on the one hand, equality of opportunity; on the other hand, there is regionalization. modern economic theories teach us, with a wealth of detail and supported by ample empirical evidence, that the success of local development policies is closely linked to the increasing autonomy of decision-making of individuals and the design of regional policies that are accepted by the voters themselves. similarly, to speak of regionalization is to design economic policies at the local level so that they respect and value the comparative advantages of each region, and local government institutions so that they make collective choices with the support of a real democratic base, subject to a constraint of control by the electorate that makes them politically accountable. the achievement of these objectives certainly requires a new kind of statistical information on the realities of economies, at local, national and community level. it is no longer enough to have per capita income data to assess individual access opportunities in european regions; much more is needed: we need indicators on the degree of access to resources, indicators that measure the enjoyment of economic freedoms, that take account of the enjoyment of fundamental human rights, that measure, more generally, the quality of life.
mr president, the statements we have heard, both from the council and from commissioner barnier, and the speeches by all our colleagues, have clearly confirmed that cohesion policies remain one of the fundamental pillars of the union's policies and that enlargement requires not only their reiteration but also their strengthening. however, i think the knots are different. here are a few: first, are the tools we have used over the years to manage imbalances that are becoming more and more differentiated still relevant? can generic indicators, such as gross domestic product, or schematic percentages, such as 75%, continue to be the only parameters for clarifying and classifying eligibility? can a false egalitarian paradigm still hold, whereby equal measures are taken for only statistically equal subjects and contexts? secondly: do the key principles of subsidiarity and additionality mean the same thing today as they did 20 years ago, when there was a different institutional set-up in the european union? is the idea, put forward a few days ago by mr giuliano amato, former president of the italian council, of a profound innovation which would leave the european commission in charge of major strategic investments and decentralize development measures at the territorial level so far from the truth and so far from the possible? i really hope that the debate in the coming months will have the courage to tackle these issues as well.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the framework proposal we are discussing here establishes the european community's successor to the ecsc. the net revenue from the investment of the assets of the research fund for coal and steel would constitute revenue for the budget of the european union. this revenue would be earmarked for the financing of research projects in sectors related to the coal and steel industries. the research fund would be managed by the commission; the amounts from the fund would be allocated to the coal and steel sectors at the rate of 27.2% and 72.8% respectively. this allocation may be amended only by a unanimous decision of the council. the proposal also provides that the administrative expenditure resulting from the liquidation, investment and management of the research fund will be covered by the general budget. in this short summary, ladies and gentlemen, i have not forgotten our role: the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. i am firmly opposed to the commission's approach, which in its framework proposal merely provides for consultation of parliament on the financial and technical guidelines for the fund. they have painted us with a role so passive that it is in complete contradiction with the present demands for transparency and democracy and with powers even less than those which our parliament exercises in budgetary matters. in my report i made a number of requests to the council: first of all, i asked for the codecision procedure to be applied. secondly, i have asked for the annual interest of the fund to be entered in full in the budget as pre-allocated revenue by creating a specific line on the revenue and expenditure side, in accordance with the principles of budgetary specificity and neutrality, in line with the provisions of the interinstitutional agreement and the financial regulation. thirdly, i have asked that the administrative costs of this item, estimated at some eur 8.4 million, be paid through this same heading, otherwise they would have to be covered by the general budget. i have also included the possibility of changing the allocation of research between the coal and steel sectors, as a result of the increase in production due to enlargement itself. i note that in the resolution before the house there is a reference to the ecb, which i ask you not to take into account. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this. as regards the request for the use of the codecision procedure, i would point out that the commission's legislative proposal is based on the treaties and the nice protocol, which states that the council, acting unanimously on a proposal from the commission and after consulting the european parliament, shall adopt all the provisions necessary for the implementation of this protocol. in practice, they take away all the power of parliament, despite the fact that the administrative expenditure of the coal and steel fund should be covered by the general budget. this means that parliament should approve additional expenditure and give the fund a discharge without being able to influence in any way the implementation of its activities. my request to use the codecision procedure is therefore not a request to change the legal basis but only the article. the commission document refers to the treaty establishing the european community, without specifying any article, and to the protocol annexed to the treaty of nice, article 2 - where it is provided that the european parliament is only responsible for consultation - a treaty which is not yet in force and which will most likely not be in force by july 2002. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. moreover, even if the protocol annexed to the treaty of nice were to enter into force, it would only refer to the procedure for the approval of the global package, and not to the annual decisions. i therefore propose to ask for the codecision procedure as provided for in article 2 (5) and (1) of the treaty establishing the european community, and on this point i hope and believe that i can have the support of this house, as i have had in the committee on budgets. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft budget for the 1998 financial year. as i have said before, ladies and gentlemen, we are facing a very special situation, one that will certainly never be repeated. the only treaty with an expiry date is the one whose legal successor depends to a large extent on a treaty which has not yet been ratified and which will probably not be ratified in time. in my opinion, and with the support of the political group coordinators in the committee on budgets, i believe that if the approach i have given in the legislative amendments is adopted by this house, we will have to enter into negotiations with the council and the commission before giving the european parliament its opinion, in order to try to increase the role of our institution. that is why, after the vote on the legislative amendments, i will ask the presidency to postpone the vote on the legislative resolution until we have checked whether there is a possibility of an agreement with the commission and the council to increase the role of parliament. i hope you'll agree with my approach.

mr president, in saying that our group fully supports the evans report, i would nevertheless like to stress two points: firstly, the need for a rapid procedure for the examination of refugee applications. the national states should be aware that many of their problems, but especially many of the problems of immigrant refugees, would be overcome if these questions were dealt with in a short time. many refugees - many people who have every right to be recognized as such - wait for months or years, without receiving benefits, without work, sliding gradually towards illegality, often drawn into areas of organized and non-organized crime. it is therefore necessary to shorten these very long periods. secondly, it must be understood and established that the notion of a 'safe country' is a notion which can be overcome by the specific test of the treatment an individual receives in his country. i am saying that the notion of safe country must be a relative assumption, because many refugees flee from a safe country because they are personally persecuted. it is therefore necessary that this concept should not be an absolute one, but that the conditions of treatment of individual refugees - that is, the conditions which lead them to flee to another country - should be examined individually, and that this could lead to the abrogation of the above-mentioned concept of a safe third country.

in writing. - (it) three reasons underlie all racist attitudes: first, ignorance of the other, which can generate fear and therefore rejection; secondly, the bad faith, linked to arrogance, of those who want to feel superior anyway, perhaps driven by an unconscious inferiority complex; third, the will - political, economic and religious - of those who, by dominating others, want to acquire more and more power. if it is clear that a strong and widespread cultural activity of teaching respect and acceptance of others is necessary, it is equally clear that the civilized world must fight by all means the political, cultural, economic and religious systems that foster the birth of racism and that are based on it. respect for differences can therefore, in the civilized world, only go hand in hand with constant and deliberate action to achieve the goal of respect for human rights and the dignity of the person everywhere on the planet. the attitude of civilized cultures, whether western or not, which oppose, for example, religious or ritual practices which threaten the physical integrity of individuals or oppress their personality, cannot therefore be considered racism. these are practices which do not yet regard women as subjects who can enjoy all their rights, but as objects subject to customs which prevent and limit their participation in social and political life. sadly, throughout human history, racism has been perpetuated by both groups and individuals. today, when condemning the racisms of the past, politics must not make the mistake of creating new ones. we cannot ignore a form of political racism which persists today: the racism of those who condemn the ideas of others simply because they express a different political opinion. we therefore call on parliament, the commission and the council to take more decisive action, both within and outside the community, to promote a culture of mutual respect among peoples and governments. in order to be such, this culture cannot tolerate attitudes, thoughts and actions which deny human dignity, whether conceived under the aegis of a religion, a cultural thesis or an economic or political project. i am therefore voting in favour of the resolution.

and i am referring in particular to my own country, italy, but also to others, such as germany - have experienced a period of cyclical economic growth that has been as favourable as the cyclical cyclone, that is, they have postponed the reforms that should have been implemented to strengthen public budgets and make companies more competitive, and have yielded to the pressure of trade unions and business associations that demanded greater state aid. in doing so, they did not prepare the european economies for the inevitable negative cycle, especially the severe one that followed 9/11. mr president, i believe that the tax burden in europe is still too high today. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. there is a risk that must be denounced - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the functioning of the internal market is only guaranteed if, in an area without internal frontiers, the appropriate welcome scientific developments. the commission has repeatedly found that consumer goods in commerce no longer meet the safety standards that are known to exist. that is why it is all the more irrespective of the form in which they are marketed. a decision which takes account of market developments, in the sense that it also covers distance selling and electronic commerce. the question of consumer safety is not just about children and the elderly as the weakest members of our society, as has been repeatedly emphasized, but about safety for all. it is also absolutely right and necessary cause damage to health there. i believe that one of the most important points in this respect is the inclusion of trade. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the safety requirements - the report (a5-0263/2001) by mr khanbhai, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the communications from the commission to the council and the european parliament on: - accelerating the fight against the main communicable diseases in the context of poverty reduction (com (2000) 585 - c5-0014/2001 - 2000/2006 (cos)) and - the action programme: accelerating the fight against hiv/aids, malaria and tuberculosis in the context of poverty reduction (com (2001) 96 - c5-0112/2001 - 2001/2006 (cos)).
- mr president, despite the global growth of recent decades, progress remains inadequate and unevenly distributed. poverty and injustice, terrible conditions, both socially and health-wise, remain the bitter reality for many developing countries. 30% of the world's population lives in extreme poverty, a situation exacerbated by continued population growth and the inadequacy - or rather, the decline - of aid, assistance and development cooperation policies. europe is a relatively exceptional case, but not to the extent that it corrects a negative world trend. in the developing world, new challenges - such as urbanization, environmental degradation and pollution, local wars and the scourge of aids, coupled with the previously unthinkable resurgence of malaria and tb - threaten to set us back. in general, i am wary of statistics, which differ - as we have seen - even between the various directorates-general of the commission and often seem to be subject to ideological prejudices. however, there is no doubt that the explosive growth of the richer countries has further alienated the poorer countries. among the indicators of poverty, the female figure stands out: the majority of the poor, the poorest of the poor, are women, as are the majority of the illiterate, and women continue to work more, earn more and count less. it is difficult to deny or underestimate the link which nevertheless remains between poverty, disease, illiteracy and population growth, a link which is most clearly demonstrated in the female indicator, in the suffering of women, in gender inequalities. on the other hand, the reports of the commission and parliament on the demographic issue seem to me to be evasive, if not reticent. the reports focus on the fight against aids, malaria, tuberculosis, and they go into sophisticated technical analysis and reform proposals that are likely to improve our response to poverty - first of all on the issue of medicines and health services - without proposing anything about how to make more effective policies of population control, healthy and sustainable fertility, free and conscious motherhood, as if this topic had disappeared from our horizon. yet this remains the crucial question. consider the facts: in purely numerical terms, never before have so many people been lifted out of poverty. yet, because of continued population growth, there are more poor people in the world today than at any time in history. since the end of the last century, the world's population has quadrupled, from 1.5 billion to 6 billion. the largest growth is in asia, india, china, indochina and, above all, indonesia. the growth trend in the rich countries has, on the contrary, now stopped, but the balance achieved depends on the increase in average life expectancy, which compensates for the birth-rate crisis. africa, in turn, has experienced a population explosion, mainly due to the drop in infant mortality rates. today, this trend seems to be more contained, not because of the success of demographic policies, but because of the epidemics, especially - as we have said - of aids, tb and malaria. africa engages us and moves us, but africa is not the world, and it is itself different in its various parts and certainly needs more than any other region a demographic policy that is more attentive to the status of women. in the rest of the world, not just in the rich countries, there is a relative slowdown in the population growth seen in recent decades but, if you look deeper, you have to see, at the same time, a lower fertility and an increase in life expectancy, that is, a population that continues to grow and age in general situations, and cases of overpopulation in some regional and local areas. in conclusion, a more effective fight against poverty cannot avoid or ignore the issue of population control, which is certainly a matter of economic and cultural growth, but which is not without targeted instruments and appropriate experience in the field of prevention and contraception. history teaches us that there has never been so much growth and so much poverty. experience shows that it is futile to try to dry a flooded room without shutting off the taps.
- madam president, i think you have been informed of the debate which took place in the chamber this morning at the opening of the sitting. i do not intend to reopen the debate, because i am sure that vice-president imbeni has referred the matter to you. we await your reply. i would like to ask you to vote at the end of the vote, because i imagine that all the members will be voting.
commission. – mr president, i will respond to each of the five issues. the un world day to overcome extreme poverty is a welcome opportunity to highlight the continuing unacceptable levels of poverty and social exclusion across the world and to stress the need to intensify efforts for their eradication. being able to lead a life free from poverty and social exclusion is a fundamental human right. while the challenge of combating poverty and social exclusion is particularly acute in developing countries, it also remains an issue of major concern within the european union. the most recent available evidence shows that 18%, or over 60 million of our population in the eu, are at risk of falling into the category of being among the relative poor. this is a very high figure. at the european councils of lisbon, nice and stockholm, member states made a commitment to promote sustainable economic growth and quality employment which will reduce the risk of poverty and social exclusion as well as strengthening social cohesion in the union between 2001 and 2010. the intention is to reaffirm and further enhance the importance of the european social model and to ensure that social policy has an equal status alongside economic and employment policies and that all three reinforce each other. to underpin their commitment, the council developed common objectives in the fight against poverty and social exclusion. it also agreed that these objectives be taken forward by member states from 2001 onwards in the context of two-year national action plans against poverty and social exclusion. furthermore, the council established a new open method of coordination which encourages member states to work together to improve the impact on social inclusion of policies in fields such as social protection, employment, health, housing and education. the national action plans and the development of comparable indicators provide the framework for promoting exchange of good practice and mutual learning at community level. this will be supported from 2002 by a five-year community action programme on social inclusion which was finalised following a successful conciliation session involving parliament, the council and the commission on 18 september. all member states submitted their national action plans against poverty and social exclusion during june this year. the commission has been analysing these reports and expects to adopt a draft joint inclusion report on 10 october. this will be the first time that there has been such an eu-level analysis documenting and comparing the situation on poverty and social exclusion across all member states. it is intended that the joint report will be adopted at the employment and social policy council at the beginning of december so that it can be tabled and reviewed at the laeken european council. parallel to the work on the national action plans against poverty and social exclusion, work has been going on to develop a list of common indicators in the field of social inclusion. this will also be presented to and adopted at the laeken european council. on the basis of these developments, the laeken european council is expected to define the priorities and approaches that will guide efforts and cooperation at community level. the issues and concerns raised in the debate on these resolutions are thus well reflected in the initiatives that are being taken. however, a key challenge for the future will be to ensure that all community decisions, in economic and employment as well as social, policies, are assessed for their impact on social cohesion. while a lot is now happening, there is no room for complacency. days like the united nations world day for the eradication of poverty provide an important opportunity to remind us of the urgency of the challenge we face if we are to build a more inclusive and peaceful world free from the scandal of poverty and social exclusion. looking at the global aspect of this challenge, the first and most important point of criticism is the pathetic level of official development assistance, which is now 0.24%, far from the 0.7% that was promised. this is where everyone will be looking on that world day and we must come up with a european answer to that problem. another issue we will be facing is financing for development in march next year. τhe policy of the european union towards vietnam, as to all other countries, is to encourage and support continued progress on human rights and democratisation, and to raise concerns both publicly and in private where abuses or any deterioration in the situation are observed. we have to draw attention, however, to the tendency of the vietnamese administration to want to control the pace of change and to maintain “social cohesion” during transition to a market economy. of course, i do not need to remind you that the european union is opposed to capital punishment. in the case of vietnam, the number of offences where the death penalty can be applied was reduced last year. juvenile offenders, pregnant women and nursing mothers were also excluded. we welcome this progress, but we want to see the abolition of the death penalty altogether. our principal concern remains that of freedom of opinion. the original “offence” of professor nguyen dinh huy in 1992 was to be a co-founder of the “movement to unite the people and build democracy” a movement supported by vietnamese exiles in north america. before that, he had been an active anti-communist. the detention and interrogation of 15 people last month reported by human rights watch was apparently linked to a request to the government to set up an independent “national association to fight corruption”. the common thread in all these cases is that, despite some real progress, vietnam remains a country little accustomed to public dissent. the situation of the montagnards in the central provinces arose from a complex set of unresolved old problems, but was certainly exacerbated by the lack of effective channels of communication between the local people and the central government. what is needed in vietnam is continued progress in the country’s reform programme, so that the administration learns to deal with a wider range of views and to appreciate the value of accommodating dissent in the system of government. when mr patten was in hanoi last july he took the opportunity to raise some of these concerns with the vietnamese foreign minister. next month, we will be holding in hanoi a meeting of the ec-vietnam joint commission, at which all aspects of our relations will be reviewed, including our shared commitment to respect for human rights. we shall continue to raise particular issues of concern and individual cases and to encourage continued progress on human rights in vietnam. on the situation in uzbekistan, the commission shares the european parliament’s concern about the present situation in central asia. it is clear that the drought is causing damage in the aral sea area and particularly in western uzbekistan. for example the amu darya, where the major problems lie, is reported to have 70% of the normal water level in its upper reaches and just 40-45% in the lower stretches. in addition to natural causes, some structural reasons can explain the present situation such as poor maintenance of water-irrigation systems, inadequate water management at regional level between the newly independent states, and agricultural practices which are water demanding such as rice and cotton. lack of sustainability would be the short version of what this is all about. the july 2001 un assessment mission to western uzbekistan has attributed the absence of water to fundamental structural problems (such as irrigation and crop policies). so what is needed are ways to improve water management and agricultural practice. these activities are of a developmental nature. the response so far here is not falling within echo's mandate as such. we are, however, looking at this region from a humanitarian aid point of view, where we see a real risk of a negative fall-out from the situation in afghanistan. in fact, echo will include a strengthening of the ability to do something relating to this part of the world in a package soon. the absence of democracy, transparency and accountability, corruption at all levels and misuse of the flow of assistance provided by the international community are all part of the problem. since the independence of these countries, no real effort for maintaining the water system has been made. in addition, national rivalries between the countries in the region have blocked cooperation and also international efforts have been made more difficult. we have been active in central asia in trying to develop long-term projects linked with the structural causes of the drought. a tacis programme has been developed to fight against the consequences of the drying of the aral sea. the commission thinks that only long-term reform by the uzbekistan government itself can solve the current problem. emphasis should be put on: the creation of alternative forms of employment in the drought-affected areas to improve the irrigation systems in use in these affected areas and, in general, improve water conservation; the introduction of more drought-resistant and less water-hungry crops through further research into new crops, pilot schemes, model farms and whatever is necessary to farm in a sustainable manner in this environment. definitely a more effective allocation of water throughout the region is needed. we hope that tacis can develop activities to address these issues, in particular at regional level, but the challenge is huge relating to our actual means. let me turn to east timor. the democratic elections on 30 august were a cornerstone in the transition towards independence. the commission was pleased to see how peacefully the electoral process took place. the outcome – with no two-thirds majority for a single party – will require the constitutional assembly to work together and to seek a consensus. this will hopefully stabilise the political landscape even further. i think we can be justly proud of the contribution made by the european union election observer team, and i am happy to congratulate mr kreissl-dörfler on his leadership of the team of 24 observers. we will certainly look into the possibility of sending another observer team to the presidential elections in 2002. in general, i am very pleased with the cooperation with the parliament and parliament can be pleased with itself because of its ability to deliver high-quality electoral observation. the next steps in the formal process will be the adoption of a constitution, hopefully before christmas this year, followed by the election of a head of state by popular vote, probably around may 2002. then will come the withdrawal of untaet and the declaration of independence. this process seems to be well on track. at the same time, the evolution of the political process appears to be equally well under way. the highly commendable performance of untaet, the recent nomination of an interim cabinet and the further “timorisation” of management functions in the administration have all contributed to this process. east timor’s regional anchorage will add an additional foundation. east timor is at an historical juncture. the emergency phase is over. we now have the chance to get the ambitious independence process right. the international community has to consider now the long-term development issues. the canberra donors’ meeting last june outlined the current, clearly unsustainable, economic situation and signalled the need for further international assistance. there is a narrow tax base, a lack of skilled entrepreneurs, and rural poverty leading to demographic pressure on the urban areas. but there is a realistic perspective for substantial oil revenues coming on stream around 2005-2006. this could change the picture dramatically. the national budget could double and could hopefully ensure financial cover for basic state functions, as well as some stimulus for the economy. we need to support the effort of the east timorese to manage these oil activities better than what we have seen in many other developing countries. statistics will tell us that it should not be very difficult to do it much better, which may not even be good enough, but definitely it is an opportunity. i would say that so far, so good. it would be wonderful to have best practice demonstrated in this field. lack of transparency in this area is case-by-case across the world the real reason for a lot of trouble. against this politico-economic background, and as one of the major donors for east timor, the commission has identified its future role accordingly. we anticipate the need to support one of the poorest countries on earth until oil revenues provide a more stable economic basis. we will seek to create a development relationship based on a partnership philosophy. this means taking a realistic view of all the requirements. we are currently drafting a country strategy paper, outlining the sectors. most likely rural development and public administration will be where we concentrate our activities, suggesting appropriate financial targets for 2002-2006 within these sectors. this is how we will try to do it: focussing both on poverty alleviation and capacity building. as was said in the debate, east timor will also be able to benefit from the 'everything but arms'initiative, helping it to develop its foreign trade. finally, i turn to colombia. the commission shares the deep concern expressed by parliament concerning the deterioration of the situation in colombia, in particular, the continuation of human rights violations. the commission is seriously concerned with the situation of the peace process in colombia after the recent events that have taken place and it is waiting for the evaluation of this process announced by president pastrana. the commission intends to maintain its support to the colombian people through echo. eur 10 m are being spent this year. in addition, the commission has approved under its human rights budget, four new ngo projects worth over eur 3 m. as announced by myself in brussels on 30 april at the third meeting of the support group for the colombian peace process, the commission is currently finalising its proposal for a programme of a “peace laboratory” in the magdalena medio region in colombia. this programme envisages the support of actions and movements already being implemented by civil society at local and regional level. the commission sincerely hopes that conditions on the ground will allow an early implementation of this programme. the commission will continue encouraging the colombian government and all other relevant political forces to remain strongly committed to the peace process in colombia, especially during this time of unrest. as mr medina ortega said, this reminds us very much of the labours of sisyphus. it is true that it is hard to see progress, but there is no doubt that any relaxation or any type of giving up would definitely make things worse. this is our simple analysis and this is why we continue.

commission. - mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate mr goebbels on his report. it is a report which is read with interest and which is studied in depth in an attempt to make progress on the various issues it raises. i think your resolution is informed and balanced. we believe that it is a constructive contribution to a fundamental political debate and that it is timely. the debate on how to achieve a better functioning international monetary and financial system is at the heart of our mission to respond to globalisation. private capital flows - and this view is also reflected in your report - are the main source of growth, prosperity and productivity. if our aim is for countries, both developed and developing, to be able to share fully in the benefits of globalisation, i see no better alternative than the integration of financial markets and their functioning. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial markets are open to competition. this will be beneficial for operations which would otherwise be excessively risky for international investors and will benefit not only developing countries but also small and mediumsized enterprises in our countries. the economic benefits of financial globalisation are the result of the intensification of the internalisation links between markets and operators. the very nature of these links means that the disruptions which are transmitted in a modern economy as a result of this process of globalisation are more rapid, precisely because of the disappearance of the frontiers that existed twenty years ago. it is true that among the risks we are going to run into are going to be financial markets with excessive volatility in exchange rates and asset prices. there may be contagion between countries and there is a possibility of fluctuations in capital flows. it is true that in the context of economic and monetary union we have stimulated stability and growth through macroeconomic policies and structural reforms, which are key ingredients for strengthening our economy and avoiding or, better, fighting these financial turbulences. economic and monetary union thus contributes to strengthening the stability of the international context in our area. but it is true that some other alternatives have been proposed on a global scale. i agree with mr goebbels' thesis in his report. i believe that there are no panaceas to the challenge of consolidating the global financial system. this point is very clear in the report and i hope that its resolution will be read not only by those to whom this document is officially addressed and who deal with these issues professionally, but also by those who have legitimate concerns about the direction of the process of international economic and financial integration. the problems and challenges of financial market integration must be seen in a broader context, as is done in your report and as we, from the commission's point of view, intend to do in the study that the liège ecofin has commissioned us to produce on the responses to the challenges of globalisation and which we intend to present in february. what has happened in the last few years? i think that substantial progress has been made since the asian crises. efforts have been made to improve macroeconomic conditions. economies today are more resilient to external turbulence. more and more countries are adhering to internationally agreed codes and standards for greater transparency in their economies in their own self-interest. the g7 and imf ministers have made progress in some significant areas. we can think of the international financial institutions, for example, which are also clearly more transparent in their actions today: the international monetary fund itself has strengthened its capacity and is refining its instruments to enable it to analyse, assess and monitor the stability of the financial system more efficiently. and i also think that the coordination between the various national supervisory authorities has been substantially improved. true, we should not be satisfied with all of this. i think there is still a lot to be done and parliament's report points in the right direction. the commission is perfectly happy to accept your view that we must ensure that the private sector is fully involved in the resolution and management of financial crises. it is not just a question of fair sharing of responsibilities in times of crisis, but also of the proper and systematic involvement of the private sector, which is fundamental to effective crisis prevention, avoiding the accumulation of dangerous and, ultimately, unsustainable risk situations. in this connection, i note your call for the commission to consider the feasibility of introducing collective action clauses on financial instruments such as bonds. you know as well as i do that this position is not fully shared by the member states, but it is a view which the commission does defend, as we do all references to the fight against the financing of terrorism. the 9/11 attacks have brought the abuses of the financial system by terrorists to the forefront. the commission has already taken some measures. you yourselves have worked efficiently to complete the codecision process for the second directive on money laundering. however, i think we must move on. we are at the beginning of a process which will be long and we will have to continue working in this direction in the coming months. it is important to make rapid progress on each of the proposals which contain useful instruments for combating the financing of terrorism. i would like to make a brief comment on a point which has always been the subject of some frustration among us: the external representation of the european union. the explanatory statement for the motion for a resolution refers to the unique absence of europe in the debate on a new financial architecture. you criticise the fact that the isolated initiatives of some member states do not translate into a european policy. the commission cannot but share your diagnosis. what is the answer? what could we do? how could we improve the situation? i think it's not just about improving coordination and speaking with one voice. it is true that the launch of economic and monetary union has transformed the foundations of financial and monetary relations at the global level, but the way we continue to address these issues in the main organisations and forums, including the imf and the g7, remains largely based on a purely national approach. so i can only agree that we must move forward. i think it is very difficult to formulate a real policy in this field if we do not express our european positions clearly at world level. and that means a more accurate and defined representation of our interests outside. i am aware, however, that it will be very difficult to move in this direction if we do not first move in substance. i believe that focusing the battle solely on our form of representation abroad is not as important as defining our own positions and getting policies coordinated abroad. those two steps must be taken in the same direction and in parallel. and on those points parliament will always count on the commission to make further progress.

can be resolved satisfactorily. in its amended proposal the commission, after the first reading, accepted in full or in part 12 of the 17 amendments tabled by parliament. the common position which you have been considering, while significantly different in format and presentation from the amended proposal, contains resonances of the ten amendments. in relation to the amendments which are now under consideration, the commission can accept nine of them in full or in part. those are amendments nos 1-8 and 14. i should like to specify exactly what i accept. amendments nos 1-3 i accept in full. in amendment no 4, i very much welcome the reference to special attention to groups subject to multiple discrimination in their access to the labour market and i share your concerns that we should be and cannot accept this part of the amendment. on amendment no 5, i am very pleased with the emphasis you introduce with regard to the importance of promoting public knowledge of the european employment strategy and further encouraging individuals and organisations at all levels to contribute to enhancing its impact and effectiveness. this programme should and will assist in the realisation of those objectives. however, assigning funding for the ‘projects’ in this context is not appropriate, and i have to reject that part of amendment no 5. our diverging views on amendment no 5 may lie more in the wording used than in any disagreement on its intent. local projects involving local actors are funded through article 6 and the european social fund regulation, as well as through another budget line – b5-503. the latter is available exclusively for the funding of local development projects. the analysis, research and evaluation work which it incorporates will include measures, informed by the outcomes of the projects delivered under other budget lines, to assess how knowledge of the european employment strategy, and local level involvement in its delivery, might be further improved. i hope that this approach will meet your concerns. with regard to amendment no 8, i again fully subscribe to the principle of consistency and accept this part but i cannot agree to specify each linked programme. amendments nos 6 and 7 are taken on board in spirit by the inclusion of amendment no 1, and amendment no 14, i can fully support. unfortunately, i am not in a position to accept amendments nos 9-13. i will briefly explain why: amendments nos 9 and 10 concern the committee. while i am grateful for your support for the commission's role and the re-institution of an advisory committee, this is a lost fight with the council. looking at the legal framework and recent precedents, a mixed committee is a fair compromise. we could look at the mandate in future discussions to see if this could be adopted to meet your concerns as part of a global compromise. on the annual plans in amendment no 11, this is an internal commission question which has no place in a parliament and council decision. amendment no 12 also has to be rejected on institutional grounds and more specifically with reference to the framework agreement on interinstitutional relationships. finally, regarding amendment no 13, we maintain the eur 55 million initially proposed. we have made a thorough analysis and this is an adequate figure for the activities envisaged. to sum up, the - the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0325/2001), on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council decision on community incentive measures in the field of employment (c5-0388/2001 - 1998/0315 (cod)) (rapporteur: mrs ghilardotti).
the rapporteur. - mr president, information, consultation and participation of workers has been a major theme in the european debate since the first social action programme adopted by the council in 1974. since then, this subject has been raised in many of our debates in this house and many initiatives have been taken by the commission, which have met with resistance. almost all member states have a legal framework, whether by regulation or by contract, to ensure that workers are informed and consulted. this directive aims to have minimum standards of information and consultation to be applied throughout the union: the directive which we are considering today, after the statute of the european company, the directive on european works councils and the charter of fundamental rights, is intended to complete the existing community and national framework, thus contributing to the ultimate aims of the law in question, namely to prepare for change, to ensure that restructuring takes place in an acceptable context and to give the employment objective the preeminence required in the present context. the commission had put forward its proposal - a good proposal - in november 1998 and the european parliament had adopted its first reading in april 1999, approving a number of improvement amendments. it was not until june 2001 that the council adopted a common position. in general terms, the common position reflects the position adopted by the commission following parliament's first reading, but if you compare parliament's first reading with the common position, you realise that there are about thirty amendments of parliament which have not been accepted. as rapporteur, i have proposed to the committee on employment and social affairs that we should not take up all the amendments at first reading but concentrate our attention on the most important points which can improve the common position. i am grateful to my colleagues for their cooperation and they have tabled 15 amendments to my proposal, almost all of them aimed at strengthening it. after a thorough discussion, we have arrived at the text which is before the house today. the amendments are 16 in number and concern: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. the definition of economic and financial information; the exact definition of the social partners to avoid any misunderstanding; the protection of workers' representatives, which needs to be further specified in terms of protection against disadvantages in terms of career, wages, training; the suspension of a decision where the application of a decision may have substantial adverse consequences for the workers, so that the adoption of the final decision can be postponed for an appropriate period, at the request of the workers' representatives, to allow further negotiation and reach a mutually agreed solution. transitional periods it's a very delicate point. we do not think that any particular transitional periods are necessary, but the implementation of this directive must take place for all european workers - precisely because we are talking about minimum standard rights - at the same time. the penalties: it is the most sensitive point, on which all the lobbies against us, all the members, have been unleashed. we abandon in our proposal the initial hypothesis of a european sanction with legal effects; we are also calling for the introduction of a new system of penalties for the infringement of the principle of subsidiarity, which is to be applied to all workers. this is an interpretation of the common position, which states that member states must define effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties. i really hope that the house will confirm the large majority in the committee and that it will come very quickly, during the belgian presidency, to provide the union and the member states with this important regulatory instrument.
mr president, the subject which mr ghilardotti's report has so eloquently tackled is not, as we know, new, but on previous occasions when it has been touched upon it has never found a clear setting. i am referring in particular to the legislation on the eac, which has not been transposed by all the member states and, of those which have done so, not transposed into law by all of them, but is regulated by a framework agreed between the social partners, often unilaterally disregarded, as has been shown by repeated events, which have been discussed by this parliament. however, this parliament, which has always been sensitive to the problem of employment and is openly committed to shaping and guaranteeing the dignity and even the quality of work, and which is also prepared to propose sanctions in the face of the aforementioned cases which even impose requirements on the use of european funds to maintain employment levels, has shown varying degrees of hesitation in discussing this report. the different sensitivities are certainly understandable, given the sensitivity of certain issues, such as the application of sanctions, which are also necessary if one wants a requirement to be respected, or the abolition of the confidentiality exempting it from the consultation procedure, which has in any case been abandoned, or the granting of a transitional period in the transposition of the directive, which is also unnecessary, given the time for its implementation. the fact is that, both because of the constant implementation of community law and the persistent desire for ever greater cohesion and, finally, because of the practical presence, in the near future, of companies governed by european law which, in comparison with other legal and company forms, would guarantee better protection for workers on the level of participation, a firm standpoint had to be taken on the matter, providing for the definition of important and related issues, ranging from the definition of the content of the information to the revocation clause, from the timing of the initiation of the procedure to the definition of the parties involved, to the areas of application, and without disturbing, on the one hand, the restriction of competition, which in this case would also be open to the various behaviours of the member states and, on the other hand, the ratio of the method of open coordination for social policies which has finally also found practical use. the subject in question is certainly suitable for consideration in the context of the principle of subsidiarity, although the concept itself is still not clearly defined, although it is a fundamental element of the union itself. however, it must be said that its definition and application cannot and must not have a single meaning, namely that of requiring the member states to deal with certain matters solely because the opposite is also inherent and correct, that of entrusting the union, in the face of strong national heterogeneity or inattention, with a basic definition of those same matters when the reflections of these are endowed with some community value.
- mr president, commissioner, rapporteur, i think that the opportunity and the need to ensure an adequate flow of information between the company and all the stakeholders, first and foremost the employees involved in the life of the company, is something that can be widely shared and is shared. it would be much less acceptable to impose on the member states, on the individual member states, solutions for involving workers in management decisions, evoking in certain respects models of joint management which are foreign to the legal and economic tradition of many european countries, as has been noted recently. i therefore believe that the directive under consideration must leave the member states, as did the commission's initial proposal and as does the council's common position, sufficient room for manoeuvre in determining the best solution to satisfy the principle of the need to inform workers. many of the amendments adopted by the commission and contained in the common position we are about to vote on, however, go in the opposite direction, in particular amendments nos 2 and 12, which are intended to give workers' representatives - i repeat, in effect - a kind of veto right over the decisions taken by the undertakings. i therefore hope that parliament will not vote for the amendments and will stick to the council's common position. finally, i want to make a note: article 3 (2) provides for specific provisions applicable to undertakings pursuing political objectives, professional or religious organisations, etc. does this mean that parties, unions and churches can make restructuring decisions without informing their employees, whereas normal companies have to do so? that's what i'm wondering.

a shared vision and a shared approach. secondly: what is the attitude after october 7? on 7 october, things changed, as the united states and the international coalition reacted in the opposite way. now, once again, a joint attitude. i think it is important to emphasize this, because there was a time in the european union when this was different. romano prodi recalled that whenever there was an international conflict, there was not one position but 15 positions within the council. that is no longer the case today. i am very much in favour of the idea that we should go a step further, and certainly go further in the field of european defence, but i think we should emphasize this positive development. finally, little by little, stone by stone, a common foreign policy of the european union is being established, something which was almost unthinkable ten or fifteen years ago. in this respect, i think mr van den berg is right to emphasize the role we must play now. because our role is different from that of the united states. the european union's role is primarily one of political, logistical support and diplomatic action which we must undertake. he is right to stress the importance of the mandate we have received from the council with regard to the middle east. we are looking together, romano prodi, myself and javier solana, at the time when we can undertake this important mission, perhaps the third week of november. i think it is up to the european union, and above all the european union, to develop an initiative in this area. but we must be realistic and not have illusions. it is not one trip - there have been many - that can solve things, but perhaps something can be brought into a flow and that can eventually lead to an initiative.

- mr president, madam president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, international trade is in crisis. the institute for international affairs estimates that there will be only 2 percent growth in 2001 compared to 13 percent growth in 2000. i think it is right to raise the question of reform of the wto, to raise the question of the legitimacy and transparency of its decisions, provided that we do not lose sight of the main and sole mission of the wto, which is to expand international trade relations. that's why doha must not fail: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. europe and the other more advanced countries bear the responsibility for making doha a failure or a success. i think that, in general terms, certain considerations, certain questions should be noted. the first thing to do - and this is my view - is to abandon the logic of reciprocity at any cost: the removal of barriers to trade, even unilaterally, is not an act of surrender but an act of foresight, above all economic foresight. i acknowledge that commissioner lamy has acted in this way with the initiative everything but the arms, although it should be explained to the european citizens that this initiative, which is rightly welcomed, provides for the bananas to be definitively exempt from customs duties in 2009, ten years from now - a geological age in many respects - and it should also be explained to them why. another problem to avoid is to propose, to dump on doha an agenda that is too broad. i repeat: the wto has a specific mission, we cannot overburden doha and the wto by wanting to reform somehow, in that place, a series of issues that we do not like in the world today. some of the positions expressed on the environment, health and working standards do not help defend against the accusation that the enlargement agenda is actually being used by the advanced countries and europe as a protectionist tool. i think the developing countries are right to say that all these politically correct issues are actually serving to slow down the opening up of our markets to goods which must first come from the less developed countries. on the agricultural question: i think we must put an end to this game of cards as soon as possible, this game of parties between europe and the united states, whereby, while waiting for someone to start reducing agricultural protection, levels of duties and subsidies for agricultural production are maintained which are incompatible with a liberalization of trade in the agricultural sector, which, as has been pointed out, is one of those which could bring the greatest benefits to the developing countries. we in europe give a dollar a day for every cow - and they are not quality cattle, they are our mad cows - when there are 1.3 billion people living on less than a dollar a day. if we really want the wto, doha, to succeed, we must act courageously on these issues and, i repeat, abandon the principle of reciprocity at any cost. unilateral acts of opening up international trade are beneficial first of all to those who have the courage to commit them.
mr president, international trade is fundamental to our system and for those who want a different kind of globalisation - and i am one of them - international trade should be based on fair and equitable trade which can bring development and wellbeing to as many people as possible. unfortunately, the trade negotiations under the auspices of gatt and the wto have not helped to create fair international rules. on the contrary, they have left entire populations defenseless against the voraciousness of multinational corporations. it is therefore logical that these institutions, in large sections of the population, are suffering from an unprecedented crisis of legitimacy, which must be met by profound reforms. the désir report clearly addresses the limitations and dysfunctions of international trade, unequal trade, lack of transparency and democracy and so on, and proposes some reforms to remedy these shortcomings. we support and will vote for this report, but we think that this can only be the beginning of a process of change. the commission and the council must remain deaf to the world's clamor.
