the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. the tragic accident in the gotthard tunnel yesterday morning reminds us of the tragic fire in the mont blanc tunnel on 24 march 1999. but before i say anything on the reopening of the mont blanc tunnel, i would like to express on behalf of the commission my deepest condolences to the families of the victims and to convey our condolences to the swiss authorities and the swiss people. even if the causes of the accident are not known at the moment, this incident raises again the question of the safety of long road tunnels in a most urgent and dramatic way. the commission's approval is not required for the reopening of the mont blanc tunnel. this decision falls within the exclusive competence of the french and italian authorities. the upcoming reopening of the tunnel has, however, reignited many controversies. the main issue is the closure of the tunnel to truck traffic, a wish that the inhabitants of the chamonix valley had long before the fire disaster. however, the commission considers that the reopening of the tunnel should be based solely on safety criteria and only on the condition that all safety requirements are met. the commission has received information that the tunnels have now been equipped with modern safety equipment under the responsibility of france and italy. an electronic control centre was set up, electrical installations were completely renewed, ventilation was upgraded and ventilated shelters were set up 300 metres apart and emergency stopping bays 100 metres apart. in addition, the training level of the operators and rescue services has been greatly improved. in order to improve safety, the minimum distances between vehicles in the tunnel have also been revised. finally, the two original operators, atmb in france and sitmb in italy, have been replaced by a single administrative structure, an important step, bearing in mind that according to various technical reports drawn up after the fire disaster, the high number of victims was due, among other things, to the poor coordination between the two operators. the commission contributed eur 22.5 million to the repair work, which amounts to some eur 200 million. following the accident and the two subsequent fire disasters in austria - the fire in the tauern tunnel on 25 may 1999 caused by a road accident, which killed 12 people, and the fire in the kapruner glacier on 11 november 2000, which killed 156 people - the commission also decided to investigate, together with experts, how to optimise the safety of tunnels. our conclusions on this are part of the white paper on transport policy up to 2010. the commission is considering a european regulation to ensure that tunnels play an important role in many crossborder transport links. the aim is to create the conditions necessary to guarantee a high level of safety for road and rail tunnel users, in particular for those in the tunnels of the trans-european transport networks. the commission will submit a proposal to the european parliament and the council early in 2002. the recent accident once again underlines the fundamental importance of controlling the traffic flow across the alps. the commission considers it a matter of the utmost priority to develop and put into operation without delay the two rail links already mentioned in the 1996 guidelines for the transeuropean transport network, namely the lyon-turin line and the line over the brenner. it has informed the relevant ministers on several occasions and asked them to take the necessary measures to speed up these projects and, in particular, to consider their financing. the aim is not to exclude public-private partnerships. in addition to the creation of new infrastructure facilities, which will cover a large part of the region's goods transit, the commission will, as announced in its white paper, formulate minimum safety requirements for tunnels. the commission also proposes a new approach to transport infrastructure charges in the white paper, in order to take greater account of the external costs of individual modes of transport. this new pricing policy should make a major contribution to achieving a balance between modes of transport, particularly in sensitive regions such as the alps, and to favouring the most environmentally friendly of them. the commission will also propose, as part of its strategy for sustainable mobility, to revise the eurovignette directive to allow cross-financing for new railway infrastructure. the commission has also proposed signing, on behalf of the european community, the protocol on transport to the alpine convention, which is a political signal for the establishment of a balanced relationship between the modes of transport, even if the relevant provisions can be applied with a certain degree of flexibility in individual cases. in general, the commission intends to make european transport systems sustainable, taking into account medium and long-term environmental objectives. the commission will be presenting a communication on this subject next year. the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, despite the importance of the initiatives under consideration, the european parliament is merely consulted in this case, that is to say that what we decide by our vote, as often happens in these cases, will not be taken into account in the slightest by the council. in spite of this - and this is the main reason - i shall stress the need and urgency of reforming europol, so that it can be subject to democratic and judicial control. for at least five years, since 1996, parliament has been making this request in mr nassauer's report. the nassauer report sent a strong political signal to the council. it had asked the member states not to ratify the europol convention until it had been assigned to the court of justice, that is to say, to a decision-making power, which had jurisdiction to give preliminary rulings on the interpretation and correct application of the convention. the report by mr nassauer was a good example of the problems which europol and the europol convention faced and which are still the same today. the solution to these problems is not a matter for political groups, it is not a matter for the rapporteur or for mr nassauer: the judicial and democratic control of europol is an institutional problem. the failure to heal this wound inflicted on european democracy - if we can speak in these terms of the system which today governs the institutions of the union - means that it is impossible to make any real progress towards the creation of an area which is an area of security, of justice and of freedom, but which we believe must be, above all and a priori, an area of democracy. the european parliament has been reaffirming the need to allow europol to be monitored since its creation. the prospect of increasing europol's powers to deal with the terrorist emergency, the scandal involving a senior europol official and the reluctance of national police to hand over their data to europol, as well as the creation of parlopol - a group of national and european meps who claim the importance of increasing democratic control over europol and decisions taken within the area of justice, freedom and security - have already prompted the council to at least reflect on the need to implement some reforms. first, the council asked the european commission to draw up a communication on the democratic control of europol by the end of the year. we know the views of commissioner vitorino, who has repeatedly expressed his support for a committee of national and european parliamentarians, but we hope to hear here that the timetable will be speeded up in view of this reform. we believe that in a democratic framework europol should be subject not only to democratic control but also to financial and budgetary control and judicial control. today, financial and budgetary control is impossible, since europol is financed by the national states and not by the community budget. the parliament and the commission thus have no power of financial control, and thus can neither censure nor direct the work of the body. judicial review is also denied. the court of justice is not allowed full powers of review. it should also be noted that europol officials enjoy such a broad immunity that it is more akin to a guarantee of impunity, which also protects them from judicial review that might be exercised at national level. finally, there is the problem of the progressive increase in mandate and powers. while europol was initially concerned with drug-related crime, the act extends its remit to cover substantially all types of crime. we therefore believe that, in order to enable parliament to express its concerns and to make requests to the council and the commission at a time when they are about to decide to extend the powers and competences of europol, other amendments are needed to solve this problem, in addition to the amendments to the two acts proposed by belgium and sweden. we believe that the proposed amendments can serve to clarify and improve the initiatives under consideration and to send a political message to the council and the member states criticising the present situation and proposing some basic lines of reform. finally, the combined nature of the above considerations and the absence of co-decision powers for parliament in the field of justice and home affairs should lead all those who value the principles of democracy and freedom to reject the two initiatives under consideration, which, in my view, would make the council and the member states more aware of the need and the urgency of reforming europol.

commission. – mr president, it is a particular pleasure to welcome the langen report and the excellent work of the rapporteur in presenting a measured and forward-looking approach to the future provision of a category of services essential to our economy and to the wellbeing of all european citizens. the commission has played its part by presenting two communications on this subject and most recently a report to the laeken european council. essentially we are all inspired by the same will to ensure that every citizen in europe has access to high-quality services of general interest. the european union has direct responsibilities with regard to those sectors for which internal market legislation has been introduced, essentially for network industries. in each case, specific provisions have been devoted to public service obligations. all this legislation has been adopted under codecision and is continuing to evolve. the package of proposals on energy adopted by the commission this spring comprises greatly strengthened elements relating to public service obligations. member states have a duty to specify and implement those obligations. elsewhere, in sectors not covered by specific community legislation, member states and their constituted authorities have the main role to play, for instance in the organisation and provision of local and social services. here the commission limits itself to ensuring compatibility with competition and internal market rules in general. those rules, as emphasised by the langen report, are quite flexible. in particular they provide for adequate financing of services of general interests. the commission has repeatedly been requested to provide greater legal security with regard to the general competition and internal market rules applicable to services of general interest. by explaining and developing its approach, it has attempted to put the fears expressed by operators and others involved to rest. the commission proposes to continue to use examples, guidelines and communications, together with proposals for regulations on exemptions, to provide further clarification, as called for in the langen report. in its report to laeken, the commission has undertaken to establish a community framework for state aid granted for services of general economic interest. that framework could, in particular, specify the conditions for the authorisation of state aid schemes by the commission, thus alleviating the notification obligation for individual aid. this may lead to the adoption of a regulation exempting certain categories of aid from the obligation of prior notification. on the issue of a proposed framework directive, the commission is not opposed in principle and has already agreed to assess the value and feasibility of such an instrument. our doubts concern mainly the articulation between such a directive and legislation at sectoral level. in the light of the european parliament's resolution, the commission will look at the subject again. another major issue concerns evaluation. i repeat that the commission has every interest in rigorous, complete and honest evaluation of the results of community legislation. that is good practice; it is also good governance and it should not be neglected, either at member state or at european level. we propose to improve on existing sectoral evaluations and we have agreed to present an annual horizontal report in the context of the cardiff process. the commission welcomes the european parliament's proposal to organise a debate in the existing forums in order to ensure a pluralist assessment and the debate ought to take place before the preparation of the cardiff report in order to take full account of its results and recommendations. in conclusion, i stress that services of general interest are an area of ongoing concern which will require new initiatives in future and further development of community legislation. the commission looks forward to involving the european parliament as a partner in this process.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr sign language interpreter, i would like to express some thoughts on the world year of people with disabilities, also on behalf of my colleague mr mario mantovani, who is particularly sensitive to this subject and who was unable to be here with us today. it's a really big problem. just look at some numbers: today, some 38 million people in the european union have a disability. this means that one in ten europeans encounters obstacles, not only in the field of work but also in access to public transport, buildings, private services, education, training, in short, to all aspects of daily life. however, there are other barriers, perhaps less visible but equally insurmountable, which limit the freedom of european citizens with disabilities: for example, barriers to movement within the union, to choices of residence in another member state. all too often, these barriers prevent people with disabilities from playing the active role in society, at work, in school, in everyday activities that they aspire to. a multifaceted strategy is needed to ensure equal opportunities for these people in full respect of the charter of fundamental rights of the european citizens. there is one right, however, that stands out among all: the right to full citizenship. that is why our group, the epp, will vote with conviction on the proposal for a council decision on the year of persons with disabilities 2003 or - as it was also called - persons with different abilities. i therefore thank the rapporteur, mrs lynne, for her good work and for having accepted the 17 amendments tabled in committee. we have presented three of them, which are of particular interest to us because they contain three concepts: first, the recognition of the role of the family in the life stage of the disabled person; secondly, the promotion of a culture of social society and solidarity, understood as the understanding that the value of the disabled person is not only expressed in what he or she does or can do, but essentially in what he or she represents as a fully fledged human person; finally, third and last, the deepening of the concept of the quality of life of a disabled person, understood not only as an occupational or training practice but also as a daily activity in all other expressions, together with the family, within and among society, but that it is indeed an excellent quality of life, the same for them too.

- mr president, the european union's foreign policy, after recent international developments, must take a breath, but the governments of the member states cannot ignore the fact that there can be no common foreign policy without common intelligence. the geopolitical situation, poverty - an ever more emerging problem - and the spread of terrorism with cells in all the countries of the planet must lead us, at the laeken summit, to consider a project for a genuine common intelligence service, a new intelligence service which is not born and developed like europol, but which is able to work in a transparent way with political, economic and cultural analysts who are able to give our foreign policy an overall vision and a timeliness without which the european union, regardless of any institutional reform, will not be able to take off. the achievement of peace in afghanistan and its subsequent reconstruction suggest that the union's role as both a mediating presence and a driving force must be identified now, if the future of afghanistan is to be marked not only by economic recovery and a democratic political system but also by the regaining of a role for women in politics and social life. the union cannot ignore the fact that, in order to achieve real peace in the middle east, it is necessary to take an active stance against those who foment, or at any rate do not oppose, local terrorism which - it is now clear - is supported at international level, and the union has the economic and political instruments to intervene in this direction. in conclusion, the success or failure of the convention depends on the convictions, the real european convictions that move us, the convictions that we have, as individual parties and individual governments, not to rely on reforms on paper but on concrete acts that can improve the situation not only of our countries but of those who turn to us.

- mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr president of the commission, mr commissioner barnier, ladies and gentlemen, i think that once again the rapporteurs méndez de vigo and leinen have presented us with a fine piece of work, but i think they have been a little too concerned with methodology. of course, it's better to have a motorcycle than a bicycle, it goes a little faster, but if you don't know where you're going, i think you're not very far. i was pleased to hear mr poettering, mr cox and mr voggenhuber put the commission at the centre of their speeches for the first time in a long time. i think we have a very serious problem today. we have a fight. everyone is taking a little bit of the cover off between the council and parliament. we are increasing our powers of codecision, but at the same time we are destroying the commission. this destruction of the commission is accompanied by a process of bureaucratisation, and i think it is useless, mrs theorin, to talk about transparency, governance, codecision and democratic legitimacy when we cannot even talk about the election of the commission by direct universal suffrage. i think that it is the balance of our institutions and that we cannot do the economics of the great american model, it is the balance of our institutions, the checks and balances, it is the division of powers and not the distribution of the cake between the various institutions that should be at the centre of our discussions, our debates and this intergovernmental conference, and before that the convention. i think that this is the only way to combat bureaucratisation, the only way to restore legitimacy to our institutions, the only way to revive the construction of europe. so, as mr salafranca said, there are no favourable winds for those who do not know where to go, and i think that it is first and foremost the problem of our parliament to know, to understand where it wants to go.

mr president, the laeken summit will be an important but difficult summit, particularly because of the importance of the subjects under discussion. in this brief speech i would like to focus on the institutional aspects of the summit. the convention will have to work to start a new phase aimed at creating a constitution which leads to the creation of a federation of nation states, but which also establishes the powers of the various institutions: the commission, the council, the member states, the regions, the large cities. these are choices which must be made in the spirit of solidarity and subsidiarity, two values which must inspire the new constitution. the timing of this march towards the new institutions will also have to be discussed at laeken. it is necessary to avoid that decisions which are crucial to the future of the union coincide with the election campaign. that is why we think it is appropriate to start the intergovernmental conference early during the italian presidency in the second half of 2003. of course, the constitutional process will not be able to do without the involvement of the peoples through the votes of the parliaments - we would have liked, for example, that the charter of nice had been discussed, that it had been amendable by parliament because there are parts, especially those concerning the person, which do not convince us at all - starting with the european part, because without the involvement of the citizens and their representatives, we will not be able to transform the europe of the euro into a political europe, destined to enlarge its borders, in the future, perhaps up to the urals: i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the future of europe, but that we should be concerned about the future of europe.
- madam president, there is a constant relationship between the restrictions on individual and collective freedoms which occur in the united states and those which occur in europe, just as there is a constant link between the two phenomena, as is the function of the united kingdom government, first with the reagan/thatcher pair and now with the bush/blair pair. the criminal act of terrorism against the united states on 11 september is providing many european governments with a pretext for passing further laws that are not related to the fight against terrorism. leaving aside the special military tribunals set up by president bush, it is enough to reflect on recent laws, enacted or proposed in italy or the united kingdom, to understand that they are aimed at controlling and repressing a growing political opposition to an unjust and inhumane world order, social and economic: the welfare, the affluence, the growth, the development of one fifth of humanity is a reflection of the hunger, the scarcity of resources, the continuing economic decline, the underdevelopment of the remaining four fifths. it is strange that we can never find the legal formula to describe all this social slaughter as an act of terrorism, while we can immediately describe as acts of terrorism all those manifestations of social opposition that have been experienced in recent times, from seattle to genoa. article 3 of the draft framework decision on terrorism contains a clear message to those who will henceforth want to demonstrate their opposition to the neoliberal single-mindedness and the social system that derives from it. women, men, workers, students, the unemployed, pacifists, environmentalists will no longer be opponents but terrorists because - - madam president, after the events of 11 september, europe too, the european institutions, must feel responsible and must have the courage to reach a common agreement as soon as possible between the member states on the fight against terrorism and, in general, the fight against large-scale organized crime. the legal instruments which can make this fight really effective are undoubtedly the european arrest warrant, which can finally replace the complex and overly bureaucratic extradition procedures which have become insufficient and inadequate to combat criminal phenomena, especially international ones. in view of all this, it is nevertheless appropriate to proceed in stages. the emotion of the tragic acts of terrorism of recent months must certainly and without hesitation lead to a strengthening of judicial cooperation between the member states, but the acceleration which is taking place must nevertheless be carried out in a progressive manner and with a great sense of responsibility. good laws do not allow for haste, for proximity and for emotions, especially in the detection of crimes for which the european arrest warrant must be applied. we therefore express our perplexity about the belgian presidency's proposal to apply the european arrest warrant immediately to a list of some 30 categories of crime. we cannot, in our view, equate terrorism or human trafficking, to give just two examples, with counterfeiting of products or falsification of administrative documents. it would therefore be more reasonable in the general interest to propose and approve, in the first instance and with the unanimous consent of all member states, a first restricted list and then, at a later stage, to extend that list gradually, thus concentrating in the first instance on the offences of terrorism, organised crime, drug trafficking, arms trafficking, trafficking in human beings and child abuse.

- the next item is the report (a5-0391/2001) by mr fiori, on behalf of the temporary committee on human genetics and other new technologies in modern medicine, on the ethical, legal, economic and social implications of human genetics [2001/2097 (ini) ].
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in june last year president bill clinton of the united states and prime minister tony blair of the united kingdom presented to the world the map of the human genome, which had been produced simultaneously by their respective research groups. a month later, nature brought the more timely findings to the attention of the world's scientific community. it's just this morning that the first trial for human cloning in the united states is about to begin. as is often the case with the prophecies of the day after, alarmed voices are being raised today, expressing in unison the most indignant condemnation and concern. the same researchers acknowledge that they have shown the way for those who would like to commit the folly of cloning a human being. there are two historical moments: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the european union. beyond the disturbing scenarios, however, i believe i can say that, between these two historical moments, a new way of doing medicine is born: curative medicine is giving way to regenerative medicine, predictive medicine. in the not too distant future we will probably be able to predict what diseases we are destined for and, more importantly, to identify the means of preventing them from coming to the fore. thus, as often happens in the history of human discovery, two opposing paths open up: on the one hand, it opens up the wonderful path of therapeutic hope. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we therefore have the paradoxical task of drawing the line in the great sea of the unknown before us. it is the greatest project of the century that has just begun, to which all mankind is called. it is precisely this awareness that has led to the need to set up think tanks to look at the ethical, social and legal implications of the new research programmes. the extraordinary possibilities of scientific and medical progress, read in the light of the potential inherent in them, have in fact immediately sounded alarm bells. it is this fear that led unesco to set up a bioethics committee to study the social implications of knowledge of the genome and, in 1997, to the adoption of the universal declaration on the human genome and human rights. later, the broad consensus of the declaration led the united nations general assembly to commemorate the 50th anniversary of another landmark document - the universal declaration of human rights - by adopting the unesco declaration on the genome. i have the feeling, however, that when we go into the details of the regulations, some of the principles we have defended so much inexplicably dissolve. while i am aware of the vastness of the subject, i will try to summarize the impact of the project on human rights and human dignity, which are the basis of our report. i would sum up the attempt and the commitment to reconcile the longed-for progress of science with the utmost respect for the sanctity of human life in four objectives. first, the progress of scientific experiments in genetics to obtain therapeutic benefits is highlighted. the knowledge of the genome requires the use of clinical trials. the medical profession itself teaches us that there always comes a time when such experiments must be carried out on humans and that it is therefore obviously necessary to take all measures to ensure the safety of those who undergo them, so that there is no risk to their health, much less to their lives, and always being able to rely on their free and informed consent. secondly, even in the light of the limited information we have today, we can say that knowledge of the genome could allow us to change our genes. it is therefore absolutely necessary to indicate today which doors we must never open. i would like to remind you that the universal declaration on the human genome and human rights prohibits any intervention in the human genome that affects the germline. what has happened in the last few days does not seem to have gone in that direction. furthermore, knowledge is a continuous process requiring constant monitoring. in the light of the information we have, the only certainty we can compare with is the human nature of the embryos, whatever their destination. thirdly, the doors that knowledge of the genome opens up present us with serious risks of invasion of privacy as a consequence of the knowledge itself. we must be able to ensure that the information deriving from knowledge of our genetic heritage does not reach operators other than those who use it for our own good. it is clear that if the news of a person's propensity to contract a particular disease could be accessed, it would easily help to create a new source of discrimination, for example, but not only, in the field of employment. we must be aware of this risk and take appropriate measures to avoid it. finally, another objective which research puts at stake for the future of humanity is its universalization. it is clear that research requires considerable investment and that economic incentives are essential for progress. it is equally true, however, that we cannot accept that the need for the achievements of progress to be the undisputed heritage of mankind should be put on the back burner. if we are not able to universalize the benefits of knowledge of the human genome, we can already say that we have failed. instead of being a means to create a more just world, science will have helped to create a further gap between rich and poor and will have established itself as a further tool for social diversification. the importance and difficulty of establishing a sound patent system, the aim of which is to ensure that the benefits are distributed equitably among all human beings, cannot be overlooked in this context: the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the council of europe, concerned about the protection of human rights in the member states, gave specific directives to oviedo: the prohibition of any form of discrimination based on genetic heritage; the prohibition of interference with the human genome for purposes other than therapeutic purposes; the absolute prohibition of the modification of the hereditary genome; the prohibition of sex selection. i think we should stick to these points. ladies and gentlemen, we are facing a set of challenges for scientists, lawyers, ethicists, sociologists and those of us in the institutions who must draw the lines of the new path. i have dealt with this report - a task that makes my veins and wrists tremble, and i do not know if i have been up to the task you have entrusted me with - guided by a principle that is essential to me: i did not feel that i had gone beyond where progress demanded a step to the sanctity of human life, where it clashed with respect for human dignity. at this juncture i felt that it was progress that had to change its course. one of these routes is already known today: it's a non-destructive alternative, just as promising as embryonic cell research but it uses adult cells. i think we should prefer this direction which, besides being desirable, does not present any kind of ethical and social conflict. respect for human dignity in biomedical research means that science must be subordinate to man, not the other way around. all human beings must be protected at every stage of their existence, from conception to natural death, particularly if they are vulnerable or disabled. i am in favour of scientific research, partly because it is a source of economic development, but i believe that we must prevent it from becoming a kind of death trap for man, because we have not paid due attention to the ethical principles which should inspire it. finally, i would like to thank all those who have contributed to my report. (applause) i would like to thank
mr president, the work of the temporary committee on human genetics has been complex and interesting. the rich and comprehensive report by mr fiori, which accompanies the motion for a resolution, is a testimony to this. the draft resolution, presented by the rapporteur in committee, was in turn a balanced summary of the conclusions to be drawn from our investigations, which have addressed the many ethical and political problems raised by the great scientific advances of recent years: the development of genetic tests, which opens up prospects for early detection and possible cures for serious degenerative diseases, but which at the same time pose risks for the protection of personal data, which in this field concern not only the individual but all his relatives, so that, alongside the right to know, the right of everyone to know the possible risks of predisposition to future diseases, is the new right not to know, to face, if you wish, the fate that life holds for us by trusting in the future. the problems raised by the application of patent discipline - a traditional industrial policy instrument which favours private funding of research - to biotechnological and biomedical innovations which deal with living organisms and therefore raise delicate questions of the boundary between invention as a product of human activity and the discovery, not appropriation, of living matter have been addressed. finally, the most compelling dilemmas of the new frontiers of stem cell research were addressed, which offer extraordinary potential for possible interventions, perhaps capable of eliminating diseases that have hitherto been invincible, but which also raise dramatic questions about ethical principles that should be considered unworkable. we are not starting from scratch, thanks also to the fruitful work of the european ethics group and to the many instruments developed at community and international level, so that our parliament was able two weeks ago to approve, by a large majority, prudent and shared criteria on this subject at the launch of the sixth research framework programme, which gives priority to the necessary research in this field, financing in particular those concerning adult stem cells and embryonic cells from abortions or from so-called surplus embryos, produced for the purpose of assisted procreation and no longer usable for that purpose, to the extent that the laws of the member states allow it. unfortunately, the original plan was twisted in committee and an orientation based on fear rather than hope prevailed. the spectre of cloning, which generates monsters, has been stirred up, leading to the absurd conclusion that it is better to let the surplus embryos perish, to destroy them, than to use them for the suffering but only to safeguard the first aggregates of embryonic cells in the early state. yet never, never in the history of mankind has the human embryo found protection comparable to that of today. the demand that lawful, regulated and controlled research should open the door to harmful speculation, as if we should ban organ transplants, which save lives, just because there may be shady organ trafficking. fight these, do not give up hope of recovery! divine laws are invoked to reject the responsibility that a strict secular ethic imposes on those who are democratically elected to make choices for the common good. it is necessary, however, to weigh the values at stake and, with all caution and prudence, with all reasonable limits, opposing all commercial logic, to allow freedom of knowledge, of research, of hope for new goals in the treatment of atrocious diseases. that is why my group hopes that the european parliament will not wish to contradict what it wisely decided just commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to warmly congratulate the members of the temporary committee on human genetics, chaired by mr goebbels, and the rapporteur, mr fiori, who has done a very good job. the recent developments in the united states in the field of human cloning have once again highlighted the need and urgency for a thorough political reflection in this area, also and above all at european level. as you know, the commission is not obliged to take a formal position on an own-initiative report. but given the political importance of the issues raised, i would like to share my thoughts on the main points raised and the positions expressed on them in the text of the resolution. i shall do so in the order in which these points have been raised. the commission can only agree with what has been said on the general conditions of human genetics. of course, when it comes to human genetics, ethical considerations are decisive. as article 13 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union states, research must be free, but on the other hand, technological progress can of course only be applied in a fully responsible manner. the idea of responsible technological progress is one of the main lines of the action plan on science and society which the commission will shortly present. i come now to the big issues at stake. the resolution very appropriately raises the question of genetic testing. there is a need to strengthen the consistency of quality standards in this field, through harmonisation or mutual recognition. the commission will undertake a study of the various technical options which may be envisaged in this respect. the need for better coordination of genetic research on rare diseases at european level is also evident. and i would remind you that in the new research framework programme, support for the networking of laboratories working in this field will be possible in the spirit of the resolution on rare diseases adopted in 1999 by the european parliament and the council. pharmacog­enics: the resolution also calls for a harmonised regulatory framework for the development of new products based on genetics. as you know, there is already a harmonised framework for the development, testing and authorisation of biomedical products. community legislation on pharmaceutical products already applies to gene therapy and medicinal products used in cell therapy in terms of general principles. however, due to the constant advances in science and biotechnology, technical adaptations will need to be made to specifically cover certain products. thirdly, the use of personal data for genome analysis. the right to privacy and the requirement of free and informed consent are obviously essential when it comes to the use of personal data. the commission will examine whether and to what extent there is a need to update and supplement existing community legislation on privacy protection. i personally think that one of the points that needs to be examined carefully is the question of the use of this data by insurance companies, which is also explicitly mentioned in the resolution. patentability: you also mention the problem of the patentability of products derived from biotechnology. this is a particularly important question, which touches on fundamental concepts, but also has many highly technical aspects. as you know, the directive finally adopted by the community in this field was after ten years of intense debate, particularly in the european parliament, and is now only translated into a number of national laws. in a context of very strong international competition, this directive provides european researchers and industry with a much-needed common reference framework. but given its importance for innovation, the most urgent thing is to establish the conditions for its effective application. at this stage, it is not a question of amending the directive or revising its content, but certain aspects of it certainly need to be clarified. this directive and the discussions it has given rise to highlight the kind of relations which will have to be established between society at large and science, between the scientific community and the legislator. science is moving fast, knowledge is advancing rapidly, and yet legislation is needed. it is up to policy-makers and public officials to do so responsibly. but the decisions taken must be reviewed continuously in the light of the progress of knowledge, in open dialogue between researchers, lawyers, policy-makers and citizens. a case law will inevitably develop. it cannot do so in a 'scientific vacuum' any more than science can develop in a 'legal vacuum'. in order to clarify certain aspects of this question of the patentability of products derived from biotechnology, and the application of the directive, the high level group on life sciences and technologies which i have set up, and which is chaired by professor axel kahn, has been asked to speak on this subject. it has recently made an important statement public, which will be reflected in the annual report to parliament and the council, which is also provided for in the directive. the group recalls that the protection of genes by patents does not apply to these elements as they exist in their natural environment, but to molecules isolated from the human body, used in the context of a well-defined technical application. it thus emphasizes the inaccurate and misleading nature of the term "patenting life". in the same vein, the group recalls that the purpose and effect of a patent is not to make the proprietor the 'owner' of the protected object, but to confer on him the exclusive right to exploit the product of his invention for a certain period of time. and it warns of the potential negative fallout of overly broad patent strategies on research and its medical applications. finally, the group draws attention to the need to develop a genuine culture of intellectual property among researchers, who are often not familiar with these realities. and he suggests engaging in a process of collective learning and sharing experience in this area, involving the scientific community, the legal world, policy makers, industry, the media and the public. in this spirit, and in preparing the annual report to parliament and the council on the implementation of the european directive on the patentability of biotechnological inventions, the commission is considering setting up a group of scientific and legal experts to clarify certain aspects of the directive. at the time the directive was being prepared, the therapeutic prospects for the use of stem cells were not as clearly identified as they are today. at the same time, the commission therefore asked the european ethics group for an opinion on the specific question of the patentability of products derived from this technique. the commission is expected to give its opinion by the end of this year. i come now to the last point i mentioned, stem cells and embryo research and cloning. the question of the use of stem cells, as this debate has shown, is a particularly sensitive subject. the announcement earlier this week of the results of therapeutic cloning by researchers from a us company has reawakened questions about the technology. it led me to recall that the commission is opposed to any form of research involving the creation of human embryos for research purposes only, or for the production of stem cells. first of all, however, i would like to recall a formal point: the community has no legislative powers in the field of bioethics. however, for reasons connected in particular with respect for the diversity of national sensibilities and cultures, it is now up to the member states to lay down the rules in this field. the questions raised are currently the subject of intense debate in the member states, here in the european parliament, and i welcome this, in the council of europe, with which the commission is working in close cooperation, and at international level. there is unanimous agreement on certain basic principles. human reproductive cloning is thus universally condemned, for example explicitly in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. in this spirit, the commission fully supports the franco-german initiative to establish an international convention prohibiting human reproductive cloning. beyond this question, the problems of the use of stem cells of embryonic origin and the use of human embryos for research purposes are, as you know, the subject of assessments which vary considerably according to sensitivities and beliefs. the ethical issues associated with them are complex, because certain basic principles and risks of drift have to be balanced against the interests of the patients and the possibilities of significantly reducing their suffering and that of their loved ones. so setting limits is never easy, and we must try to find the balanced position that is most widely acceptable. in my view, the position of prohibiting the creation of human embryos but allowing, under strictly controlled ethical conditions and in compliance with national laws, the use of already existing embryos, so-called surplus embryos, in particular for the production of stem cells, achieves this balance. this position reflects the opinion of the european group on ethics, which considers that the creation of human embryos by somatic cell nucleus transfer for research purposes would be premature, given the vast field of research to be explored using other sources of human stem cells, in particular from existing so-called surplus human embryos. can we close down certain research possibilities altogether, at the risk of depriving ourselves of the means to alleviate severe suffering and of jeopardizing europe's chances of remaining at the cutting edge of knowledge? in the present state of knowledge, many questions remain open, even in purely scientific terms. that is why the commission will be organising - and i would like to reiterate my invitation to all interested members - a conference here in brussels on 18 and 19 december on the subject of 'stem cells: therapies for the future?' discussions should focus on the promises and priorities of stem cell research, but also on the challenges of all kinds it faces. i would like to conclude with a final point, which is governance and public debate. in this context, i can only endorse the report. i can tell you that the science-society action plan we are preparing is in that direction. it aims to encourage public debate on these issues. it is absolutely essential that the debate be as wide and as public as possible. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on matters which are of major importance for the future of european society, i am very pleased to note that your assembly has played the role of a key forum for high-quality debate. in a europe where citizens share the same fundamental values but may differ in their opinions on certain subjects, the european parliament is the place where democratic debate of opinions should take place. the commission is willing to continue to support your efforts in this field and will continue, in close cooperation with you and the member states, the essential effort of information, reflection and exchange which is required for responsible scientific and technological progress.

the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner liikanen, the new regulatory framework for telecommunications replaces the community regime which opened up national markets in europe and brought an end to the age of monopolies. the european commission had indicated its intention to reduce regulatory burdens on the basis of the liberalization objectives achieved on the basis of the model still in force, as a basis for the review of the community telecommunications framework. the aim was to ensure greater confidence in market forces to promote the competitiveness of the european market and to encourage investment in emerging markets by encouraging the supply of innovative services. the revision of the current model should therefore aim to gradually move the telecommunications market from the phase of liberalisation to a phase of effective and consolidated competition. the relationship between the evolution of the regulatory framework and market dynamics should be pursued by a forward-looking approach that fosters competitive conditions, ensuring the rapid diffusion of innovative services, so as to orient the market and the future exclusive application of antitrust rules gradually replacing ex ante regulatory rules. the new model should provide a transitional phase to facilitate this transition towards a telecommunications market which can be managed in the same way as any other economic sector, in strict compliance with the competition rules. this can be achieved by a body of ex ante rules harmonised at european level, characterised by transitional and exceptional characteristics; in other words, the regulation we are discussing and approving ex ante must provide the conditions for its elimination once a sufficient level of competition has been reached. these ex ante rules should be kept to a minimum in terms of requirements and intensity, to ensure that the intervention is proportionate to the regulatory objectives. given the flexibility of the new model, which extends the areas of intervention of international regulatory authorities with great discretion, the underlying structure of the new regulatory framework must be represented by the need to ensure the supervisory power that the commission has provided for national authorities, in order to ensure a correct interpretation of the new framework, such as to avoid distortive effects on the competitiveness of the european market in one geographical area compared to another. in fact, in the absence of a centralised power at european level to assess the final consistency of national decisions with community objectives, the new regulatory framework risks not achieving the objectives it set itself. to this end, mr president, commissioner liikanen, i would like to make a point of introducing an amendment which i tabled with 51 other colleagues from various political groups to the directive of mr paasilinna, who has worked so well on his proposal for the telecommunications framework directive. the amendment aims to provide greater clarity for operators, to avoid fragmentation in the application of community law in the various member states and to ensure the development of a genuine internal telecommunications market. the adoption of my proposal would facilitate harmonization, which can only be achieved by providing for a power that is clearly defined and that allows the european commission to intervene to ensure that the application of community rules is consistent with the objectives and pursues the same objectives in all member states. harmonisation and centralised power are the basis for the construction of the pan-european telecommunications market. that is what the operators want, that is what the market wants, mr daems, commissioner liikanen. the market wants to build a pan-european telecommunications market, but the short-sightedness of the national authorities often tends to hold back this development at this stage. i therefore propose this amendment, which i hope will be taken up positively by the belgian presidency, the council, the commission and this house.

- the next item is the joint debate on the following four reports, drawn up on behalf of the committee on budgets: - a5-0400/2001 by mr costa neves and mr buitenweg, on the draft general budget of the european union for the financial year 2002, as amended by the council (all sections) and on letter of amendment no 2/2002 to the draft general budget for the financial year 2002; - a5-0427/2001 by mr colom i naval, on financial programming for the period 2002-06; - a5-0447/2001 by mr wynn, on the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument; - a5-0439/2001 by mr turchi, on community financial assistance in the field of transeuropean networks.
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission's annual report on transeuropean networks provides an overview of community assistance in the three main areas of the tens - transport, energy and telecommunications - from both the general budget of the union and other community sources such as the eib and the cohesion fund. i think that overall it is a good report, if one also takes into account that 1999 was a crucial year for this sector; in 1999, the financial regulation was amended, the 2000-2006 financial framework was approved and ispa was set up. this year, 50% of the funding was allocated to transport infrastructure works and the identification of galileo as a new priority ten project. this does not mean, however, that there are no notes to be made to the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. the first point i would like to make about the report is the lack of reference to the qualitative development of ten projects. very often the start and completion of projects took much longer than expected, due to differences in procedures and a lack of coordination. in many cases, member states have had different priorities, while the notion of partnership, public or private, is still not very developed. in future, therefore, the commission should be required to attach to its reports additional information relating to projects, such as original plans, timetables, results achieved. this would first of all increase transparency and, consequently, also the possibilities for effective and productive monitoring of the situation. secondly, the financial evaluation of the tens should also include information on funding from local, regional and national budgets as well as from private sources, considering that these sources account for about 80% of total funding. this would enable a global picture to be taken of the state of financing and the member states' compliance with their commitments. thirdly, i believe that the financial resources available for the tens are too limited in relation to the continuing changes that the transport sector has to face. the share of tens financed from the general budget is steadily declining, while eib loans cover more than three quarters of the financing in this sector, and this should be emphasized. i believe that the ten transport financial package should be reviewed and adjusted to real needs, especially in view of the impact on other areas such as the environment. finally, i believe that the question of road traffic, whose constant increase runs counter to the objectives set for the creation of the tens, should be seriously addressed. i believe that this is due to the lack of crossborder cooperation, which necessarily undermines the viability and promotion of the rail system. to remedy this problem, i believe that we need to gradually shift the focus from essen priority projects and national infrastructure projects to transit projects and cross-border projects, in order to strengthen sustainable transport policy and promote integration between different modes of transport. i would also like to end by mentioning the budget we are about to vote on. i believe that we have come to two not indifferent political nodes, reflecting the additional needs that have arisen in the light of the changed international situation. we have left a large margin for assistance to afghanistan and its neighbouring regions at second reading and have agreed with the council on eur 488 million for cooperation with the developing countries of asia. we have therefore once again demonstrated our political sensitivity and our support for the common foreign and security policy. it was not possible to assume that the union would be absent at a time like this, nor was it possible to assume that parliament would defect at the explicit request of the council. on the other hand, this does not mean that everything is fine and that criticism should not be raised. but i must congratulate above all the rapporteur, mr costa neves, mrs buitenweg and the whole secretariat, who have assisted and supported us even in difficult times.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as we know, the debate taking place today in this chamber is taking place in an international context which only underlines the need, the very urgency, of implementing the objectives of the treaty of amsterdam and of respecting the programme defined in 1999 in tampere by the heads of state and government of the union countries. it also comes on the heels of a jha council whose busy agenda reflected the intensity of the work in progress and on the eve of the laeken summit, a mid-term meeting which will allow us to assess the progress made since tampere and hopefully give a new impetus to the efforts undertaken to implement our programme. it also examines the medium-term prospects for the intergovernmental conference in 2004, against the background of enlargement of the union. and some of the questions raised - notably the role of the european parliament in the field of justice and home affairs or the protection of the fundamental rights of the citizen in the european judicial area - will be very present in this debate. i shall therefore try to answer the questions of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs on the basis of the questions put by mrs boumediene-thiery. the first question raised concerns a matter of principle: the objective of protecting citizens, which is set out in the treaty of amsterdam and which is placed at the forefront of the union's political agenda by the dramatic international events and the increasingly close deadlines, such as enlargement. can this objective be achieved at the expense of respect for the fundamental rights enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights? i certainly don't. and the commission is very keen to ensure that the proposals made to guarantee internal security and the protection of our citizens are balanced and proportionate and are part of a system of values at the heart of which is the rule of law. firstly, a number of texts of a quasi-constitutional nature guarantee these rights in the european union and are systematically mentioned in the proposals made by the commission. this is true not only of the european convention on human rights but also of the european charter of fundamental rights. these texts are binding on the union's laws, but also on national laws. i also believe it is imperative to recall that the union's objectives in protecting citizens are not only not contrary to the fundamental rights as set out in the charter of the european union, but are based on those rights. in this respect, the recommendations of the watson report on events organised on the margins of the european council are welcome. these are reasonable recommendations which we believe strike a balance between, on the one hand, the freedom of expression of citizens and the full exercise of the fundamental right to demonstrate, and, on the other hand, the need not to leave the field free to those who, in reality, refuse democratic debate and believe that they can get their message across through violent confrontation with the police. as for the recommendation to open a de facto dialogue on the internal and external impact of globalisation, i can say that this concern will be reflected in the communication which the commission will present next january on the external aspects of sustainable development policy. as regards the second point raised, as regards possible exceptional measures, as mentioned by mr boumediene-thiery, to deal with the terrorist threat, i do not think that the european union is on the path to do so. once again, while it is true that there is a certain degree of urgency in taking decisions, including measures to strengthen police and judicial cooperation in the fight against the most serious forms of attacks on our freedoms, values and institutions, i do not believe that the initiatives taken or proposed at european union level can be described as exceptional measures, that is to say, measures derogating from essential principles because of exceptional circumstances. no, the measures proposed are substantive measures, taken, it is true, in an exceptional context, but they are not improvised and in fact they respond to the mandates which our governments and our nations have given us by adopting the treaty of amsterdam. and i take this opportunity to welcome and congratulate the belgian presidency for having succeeded yesterday in rome in consolidating the decisions taken by the jha council in the direction of adopting the framework decision on terrorism and the framework decision on the european arrest warrant. the rapporteur's suggestion to include a temporary validity clause or a revision clause is interesting for the principle she proposes, namely the obligation to assess the impact of a proposal adopted in the light of the objective pursued. the third point underlined concerns the delays in the achievement of the tampere objectives. it called on all the institutions and authorities responsible for implementing the programme defined in tampere to take the necessary steps to ensure that the programme is implemented in a transparent and effective manner. the latest edition of the commission's scoreboard includes a first assessment of progress made. and indeed, there have been delays, particularly in certain areas such as asylum and immigration, or the minimum harmonisation of criminal sanctions. the mid-term evaluation which will take place, as you know, at the laeken european council, is therefore a crucial step. it is time to see whether the commitments made in tampere and reiterated on 21 september are translated into a real will on the part of the member states to move forward. it is also a time to learn from the successes and difficulties of the past. the reassessment of the tampere objectives, and in particular the questioning of the deadlines, would lead to a crisis of public confidence in a political project which everyone feels is essential and a priority, whatever the difficulties that remain. so, is it the will as well as the method that we need today to not disappoint the legitimate expectations of the public, but also of men and women whose job it is to protect our freedom, to guarantee our security and to ensure more accessible justice? the council of justice and home affairs ministers last week produced encouraging results on the willingness of the member states to act in accordance with the commitments they have made. but it also illustrated all the limitations, even the ambiguities, of a decision-making process entirely subject to unanimity. the commission will stress at laeken that the reluctance to make progress will only be overcome if we start by injecting a new dose of political will. but the laeken summit will also be the moment, as the heads of state and government engage in a more general debate on the future of europe, to link the progress made, the progress to be made and the future of the union and its functioning. the next intergovernmental conference should be devoted to considering how institutional changes and reform of decision-making mechanisms could be introduced in the direction needed for the area of freedom, security and justice to be fully realised. the fourth question concerns harmonization in the criminal field. i would first like to remind you that the treaty specifically deals with the harmonization of substantive criminal law. the purpose of this harmonisation is not to allow mutual recognition; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is a complementary tool to the mutual recognition of judicial decisions. of course, as i have always said and i repeat today, harmonization must be used with discernment and only where it is necessary. the tampere european council listed the areas where such approximation is necessary. all these areas have been the subject of initiatives by member states or proposals by the commission. several of these have been adopted; the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to take them up in the near future. as regards procedural law, however, i have already had the opportunity to say that the commission is considering a communication on this subject, which has become even more necessary in the light of the very interesting political debate on the european arrest warrant. the purpose of such a communication would be to specify common standards for the protection of individual rights in criminal proceedings on a number of aspects as they result from the convention on human rights and the case law of the court of strasbourg. such an approach would help to strengthen the mutual trust on which the construction of the european judicial area is based, both within the union today and, later, in an enlarged europe of 25 or 30 member states. the fifth point refers to the democratic deficit which persists within the union in the fields of justice and home affairs. the question is twofold, since it concerns both the role of your institution in the decisionmaking process in the field of justice and home affairs and the proper exercise of its powers. it is very important that our desire to make progress towards our objectives be combined with improved democratic and judicial controls. i should first of all like to say that the commission has made every effort over the last two years to inform and involve the european parliament as closely as possible in the definition of its strategic guidelines and initiatives. the fact remains that the involvement of parliament, not only in defining the union's strategy but in implementing it, is a point that needs to be further developed and that the commission considers crucial in the progress still to be made. the intermingling of subjects falling under the first pillar and those considered to fall under the third pillar is a source of permanent difficulties. this situation also entails the risk of blocking the decision-making process, which, even if overcome by artificial separation between acts having the same objective, renders the union's action illegible to the citizens. i therefore welcome the council recommendation adopted by your assembly on 15 november on criminal sanctions and community law, which calls for at least the community-wide introduction of judicial cooperation in criminal matters. as regards parliament's access to sensitive information held by the commission, which is one of the practical conditions for the proper exercise of control by your institution, i must remind you that there is a framework agreement between our two institutions, dated 5 july, and that the commission will apply it to the fullest extent. finally, ms boumediene-thiery raised the question of strengthening the institutional capacities of the candidate countries. i believe that in the reports we have published and in the continuous evaluation we are making of the capacity building of the candidate countries, we have made our assessment of each of the candidate countries known and given it the publicity it deserves. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as regards the increased cooperation between the union and the united states in the fight against terrorism, i believe that this cooperation illustrates how the european dimension is today inseparable from any international action against transnational phenomena that is intended to be comprehensive and effective. of course, it's still fairly new. it raises problems, particularly in ensuring full respect for the principles of our european law and even international law. i see in the development of this european dimension a chance to put forward our values and principles, rather than sacrificing our principles on the altar of cooperation. in conclusion, madam president, mr president, ministers, ladies and gentlemen, in the face of the challenges and challenges of our time, the union's response must be thoughtful but rapid, transparent but effective, flexible but coordinated. it is in this spirit that i envisage the future of the vast area of freedom, security and justice and that i intend to continue the cooperation with the european parliament that has been established over the last two and a half years. i am personally very grateful for the commitment of all the members of the committee on civil liberties and in particular its chairman, mr graham watson, to whom i would like to express my particular thanks.
- mr president, i congratulate commissioner vitorino and the rapporteurs, mr boumediene, mr hazan, whose report was unanimously approved in committee, and mr watson, whose report on security at international summits is drafted with legal scruples and political balance: the report makes us reflect on the need to tackle politically the problems posed by globalisation in order to contribute to the political, social and economic progress of the international community and to overcome violence. too much violence has been committed in the demonstrations on globalisation, too much violence in some cases against the protesters, even against prisoners, as in the dramatic events in genoa where a young man was killed, shot in circumstances that are still unclear. fortunately, in my country there is an independent judiciary which is still able to render justice even posthumously. there has been too much violence, too many violations of the rules and principles governing the european union. we cannot allow alarming events to prevent us from respecting the fundamental rights which we solemnly affirm and which we demand that third countries, perhaps those which have just entered the democratic area, respect. we must remember that these rights were won in europe at the cost of the hardest of hardships. they cannot be valid only on holidays, for periods of serenity. they exist to protect us in times of grief and danger. we are therefore prepared to defend ourselves against terrorists, enemies of human rights, by all legitimate means, but we reject, even in the face of pressing authoritative demands, any temptation to use instruments which would take us away from the levels of civilization of which we are proud. the ends do not justify the means, when it is above all the means - mr president, one of the most lasting impressions of those who have been victims of the violence in nice, gothenburg and genoa is the impotence of the national authorities, who are increasingly closing borders indiscriminately and illegally, expelling citizens with clean criminal records - as recently happened to a swedish citizen, a member of a non-governmental organisation, who was expelled from belgium just these days, without any real reason - arresting and subjecting to unacceptable procedures, if not to torture and terrible violence, as happened in genoa, defenseless demonstrators. how can there be nothing to do? how is it possible that, with all the discussions that have been held on rights, respect for dissent and freedom of expression, with all the talk about a people's europe, that europe cannot act alongside national courts? the merit of the watson report is precisely that it points the way forward so that europe is no longer silent. the open declaration that schengen has been violated repeatedly and that this must not happen again; the dangers to individual freedom of secret blacklists, compiled in an illegitimate manner; the need to punish, including through international instruments, disproportionate use of force by law enforcement agencies; the prohibition of discrimination between european citizens: all this, contained in the watson report, represents the work plan of this parliament which, unlike other parliaments in the member states, is able to find a truly unified spirit on these issues. i hope that this is also the commission's programme, and i hope that this work plan will prevent the horrors we saw in nice, gothenburg and genoa, and that it will make a valuable contribution to all the measures being taken against terrorism.
- mr president, i would like to speak only about the draft agreement between the european union and the united states on extradition. on 7 december 2000, in nice, we signed, proclaimed and emphasized the charter of the rights of european citizens, in which article 2, under the chapter on dignity, states very clearly that no one may be sentenced to the death penalty, nor may he be executed, thereby making a clear distinction between the two and stating that for us european citizens the prohibition on execution is not enough, but that the prohibition on the death penalty must also be applied. we are engaged in cooperation with the united states, which maintains the death penalty, which condemns and applies the death penalty, which has a judicial system based on military courts, which holds a thousand arabs without charge or defence, and we are about to vote - we will of course vote against - a joint resolution with the other groups stating that extradition can be granted provided the united states guarantees not to apply the death penalty; this means that the courts of the united states can issue death sentences, provided they then refrain from enforcing them, and this is in defiance of the charter of civil, human and fundamental rights that we have been so emphasizing lately. we are opening a tremendous breach in our defense against the death penalty. friends of the people's party, friends of the greens, socialists, british liberals, please listen! we are saying that we can extradite our citizens who are sentenced to death in the united states, even if that country then undertakes not to execute the sentence. it's a total break with our tradition, it's a total break with our commitment! today we heard commissioner vitorino speak, and he made many references to our values and principles. well, what are our values and principles? commission. – mr president, the commission has passed its opinion on the amendments to the sittings directorate, and this is widely known by parliament. in addition to that, i wish to reply to the rapporteur's question. if this directive is adopted as now proposed, the commission will publish the relevant mhp multimedia home-platform standards in the list of standards published in the official journal of the european communities under article 16 of the framework directive. according to this directive, member states have to encourage the implementation of the standards contained in the list. one year after the date of application of these directives, the commission will examine whether interoperability and freedom of choice for users have been adequately achieved in the member states. if that is not the case, the commission can propose making implementation of relevant european standards mandatory. the directive requires the commission to carry out a public consultation on such a proposal. following the public consultation, the proposal would be submitted to a regulatory committee procedure requiring support from a qualified majority of member states before being adopted as a formal commission decision.

very sensitive to this complete review of the way the commission conducts its work seems to me to be a healthy attitude. it would be worrying if they were to show their sensitivity on such matters, which do not even excite us members, since we did not perceive the radical aspect of this revision, which is emphasized to us. however, we feel, as do the citizens of europe, that europe is increasingly alien to their concerns and seems ever more distant. perhaps the introduction of the euro, once the initial difficulties caused by the recognition of its value in relation to the old currencies have been overcome, will help to make europe a reality shared by many peoples, even if, probably, especially for the older generations, the feeling of having been deprived of their old currency, disappeared without anyone having asked their opinion, will remain. the feeling of a distant europe is real and increasingly widespread among citizens. in the crucial moments of collective life, it does not manifest itself as such, but as the opinion of this or that government. these are legitimate views, but they do not confirm membership of a common entity, membership which in the past has always been expressed symbolically by the commission. it was the commission that gave the go-ahead by statements and concrete proposals. today, however, because the commission does not emphasized, is contradictorily perceived by european citizens as a weakness rather than a strengthening of europe. if i do not share the enthusiasm about the 'ways of doing business' expressed in the communication, it is not because i consider that the arguments discussed and the commitments stated are not going in the right direction or because the legislative initiatives are quantitatively unsatisfactory. as we all know, quality is not a function of quantity. it should be stressed, however, that too much regulation gives a distorted image of europe and identifies it with that bureaucratic monster so feared by the productive classes and the citizens. - no , please ! the so-called work programme must be a political document and not an administrative list. it must identify the reasons for certain delays and the real obstacles that have prevented certain objectives from being achieved; it must identify certain priority objectives through which to advance the unification
